text: I sat down across from him. He moved his cup an inch toward himself, as though I might take it. ¶ “Mr. Abramowitz. You were at the Thalia tonight when Mr. Prentiss was telling the room where he keeps his key. Where did you go after?” ¶ He had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “At eight I took a letter round to a lodger at the Delmonico rooms. Mrs. Cheatham let me in. At nine I went to the Thalia, because a friend was in the show, and I stood with Miss Feeney. At ten I came here for coffee and a newspaper, on my own. At eleven I went back to the Thalia for the second show, on my own.” ¶ I checked it against what I had. Eight, nine and ten were fine, or at least nobody said otherwise. Eleven wasn’t. Coffin had Feeney, Ashby and Pardo at the Thalia at eleven, and nobody else. Coffin seats everybody. One of them was wrong, and it wasn’t the man with the torch. ¶ Abramowitz turned a page of the newspaper he wasn’t reading. That was twice tonight I’d seen it done.
The woman let out a breath she’d been keeping since I sat down.
The man heard me out and turned one hand palm up.
The thing had gone from here, and a room is worth a second look once you know more.
The man hadn’t told me his evening yet, and he was at the place.
The cold was at its worst, the kind that finds the hole in your glove you didn’t know you had.
I went over to where the woman could see the whole room, which was where she always was.
I found the man at the back and stood where I wouldn’t be in the way, which turned out to be nowhere.
I sat down where the woman could see me, and didn’t hurry.
I asked the man for everybody he’d seen tonight, in order, and nobody left out because he liked them.
“Take me through the evening,” I said. “Everybody, every hour. Even the ones who tip.”
He thought for a second, the way anybody does, and started at the beginning.
The man gave it to me in as few words as the evening would go into.
The man was in the room, and I hadn’t had his evening yet.
That pointed me at the man, and he was at the place.
I’d have to put that to the man, and see what he did with it.
Somebody went by with a plate of eggs, and my stomach reminded me it had been a long night.
I sat down at a table at the back of the place with the form and a glass of water I hadn’t asked for.
I thanked the man, and he nodded without taking his eyes off the room.
Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants.
A bartender who stands behind a bar all night knows who drank at it.
The man was in the change booth, stacking nickels into columns of exactly twenty.
Everybody who drank here tonight bought it from the man, and a bartender remembers a face longer than a name, and a tab longer than either.
Everybody who comes up to the surgery has to stop at the man’s desk, because there isn’t anywhere else to stop.
The woman keeps the members’ book, and nobody gets past the front room without her say-so.
The woman was behind the register, doing the crossword in pencil and the day’s takings in ink.
The woman was behind the counter with a magnifying glass, looking at something very small as if it owed her money.
The man sat at a little table by the wall, with a beer going flat in front of him.
The man was at the sink with his sleeves rolled up, and dried his hands slowly before he turned round.
“We haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill,” the man said. “My client and I. You can ask my client why. I’d like to hear the answer myself.”
The dead man was on the floor between the table and the door. Nobody had covered him yet, and nobody had closed his eyes.
The place was shut for the night, with the blinds down and the lamp lit in the waiting room. It smelled of clove oil and carbolic soap, the two smells of somebody being brave.
The dead man was face down just inside the door, with his back to the room, the way he must have been standing when it happened.
My client took me straight to the place where the thing had been and stood beside it like a museum guard with nothing left to guard.
The plaster mask grinned down at me the way it grins at everybody, as if we were all in on it.
A coffee urn stood by the wall, dented on one side and never off the boil.
The sloping ceiling knocked my hat crooked, to keep me humble.
The woman stood in her own hall like a visitor, with one hand on the banister.
The woman had been waiting to be asked. Most people have. They just don’t say so.
I asked the man about the dead man.
I wrote it down. It was the woman’s story of her night, and so far it was the only one I had.
I went over my client’s parlor from the door to the far wall, slowly.
So that was the woman’s reason. Most people in this city have one in a pocket somewhere.
I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it.

“So. A man can only keep a thing so long before the interest is worth more than the thing.”

Gus is good for it. Gus is slow for it, but he’s good.

It was a clear night over Orchard Street, the kind that shows you every washing line strung between the buildings, and the tenement over Lipsky’s had more than its share. A whole family’s shirts hung out over the street on a pulley, white as a surrender, waiting for a sun that wasn’t due till six.
the bottom layer of the cigarette tray
The back room, where the unredeemed coats hang in rows, and a tuba and a barber’s chair share a corner with the clerk’s cot.

One oil stove and the tempers of the players were heating the card room over the garage against the cold, and the stove was losing. One man had kept his overcoat on and was playing in his muffler, and winning, so nobody said anything about the muffler.
Windows painted black on the inside, so nobody can see in and nobody inside can tell the time.
Brass mailboxes with little windows, so the whole building can see who gets letters and who gets bills.

From there to the Schilling flat was a good walk. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ The Schilling flat on the third floor of 40 Avenue B was neat as a pin and twice as sharp about it. There were lace mats on every chair back and photographs on every wall, looking down at me as if I’d come in with my boots on. A china shepherdess stood on a doily, looking at the room with painted patience. ¶ Schilling had left everything just as it was, so that Duchess would know the way home. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ If she went at ten, whoever took her had a key, and the spare key lives on the nail in the hall at the Delmonico rooms. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, downtown and west to the Delmonico rooms, a couple of blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. A holy picture hung in the hall, with a little lamp in a red glass under it. ¶ Mrs. Callahan was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Bernstein was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ The spare key lived on the nail in the hall here. That settled where I was going. ¶ A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them. ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

The chop house was a couple of blocks uptown, and I took it at a good clip. The street was empty and clear and very quiet, and my heels were the loudest thing on it. ¶ The Grand Street chop house had served steaks to three generations of men whose doctors had told them to stop. The doctors were right, and so were the steaks. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Mulcahy stood by the reservation book at the door with a pencil, crossing out tables nobody would want now. Margolis sat with her coat on and her plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. She smelled of gasoline and cold coffee and kept her gloves on indoors, the fingertips cut out of them. Alfano had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. ¶ Nobody sits down in a restaurant without the head waiter deciding where, and Mulcahy had been doing the deciding. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Alfano had said she was here at nine. The head waiter sees everybody and says nothing, unless somebody asks. I was going to ask. I asked Mulcahy for a minute, and she gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. ¶ I asked her to give me the night the way only the head waiter could: every face, every hour. She counted it off on her fingers, and ran out of fingers before she ran out of night. ¶ “Lou the bookmaker was in his back booth all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Margolis and Shapiro. Nobody else. Nine, Alfano and Shapiro. Nobody else at all. Ten, Margolis and Shapiro. Nobody else, that hour. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Lou, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “What was it?” I said. “Under the coat.” ¶ “Something alive. It moved about.” ¶ Mulcahy had Alfano here at nine, same as she said. That put Margolis here at ten, by her count. Whatever went out of the Schilling flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Lou. ¶ I could have used a glass from the samovar. I could have used a lot of things.

Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. My ribs hurt when I breathed deep, so I breathed shallow. Rain ran down the window in the lamplight, and I sat and listened to it and did not move much. ¶ Somebody came up the stairs. Nobody comes up those stairs after midnight with good news; the good news waits for morning, like a gentleman. My visitor wiped his boots on the mat from habit, not respect. Nobody respects my floor. ¶ “It’s Mimi,” Hargrove said. “My Persian. She’s gone from the window seat.” ¶ I offered him the chair. He sat on the front half of it, which is the half I keep for clients. ¶ “I sat in the Velvet Room from eight until ten,” he said, “telling anybody who’d listen that I was off to my sister’s for the night, and the key was under the mat.” ¶ “And when did Mimi go missing?” ¶ “I can tell you when, near enough,” he said. “Whoever it was knocked the parlor clock off the shelf, and it stopped at ten past ten.” ¶ “Anybody you can think of who’d want Mimi?” ¶ “I keep thinking about Havemeyer,” Hargrove said. “She stood at my elbow at the Velvet Room the whole time, and I didn’t think anything of it at the time. And she is three weeks behind on the rent, and has been heard to say what a Persian with papers fetches.” ¶ He hesitated, then went on. “Doyle, a switchboard operator, lost her job on Friday, and asked me what Mimi was worth. And Pickering, a sewing-machine operator, owes Lou the bookmaker forty dollars, and Lou takes things in kind.” ¶ He put ten dollars on the desk and smoothed it flat with his palm. “Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

I went over Hargrove’s parlor from the door to the far wall, slowly. ¶ Hargrove sat on the arm of a chair and watched me go over his own parlor like a stranger’s. ¶ The window seat was empty but for white hairs. The key was back under the mat, and there wasn’t a mark on the door. Whoever it was had known exactly where to look. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Hargrove at the Velvet Room between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made the Velvet Room the place to start counting. ¶ The one to ask was the bartender at the Velvet Room, who’d been there all night. ¶ The sampler went on blessing the house in red cross-stitch, whatever the house was up to.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Quill. ¶ I waited for a gap in his night, and when one came I stepped into it. I asked him to count the night for me, face by face. ¶ He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Lou the bookmaker was in his back booth all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Havemeyer, Pickering and Mr. Hargrove telling the room about his key. Nobody else. Nine, Havemeyer and Mr. Hargrove, still telling it. Nobody else at all. Ten, just Lou. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Lou, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “Under the coat,” I said. “What was it?” ¶ “Something that moved.” ¶ Havemeyer and Pickering heard about the key at eight. Doyle never heard Hargrove tell the room. Whatever went out of the Hargrove flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Lou. I wrote down what Quill had at ten, the hour that mattered: Lou. ¶ Somebody came in behind me. The eyes went to the door and came back, and I was glad to see I’d been promoted to furniture.

Kowalski’s lay a couple of blocks east. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ I went to Mrs. Kowalski’s boarding house on Orchard Street. It was a narrow brick house with a scrubbed stoop and a smell of beet soup that had got into the walls and settled. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Havemeyer answered the door in her stocking feet, with the lamp behind her. Colquitt was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. ¶ Pickering had said she was here at nine, and that Havemeyer was with her at the Velvet Room at eight. That was reason enough. ¶ Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Kowalski had the look of a landlady who made a point of it. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

I took the form out and smoothed it flat on my knee. It was my name at the bottom, so it had better be my reasons above it. ¶ My ribs had let me breathe through all of it, if shallow. I thanked them and didn’t push my luck.

It was a long walk from there to the Coffin flat, uptown and east, with my collar up. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ The Coffin parlor floor on Stuyvesant Street was two tall rooms with folding doors between them, a thick carpet and a smell of beeswax. A framed sampler on the wall said Bless This House in red cross-stitch. ¶ Coffin showed me in and stood by the place where Duchess belonged, holding Duchess’s dish as if it might be wanted any minute. ¶ Nobody minded who came and went. ¶ If she went at ten, she went after the supper, and everybody at the supper had known the way in. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

Mrs. Nagy’s was a couple of blocks downtown and east, and I took it at a good clip. A lit window hung in the fog above me with nothing holding it up. ¶ Mrs. Nagy’s, on East Fourth Street, was quiet at this hour. The hall smelled of paprika and floor wax, and a lamp had been left on at the turn of the stair. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Nagy sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Sirkin was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. ¶ A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them. ¶ I took it all in, which didn’t take long, and then took it in again.

I headed downtown and west for the print shop, a long walk away. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ I went in at the print shop on Centre Street, which runs a night shift. The presses were running with a noise like a train going over a long bridge, and everything in the room smelled of ink and hot oil. A wooden chair with one short leg stood by the wall, and rocked whenever anything touched it. ¶ Callahan was at a desk on a raised step at the end of the room, where she could see everybody and everybody could see her seeing them. ¶ Whoever runs the floor at night keeps the book of who came on and who went off. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

The Orpheum lay a few blocks east. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ I went in at the Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight. The last show had let out, the screen was a big gray blank, and the rows were full of peanut shells and dropped programs. Above the lobby doors a painted plaster mask grinned down at everybody who came in, with the tip of its nose missing. ¶ Mulcahy stood at the back of the house with a flashlight, pointed at the floor, ready. She had a roll of tickets on a spindle and a coin changer on her belt, and a callus on one thumb from tearing stubs, the only part of the job that showed. Cheatham was sitting near the front, very upright, with both hands on the back of the seat in front. Weisglass stood at the back with her hat in her hand, as if she had just come in or was just going. Petrosino sat in the back row with her hat on her knee, watching the picture without looking at it. ¶ Cheatham had been at Coffin’s at eight, for the supper. Sirkin had said Petrosino was with her at her place at nine. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Mulcahy. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

I asked Mulcahy for a minute, and she gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. I asked her to count the night for me, face by face. ¶ She answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Pardo was there all evening, every hour of it. He buys things. Eight o’clock, Weisglass. Nobody else. Nine, Cheatham and Weisglass. Nobody else at all. Ten, Weisglass and Petrosino. Nobody else, that hour. Eleven, Cheatham, Weisglass and Petrosino. Nobody else.” ¶ Cheatham said the Orpheum at ten. Mulcahy had Weisglass, Petrosino and Pardo here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. Two stories about her at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. ¶ The thumb with the callus was twitching for a stub. I didn’t have one. I rarely have a ticket for anything.

I sat down with the form and a pencil. I read the night back to myself, from the office to here, and started at the top of the form. ¶ The office stairs had done their bit for the night. They’d brought me the case.

Rosenbaum’s place was only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. The cold had come down with the dark and meant to stay, and people were walking fast with their collars up and their opinions to themselves. ¶ I went up to Rosenbaum’s two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street. Two rooms, a front and a back, with the police gone and the clock on the shelf still ticking, as if nobody had told it. A radiator under the window knocked every so often, as if it wanted to be let in on something. ¶ Rosenbaum was where they’d found him, in the chair by the table, as if he’d sat down to wait for something and it had come. ¶ Colquitt, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I stood in the doorway a while before I went in. Rooms like that don’t like to be rushed.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I wanted to read them properly. I went through his papers with the lamp pulled close, the way you read a will you aren’t in. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge against him, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and he’d written every one down. ¶ Ellery: the lease on a shop, the rent owing, and a carbon of his letter calling it in. Whitfield: a court transcript, his own testimony against his brother. Salerno: the order that closed his business, with his signature on it. Bledsoe: one line, where he was in 1921, and an address. ¶ Everybody in Rosenbaum’s box had a reason. Fewer of them had been at Mrs. Nagy’s to get the chloral. ¶ The one to ask was the bartender at Hanley’s, who’d been there all night. ¶ The radiator knocked again. I didn’t answer it.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mosley. I put a coin on the bar so she would have a reason to come over. She came over and left the coin where it was. ¶ I asked Mosley for everybody she’d seen tonight, in order, and nobody left out because she liked them. She didn’t look at the room to answer. She didn’t need to. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Salerno and Ellery. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Whitfield, Ellery and Rosenbaum. Nobody else at all. Ten, Bledsoe and Ellery. Nobody else, that hour.” ¶ Ellery hadn’t been at Mrs. Nagy’s while it was there to take. That put Bledsoe and Ellery here at ten, by her count. Colquitt had said nine or ten. Rosenbaum was at Hanley’s at nine, alive. ¶ Whitfield was right here, and his evening was still a blank in my notebook. ¶ Somebody came in behind me. The eyes went to the door and came back, and I was glad to see I’d been promoted to furniture.

From there to Mrs. Nagy’s was a few blocks. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ Mrs. Nagy’s, on East Fourth Street, was quiet at this hour. The hall smelled of paprika and floor wax, and a lamp had been left on at the turn of the stair. A holy picture hung in the hall, with a little lamp in a red glass under it. ¶ Mrs. Nagy sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. ¶ Whitfield had said he was here at seven. That was reason enough for the walk. Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Nagy had the look of a landlady who made a point of it. ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

I set off downtown and west for Sokol’s back room. It was a couple of blocks. My knees had the temperature a block before any thermometer did. They’ve had more practice. ¶ I went round to the back of Sokol’s bakery on Rivington Street, where the numbers are taken. It was warm from the ovens, with sacks of flour along one wall and a table by the other where a nickel bet on a three-figure number bought you a reason to get up tomorrow. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Salerno was on a hard chair by the wall, turning his hat round and round in his hands. ¶ Mrs. Nagy’s list had Salerno at Mrs. Nagy’s at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ No one was posted to see who came and went. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Salerno had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Nagy’s list said otherwise. It was time to say so to his face. I turned back to him with my notebook open, which is never good news for anybody. ¶ “One thing,” I said to him. “You said home at ten. Mrs. Nagy had nobody at Mrs. Nagy’s at ten o’clock.” ¶ He let out a breath he’d been keeping since I sat down. “All right. I wasn’t at Mrs. Nagy’s. I was at Sokol’s, in the back, putting a nickel on a number. I swore I’d stopped. Ashby was there. Ask him.” ¶ That was a hole in Salerno’s story, all right. I wasn’t sure yet it was the one I was looking for. An owned-up story is only as good as whoever’s in it with you. If it held, he had been at Sokol’s back room at ten, not home. ¶ It turned out Ashby was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ The tin sign on the wall had outlasted the company and would outlast me.

I found a chair at Sokol’s back room and sat down with the form. Whatever I wrote down, I’d have to be able to say whose word it stood on. ¶ My cigarette had burned down to my fingers again. A man with a bank account would have noticed sooner.

A couple of blocks east, and I was at Obermann’s place. The sky was clear and the city was still up under it, with a lit window on every other floor and a radio arguing in one of them. ¶ I went up to Obermann’s two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street. The bakery downstairs had its ovens going, and the warm smell of bread came up through the floorboards, which didn’t seem right, and wasn’t anybody’s fault. A coal merchant’s calendar hung by the stove, still turned to last month. ¶ Obermann was in the chair with his head back and his mouth a little open, the way a man sleeps when he’s too tired to care how he looks. ¶ Rosenbaum was there ahead of me, hat in her hands, turning the brim. ¶ It was the kind of place nobody kept an eye on. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I looked the place over the way you read a bill: twice, and slowly.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, so I went through them. I went through his papers with the lamp pulled close, the way you read a will you aren’t in. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge against him, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and he’d written every one down. ¶ Vitale: a court transcript, his own testimony against her brother. Bellucci: a file he’d kept on her, thick enough to matter. Ellery: a column of payments, every month for years, and her name at the top. Doyle: an IOU for four hundred dollars, in his hand. ¶ A reason is the easy half. The other half was a way to the chloral, and that was at Mrs. Nagy’s. ¶ Rosenbaum had pointed me at Doyle, and that was worth the walk to the Kit Kat. ¶ The calendar by the stove was still on last month. Nobody was going to turn it now.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Doyle. I sat down one stool away from him, which gave him room to decide about me. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, he wore clothes too good to have been bought. He’d made every stitch. ¶ I asked him for his evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. He thought about it the way you’d think about a step in the dark, and then took it. ¶ “At seven I went round to Mrs. Nagy’s to borrow a collar stud. Around eight I went to the Kit Kat to dance, with Ellery and Obermann. At nine I went to the Eagle club office to write letters. Ten o’clock I went down to the Kit Kat to hear the trumpet. I had nobody with me at seven, nine or ten.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Doyle said the Eagle club office at nine and the Kit Kat at ten. That was his word for it, and I took it down as said. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it.

Lefkowitz’s list had Ellery here at seven, eight and ten, and I wanted the rest of that evening. I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. ¶ I asked her where she’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ Ellery took a moment to put the evening in order before she handed it over. ¶ “I was at the Kit Kat from seven through eight. Vitale was there at seven; Doyle and Obermann were there at eight. Come nine, I went up to Mrs. Nagy’s to see about some money owed, with Vitale and Bellucci. Around ten I had a table at the Kit Kat, with Vitale. Walking over to the Kit Kat at ten I passed Bellucci on Hester Street, going fast, no hat.” ¶ So here at ten and seven, with Vitale, which was what Lefkowitz had. One evening that held, at an hour that mattered, where I could check it. The part worth keeping came last. Hester Street was where Obermann lived. ¶ The paper lanterns swayed a little as the door went, pink and tired, like the rest of us.

It was no distance to the Eagle club office: round the corner, and there it was. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ The back office of the Eagle Social Club was where the club did the business it didn’t do in the front room. There were a lot of chairs for an office, and not much paper. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Callahan was at the steward’s desk, sorting the club’s letters into pigeonholes. ¶ A club steward knows every member by the back of the head, and every visitor by the fact that she doesn’t. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

I headed downtown and east for Bellucci’s flat, a good walk away. A baker’s boy went by with a tray of rolls on his head and the look of somebody who’d been up longer than me. ¶ I went round to Bellucci’s flat on Cannon Street. It was a walk-up like every walk-up on Cannon Street: a hall that smelled of other people’s suppers and a stair with a bend in it. A kettle sat on a gas ring on the shelf, gone cold. ¶ Bellucci was at the sink with her sleeves rolled up, and dried her hands slowly before she turned round. ¶ No one was posted to see who came and went. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

Midnight. The office on Mulberry Street had one lamp, one chair worth sitting in and one detective, and the detective was in the worst repair of the three. More money in the drawer than bills on the desk. The telephone company and the landlady were paid, and some was left over. I didn’t know what people did with that. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. My visitor didn’t sit until I told her to. She needed help, she said. That was the speech. ¶ She didn’t wait to be asked. “Hattie Hargrove. Abraham Shapiro’s sister. He’s dead, and nobody is doing anything about it.” ¶ Shapiro had been a buildings inspector. He was found in his own flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street at half past eleven. The one who found him was Hanrahan, who heard his radio still going and knocked. The police wrote it down as his heart. ¶ I pointed my client at the chair. She took it, and held her hat on her knees. ¶ “When did it happen, as near as anybody can say?” ¶ “The police can call it what they like,” she said. “The woman across the landing heard him laugh with somebody and then go quiet at nine or ten o’clock; she’d dozed off over the radio and can’t say which.” ¶ “He’d been at the Thalia earlier in the evening,” she said. “His usual.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad he’s gone?” ¶ “Talk to Lindemann,” Hargrove said, without having to think about it. “He closed his business.” ¶ She opened her bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.

I went over Shapiro’s table slowly, touching nothing I didn’t have to. ¶ I worked slowly. Hargrove waited in the hall, and the stairs creaked every time she shifted her weight. ¶ There were two glasses on the table. One smelled of rye and nothing else. The other smelled of rye and something sweet and chemical, like a hospital left out in the sun. Under the table, where it had rolled, was an empty brown bottle with a paper label from the Delmonico rooms. The lodgers there keep it on the hall shelf. He had been drinking with somebody he knew. ¶ So the chloral came from the Delmonico rooms, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Shapiro had been at the Delmonico rooms earlier, to get it. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

It was a fair few blocks to the Delmonico rooms, downtown. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Quill sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Ruggiero, in a camel coat, was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. Hanrahan, in a green hat, was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ The chloral had come from here. Hanrahan had found Shapiro. That was reason enough. A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them. ¶ The stairs had opinions about my weight and shared them all the way up.

Broadnax’s flat lay a few blocks uptown and east. Pitt Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ Broadnax’s flat on Pitt Street was two rooms and a kitchen at the top of the stairs, behind a doormat that had given up saying welcome years ago. A gramophone with a big tin horn stood in the corner, with a record still on it. ¶ Broadnax, in a fur collar, was at the sink with her sleeves rolled up, and dried her hands slowly before she turned round. She had fingertips gone flat from typing all day, and was dressed for an office in a good plain way that no office would ever notice. ¶ Mrs. Quill’s list had Broadnax at the Delmonico rooms at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

The Thalia was a good walk uptown and west. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ I went in at the Thalia, a Yiddish theater on the Bowery. The play was over, but the stage still had its painted village up, a little wooden town waiting under one work light for the next performance. The lobby carpet was red and gold swirls, worn down to the threads in a path from the door to the seats. ¶ Lanza stood at the back of the house with a flashlight, pointed at the floor, ready. Lindemann, in a grey fedora, was in the lobby, reading the bills for next week as if they might change. He smelled of gasoline and cold coffee and kept his gloves on indoors, the fingertips cut out of them. ¶ Broadnax had said she was here at nine, and that Lindemann was with her at her place at ten. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Lanza. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Broadnax had said Lindemann was with her at her place at ten, so I went over. I sat one seat over. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” ¶ He answered straight off, the way people do with an evening they’ve only just finished. ¶ “At seven I went to the Delmonico rooms for the company, and stayed through nine. Ruggiero was there at seven; Tramonti, Broadnax and Ruggiero were there at eight; Tramonti and Ruggiero were there at nine. Come ten, I went round to Broadnax’s for a game of gin.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Lindemann said Broadnax’s flat. That was his word for it, and I took it down as said. ¶ I could have used gloves like that. Mine have all ten fingertips, and they still let the cold in. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. Hargrove had said nine or ten o’clock. The chloral had come from the Delmonico rooms. I had evenings from Broadnax and Lindemann, and lists from Mrs. Quill and Lanza. I didn’t have Tramonti’s, Ruggiero’s or Hanrahan’s evenings yet. ¶ Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t, and I didn’t know yet which was which.

I found Tramonti at the far end, where the light gave up, and stood where he could see me without having to want to. ¶ I asked him where he’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. He went slowly, the way people do who like to get things right. ¶ “I was at the Thalia at seven, with Hanrahan. Come eight, I went to the Delmonico rooms to help write letters home, and stayed through nine. Lindemann, Broadnax and Ruggiero were there at eight; Lindemann and Ruggiero were there at nine. Around ten I went round to Sokol’s for coffee with Sokol, with Zeldin.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Tramonti said Sokol’s back room. It went in the notebook in his own words. ¶ It turned out Zeldin was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ My hat had left a mark in my hair too. Nobody was paying me by the hour for mine.

I took the form out and smoothed it flat on my knee. Whatever I wrote down, I’d have to be able to say whose word it stood on. ¶ There’d be more money in the drawer now. I still didn’t know what people did with it. I was prepared to find out.

From there to the Greco flat was a few blocks. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There were marble stairs to the second floor and plain wood after that, where the builder ran out of marble or interest. ¶ Mrs. Greco had left everything just as it was, so that Fritz would know the way home. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ If he went at ten, the flat had been empty, and anybody who’d heard Mrs. Greco at Steinmetz’s had known the way in. That was a room, more or less. It was a big room. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, west to Steinmetz’s, a couple of blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ Closing a chop house of the old kind takes an hour, and Steinmetz’s was in the middle of it: the chairs going up table by table, slowly, so as not to hurry anybody who might still order pie. The head waiter stood at his stand by the door, writing the last covers in his book in ink. The sawdust had been swept into the corners to think over what it had heard. There was a rack of bone-handled steak knives by the kitchen door, counted out at noon and counted back at closing, more or less. ¶ Demos was holding a fork up to the light. He had hair parted dead center and flattened with something that smells of violets. Russo sat at a table near the kitchen door with a newspaper folded to the crossword and a cup of coffee going cold. Teitel sat at a table by the mirror with a glass of tea, drinking it the old way, through a lump of sugar held in his teeth. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “I seat every table myself, and I write the covers in the book with the time beside them. Nobody sits in my room without my say-so.” ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

Teitel had moved to a table by the wall, where nobody could come up behind him. ¶ There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. He had a necktie of his own so loud it seems to be shouting for the others. ¶ “Demos has you here at nine. I’d like the rest of your evening to go with it.” ¶ He put down what he was holding and gave me his attention. ¶ “For you, a special price: the whole evening, free. Nobody gets that from Teitel. Listen. I was at the Lyric at eight, with Miss Moskin. Around nine I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee and pie, and stayed the rest of the evening. Nine, business. I think about it; it doesn’t think about me. Russo, Mrs. Sobel and Mrs. Krantz were there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ Teitel said Steinmetz’s at ten. The head waiter had Russo, Mrs. Krantz and Benny here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. They couldn’t both be true, and Demos had no reason to be the wrong one. ¶ There was the slate by the door with the specials chalked on it, where the soup is crossed off at whatever hour you come in. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. He went at ten o’clock. Russo was at Steinmetz’s at ten; Demos said so. Teitel had told me Steinmetz’s at ten, and Demos’s list said otherwise. Mrs. Sobel hadn’t told me where she was at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Benny at Steinmetz’s at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Teitel now. Or I could find out first from the usher at the Lyric who’d been in. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

Pinsky was pointing his flashlight at a man who was talking. ¶ I asked him to give me the night the way only the usher could: every face, every hour. He looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶ “Eight, the curtain goes up, and I go to the back of the house, where an usher belongs and an actor once didn’t. Eight o’clock, Teitel and Miss Moskin. Nobody else. Nine, Miss Moskin. Nobody else at all. Ten, Mrs. Sobel and Miss Moskin. And nobody else. Every cross on the chart has a face, and I’ve given you every face.” ¶ Pinsky had Teitel here at eight, same as he said. That put Mrs. Sobel here at ten, by his count. ¶ Marking crosses on his seating chart: that was the last I saw of him.

Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. My ribs hurt when I breathed deep, so I breathed shallow. Rain ran down the window in the lamplight, and I sat and listened to it and did not move much. ¶ Somebody came up the stairs. Nobody comes up those stairs after midnight with good news; the good news waits for morning, like a gentleman. My visitor wiped his boots on the mat from habit, not respect. Nobody respects my floor. ¶ “It’s Duchess,” Belkin said. “My Pomeranian. She’s gone from her cushion by the radiator.” ¶ I offered him the chair. He sat on the front half of it, which is the half I keep for clients. ¶ “I had people in at eight for a birthday supper,” he said. “Miss Moskin and Mrs. Krantz. Nobody else.” ¶ “I went out after them,” he said, “and I left the key under the mat for my sister. I told the table I would.” ¶ “And when did Duchess go missing?” ¶ “And I know when,” he said. “The woman upstairs heard feet on the stairs in the middle of the Cliquot Club Eskimos, which runs from ten o’clock.” ¶ “Who’d want her badly enough to take her?” ¶ “If you want a name, it’s Mrs. Krantz,” he said. “She says my IOU to her is overdue, and that Duchess would square it.” ¶ There was more, and he didn’t much want to say it. “Miss Moskin, the ingénue, works in my business, and hasn’t been paid since the first of the month. And Lieb, the pawnbroker’s clerk, hasn’t forgotten what my family did to Wexler, his boss.” ¶ Belkin counted out ten dollars in ones and change, and the change was the part that got to me. “Who, and where. That’s all I’m asking.” ¶ I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.

I went over Belkin’s parlor from the door to the far wall, slowly. ¶ Belkin sat on the arm of a chair and watched me go over his own parlor like a stranger’s. ¶ The cushion by the radiator was empty. The key was back under the mat, and the door hadn’t a mark on it. Whoever it was had let themselves in and put the key back after, which is manners of a kind. ¶ So whoever it was knew the way in, and the people who knew were the ones at the supper in the Belkin flat at eight. Belkin had given me their names. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Miss Moskin. The barman counts the glasses onto a towel at closing, and when one is short he knows whose it was. Miss Moskin had a copy of Variety rolled in her coat pocket, folded open at the uptown casting news. ¶ “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” She told it the way you give somebody directions, landmark by landmark. ¶ “Oh, my evening. Let me do it properly. You have to set the scene, or it doesn’t play. I was at Belkin’s at eight, for the supper, with Mrs. Krantz. At nine I left the supper when the gin ran out and couldn’t settle, so I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee, with Dr. Hirsch. Ten o’clock I stopped in at Sokol’s to get warm, alone. Ten’s when I think about uptown. Everybody on Second Avenue thinks about uptown at ten.” ¶ So the Belkin flat at eight, with Mrs. Krantz, which was what Belkin had said. That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for. For ten, the hour that mattered, she said Sokol’s. I put it with the rest and didn’t argue with it yet. ¶ Flour gets on everybody who goes through to the bar, and the whole block could find Sokol’s by the white footprints, the police included.

Steinmetz’s lay a couple of blocks downtown and east. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ The front of Steinmetz’s was dark, but the kitchen door at the back stood propped open on the alley, letting out steam and the sound of a pot being scrubbed by somebody with opinions about it. The chop house window still said CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS in gold, with the R gone from OYSTERS. There was one curtained booth at the back, for parties who don’t want to be a party. ¶ Demos was holding a fork up to the light. He had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty; he says he feels undressed without it. Mrs. Krantz sat with her coat on and her plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. Dr. Hirsch had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. ¶ Miss Moskin had said she was here at nine. Sokol’s list had Mrs. Krantz at Sokol’s at nine. That was reason enough. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “I seat every table myself, and I write the covers in the book with the time beside them. Nobody sits in my room without my say-so.” ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Midnight. The office on Mulberry Street was dark except for the desk lamp, and the street under the window had gone quiet. I gave up on bed around eleven and made my peace with the desk chair, which had never once let me sleep. The stairs outside creaked twice, some tenant getting home. ¶ I heard steps on the stairs, stopping on every landing to think it over. My visitor wiped his boots on the mat from habit, not respect. Nobody respects my floor. ¶ “It’s Mimi,” Belkin said. “My Persian. She’s gone from the window seat.” ¶ I offered him the chair, and dusted it first, which I don’t do for everybody. ¶ “I had people in at eight,” he said, “for the burial society’s meeting. Miss Moskin, Lieb and Mrs. Krantz. Nobody else came.” ¶ “I went out after them,” he said, “and I left the key under the mat for my sister. I told the table I would.” ¶ “When did this happen, as near as you can say?” ¶ He had it worked out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “Whoever it was knocked the parlor clock off the shelf, and it stopped at ten past eleven.” ¶ “Who’d want to take her?” ¶ “If you want a name, it’s Mrs. Krantz,” he said. “She says my IOU to her is overdue, and that Mimi would square it.” ¶ There was more, and he didn’t much want to say it. “Lieb, the pawnbroker’s clerk, hasn’t forgotten what my family did to Wexler, his boss. And Dr. Hirsch, the dentist, owes Russo money, and he isn’t a patient man.” ¶ He wasn’t finished. People who have been up all night with a list never are. “Miss Moskin, the ingénue, works in my business, and hasn’t been paid since the first of the month.” ¶ Belkin counted out ten dollars in ones and change, and the change was the part that got to me. “Who, and where. That’s all I’m asking.” ¶ I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.

I asked Belkin to wait in the hall, and went over the parlor by myself. ¶ He told me twice where everything usually was. I let him. It was his flat, and it was the only thing he could do. ¶ The window seat was empty but for white hairs. The key was back under the mat, and the door hadn’t a mark on it. Whoever it was had let themselves in and put the key back after, which is manners of a kind. ¶ So whoever it was knew the way in, and the people who knew were the ones at the meeting in the Belkin flat at eight. Belkin had given me their names. ¶ That was all the room had to tell me, and it had told it without being asked twice.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Lieb. I sat down where Lieb could see me, and didn’t hurry. ¶ “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” He thought for a second, the way anybody does, and started at the beginning. ¶ “Sure, I’ll tell you. I tell everybody everything. That’s my trouble, my uncle says. I was at Belkin’s at eight, for the meeting, with Miss Moskin and Mrs. Krantz. Then at nine I left the meeting when the cards went badly and went to Steinmetz’s for supper, and stayed the rest of the evening. Dr. Hirsch was there at nine and ten; at eleven it was just me. Eleven’s my hour. A fellow’s got to have one.” ¶ So the Belkin flat at eight, with Miss Moskin and Mrs. Krantz, which was what Belkin had said. So far as it went, it stood up. For ten, the hour that mattered, he said Steinmetz’s. That was his word for it, and I took it down as said. ¶ That was one more evening on paper. They pile up.

There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. Miss Moskin had a copy of Variety rolled in her coat pocket, folded open at the uptown casting news. ¶ I asked Miss Moskin where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. She told it the way you give somebody directions, landmark by landmark. ¶ “Sure, ask me anything. I’m rehearsing for being famous, so I might as well practice my interviews. I was at Belkin’s at eight, for the meeting, with Lieb and Mrs. Krantz. Then at nine I left the meeting to get some air and went home to listen to the radio, and stayed the rest of the evening. Mrs. Krantz was there at nine and ten; at eleven it was just me. Eleven, I’m tired, and I won’t admit it, because tired is for the chorus.” ¶ So the Belkin flat at eight, with Lieb and Mrs. Krantz, which was what Belkin had said. That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for. For eleven, the hour that mattered, she said home at the flats over Lipsky’s. Whether anything else I held touched it, I’d have to see. ¶ Demos would have seen everybody who came in. ¶ There was the slate by the door with the specials chalked on it, where the soup is crossed off at whatever hour you come in.

The flats over Lipsky’s were round the corner. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s were waking from the top down, a light on the fifth floor, then the fourth. In the street the first pushcart man was already untying his tarpaulin. In the cloth shop’s window a dressmaker’s dummy wore a hat it had been wearing since spring, and wore it well. There was a row of tin mailboxes in the hall, with the names in five different hands and two crossed out. ¶ Wojcik was sitting on the cellar steps with his pipe. He had a ring of keys on a bootlace round his neck, worn under his undershirt where nobody can borrow them. ¶ Miss Moskin had said she was here at nine, ten and eleven. That was reason enough. From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe from supper till bed, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

Getting to the undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock meant a couple of blocks west. The fog had swallowed the far end of the street and was in no hurry to give it back. ¶ The undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Lieb was sitting where he could see the door, with his hat on and his coat buttoned. ¶ There was one light, and everybody had arranged to be just outside it.

Lieb had named Doyle: the undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock at eleven, the two of them. Whether that held was the next question. I sat down near him, in a corner nobody else was using. He had a right hand already out and reaching for yours from across the room. ¶ I asked him to tell me his evening, and who he’d seen. ¶ Doyle put down what he was holding and gave me his attention. ¶ “Where was I? Serving the public, my friend, as always. Let me tell you how. I was home from eight through ten, on my own. Ten, I start remembering who I promised what. It’s a long list. I keep it short by forgetting. Eleven o’clock I went to the undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock to meet Lieb.” ¶ That put Lieb here at eleven, and he would swear to it. ¶ I wrote it all down. My handwriting at that hour looks like a spider fell in the ink, but I can read it, mostly.

Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants. Money sat in the office for once instead of a promise of it. I lit a cigarette slowly, like a man with a bank account. The cold stayed outside the glass where it belonged. ¶ Feet on the stairs, four flights of them, taken slowly. Nobody climbs four flights at midnight for the view. My visitor didn’t sit until I told her to. She needed help, she said. That was the speech. ¶ “Bertha Krantz,” she said, and put her hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Francis Doyle’s old sweetheart. He’s dead, and I don’t like how.” ¶ Doyle was the alderman’s clerk. At half past eleven, Teitel, who’d come to settle a bet, found him in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street. The police had a look and called it his heart. ¶ I offered Mrs. Krantz the chair and turned the lamp away from her. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ “Here’s what they don’t want to hear,” she said. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “He ate at Steinmetz’s most nights,” she said. “He was there earlier tonight. His usual.” ¶ “Who had a reason?” ¶ “Ask about Mabry,” she said. “He was squeezing Mabry’s friend for money. I had that from the woman downstairs.” ¶ Mrs. Krantz put fifty dollars on the desk in tens, squared the edges and pushed them across. “I want a name. The right one.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

I went over the table. ¶ Mrs. Krantz didn’t come in. I didn’t ask her to. ¶ There were two glasses on the table. One smelled of rye and nothing else. The other smelled of rye and something sweet and chemical, like a hospital left out in the sun. Under the table, where it had rolled, was an empty brown bottle with a paper label from Rafferty’s. The lodgers there keep it on the hall shelf. Doyle had been drinking with somebody he knew. ¶ So the chloral came from Rafferty’s, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Doyle had been at Rafferty’s earlier, to get it. ¶ I hadn’t been through the papers at Doyle’s place yet, and a dead man’s papers can be talkative. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

A fair few blocks uptown and west, and I was at Rafferty’s. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ Rafferty’s had gone to sleep the way rooming houses do: one radiator knocking, one lodger coughing, and a kettle somewhere at the back that never quite goes off the boil. The stair carpet was worn pale down the middle, a path laid by everybody who ever came home later than they said. There was a row of umbrella hooks in the hall, each with a lodger’s name inked over it, and one with no name that nobody will explain. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was counting the umbrellas on their hooks. She had a ring of keys at her belt the size of a saucer, and she knows each key by the sound it makes. Miss Nowak was writing a letter home to Scranton. ¶ From her post Mrs. Rafferty could see the front door, the stairs and every landing to the top. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Mrs. Rafferty’s list had Miss Nowak here at eight. I wanted to hear the other side of it. ¶ She was counting out change for a horse she likes. She was a girl in a kimono halfway up the second flight with her shoes in her hand, stopped as if somebody had called her name. “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” ¶ She took a moment to put the evening in order before she handed it over. ¶ “I don’t mind telling you. I’m very good at times; it’s my whole job. I was at Steinmetz’s at seven, with Amato. Seven, I still hear the switchboard in my ears. It takes till eight to stop. Then at eight I went home, because my feet hurt, with Mabry. Come nine, I couldn’t settle, so I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee, with Amato and Doyle. Around ten I went home to iron a shirt for the morning, on my own.” ¶ Miss Nowak said home at ten. Mrs. Rafferty had nobody here at ten o’clock. They couldn’t both be true, and Mrs. Rafferty had no reason to be the wrong one. ¶ Painting her nails a red her landlady disapproves of: that was the last I saw of her. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. It happened at nine or ten o’clock, and I didn’t know which yet. The chloral came from Rafferty’s, so whoever used it had been there first. Teitel, Mabry and Miss Nowak had been at Rafferty’s earlier, when the chloral was there for the taking; Amato hadn’t. Mabry was at Rafferty’s at nine; Mrs. Rafferty said so. Miss Nowak had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Rafferty’s list said otherwise. Teitel and Amato hadn’t told me where they were at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out what Teitel had to say for himself. ¶ That was the night so far: a lot of people who were somewhere, and one hour nobody wanted to talk about.

I sat down where Teitel could see me, and didn’t hurry. Teitel had a white beard trimmed square, and fingerless gloves from which he can produce change faster than you can see it. ¶ “Mrs. Rafferty has you at Rafferty’s at seven. That’s one hour. Tell me about the others.” ¶ He thought for a second, the way anybody does, and started at the beginning. ¶ “For you, a special price: the whole evening, free. Nobody gets that from Teitel. Listen. At seven I went round to Rafferty’s to return a borrowed umbrella, with Mabry. Seven, I count the day. It never takes long. Come eight, I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee and pie, with Amato. Around nine I went up to the card room over Feingold’s garage to watch the game and not play. At ten I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee. I had nobody with me at nine or ten.” ¶ So Rafferty’s at seven, with Mabry, which was what Mrs. Rafferty had. That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for. For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, he said the card room over Feingold’s garage at nine and Steinmetz’s at ten. It went in the notebook in his own words. ¶ Demos would have seen everybody who came in. ¶ There was the slate by the door with the specials chalked on it, where the soup is crossed off at whatever hour you come in.

Getting to the card room over Feingold’s garage meant a couple of blocks uptown and east. The streetlamps went out all at once while I was under one, which felt personal. ¶ The card room had shut for the night: the lamp off, the chairs pushed in, and the ashtrays not emptied by anybody, ever. The smell of the garage came up through the floor, oil and rubber, and met the smell of the night coming down. There were windows painted black on the inside, so nobody can see in and nobody inside can tell the time. ¶ Russo was sitting with his back to the wall. He had soft white hands that are always shuffling a deck, even in church, his mother-in-law says. ¶ Russo had the room from the hour that mattered, and not before. Before that, he said, it was anybody’s. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

I took the form into a corner of the card room over Feingold’s garage and sat down with it. I read the night back to myself, from the office to here, and started at the top of the form. ¶ My cigarette had burned down to my fingers again. A man with a bank account would have noticed sooner.

A few blocks east, and I was at Belkin’s place. The sky was clear and the city was still up under it, with a lit window on every other floor and a radio arguing in one of them. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There were brass mailboxes with little windows, so the whole building can see who gets letters and who gets bills. ¶ Belkin was on the floor in the middle of the room. A man looks smaller on the floor than he ever did standing up. He had his greasepaint still on and a program in his coat pocket, signed to himself. ¶ Doyle was there ahead of me, hat in his hands, turning the brim. ¶ It was the kind of place nobody kept an eye on. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I looked the place over the way you read a bill: twice, and slowly.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, so I went through them. I went through his papers with the lamp pulled close, the way you read a will you aren’t in. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge against him, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and he’d written every one down. ¶ Amato: a page on his old flame, with his name at the bottom. Lieb: a debt to Wexler, with his name beside it. Miss Moskin: a letter letting her go, written and not yet sent. Mrs. Krantz: a letter from her asking for her money, never answered. ¶ A reason is the easy half. The other half was a way to the revolver, and that was at Rafferty’s. ¶ Belkin had been here earlier in the evening, and that was worth the walk to the Peacock. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Lieb. I leaned on the bar next to him and ordered nothing, which got noticed. He had a silk scarf with somebody else’s monogram on it, worn with the monogram tucked in. ¶ I asked Lieb for his evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. He had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “Sure, I’ll tell you. I tell everybody everything. That’s my trouble, my uncle says. I was at the Peacock from seven through eight. Seven, I’m always starving. A fellow stuck behind a counter all day gets an appetite for everything. Belkin was there at seven; Amato was there at eight. At nine I went round to Rafferty’s to borrow a collar stud, with Mrs. Krantz and Miss Moskin. Ten o’clock I went down to the Peacock to hear the trumpet, with Miss Moskin. Walking over to the Peacock at ten I passed Mrs. Krantz on East Houston Street, going fast, no hat.” ¶ The part worth keeping came last. East Houston Street was where Belkin lived. ¶ There was a stuffed peacock by the bar, molting, with one glass eye; the other was lost in a bet in 1924, and nobody will say who won it.

Mrs. Szabo’s list had Amato here at eight, and I wanted the rest of that evening. I took the stool next to him. He was a stocky man in a leather jacket and a chauffeur’s cap pushed back, moving a toothpick from one side of his mouth to the other to show he’s thinking. ¶ I asked him where he’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ He nodded, as if it were a fair question, and maybe it was. ¶ “Where to? Ha. Sorry. Habit. Go ahead, ask. At seven I went to Rafferty’s to collect a debt, with Miss Moskin. Seven’s the worst hour for a cab. Everybody’s late, and everybody thinks it’s my fault. I take seven off when I can. Come eight, I went to the Peacock to dance, with Lieb. Around nine I went round to the bakery cellar at Sokol’s to see a man about a horse. At ten I went to the Peacock, because a friend was on the door. Nobody was with me at nine or ten.” ¶ Amato said the Peacock at ten. The doorkeeper had Lieb and Miss Moskin here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. They couldn’t both be true, and Mrs. Szabo had no reason to be the wrong one. ¶ Everybody’s evening sounds tidy when they tell it. I wrote it down anyway. ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. Doyle had said nine or ten, and Belkin was at the Peacock at nine, alive. The revolver came from Rafferty’s, so whoever used it had been there first. Lieb hadn’t. Amato had told me the Peacock at ten, and Mrs. Szabo’s list said otherwise. Lieb was at the Peacock at ten; Mrs. Szabo said so. Miss Moskin was at the Peacock at ten; Mrs. Szabo said so. Mrs. Krantz hadn’t told me where she was at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ That was the night so far: a lot of people who were somewhere, and one hour nobody wanted to talk about.

The bakery cellar at Sokol’s was a couple of blocks west, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ The bakery cellar at Sokol’s didn’t have a sign, which was the sign. Somebody let me in and then looked at me as if they’d made a mistake. There was the door from the bakery to the bar, with FLOUR painted on it, which has fooled nobody for years. ¶ Fishel was behind the counter, writing in a ledger by the light of a green-shaded lamp. He had a diamond pinky ring a size too small, so that the finger has grown around it. ¶ Fishel had the room from the hour that mattered, and not before. Before that, he said, it was anybody’s. ¶ It was the sort of room people say they were never in. I made a note that I was.

I headed downtown and east for Mrs. Krantz’s flat, a couple of blocks away. A baker’s boy went by with a tray of rolls on his head and the look of somebody who’d been up longer than me. ¶ The milkman had been to the Excelsior and left a bottle outside every door on every floor, and nobody in the building had seen him come or go. That’s the kind of building it is: no doorman, no janitor in sight, and a landlord who lives uptown and sends a man on the first of the month. There was a tall mirror in the lobby, so that everybody who comes in meets somebody who looks worse. ¶ Mrs. Krantz was drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in. She was a stout woman in gray, buttoned to the throat, carrying a leather satchel with a brass lock on it. ¶ There was nobody on duty, and nobody to ask who had been by. ¶ The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

Midnight. The office on Mulberry Street had one lamp, one chair worth sitting in and one detective, and the detective was in the worst repair of the three. More money in the drawer than bills on the desk. The telephone company and the landlady were paid, and some was left over. I didn’t know what people did with that. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. My visitor didn’t sit until I told her to. She needed help, she said. That was the speech. ¶ She didn’t wait to be asked. “Assunta Greco. Lazar Belkin’s neighbor. He’s dead, and nobody is doing anything about it.” ¶ Belkin had been the leading man. He was found in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street at half past eleven. The one who found him was Russo, who’d come up for the Thursday card game. The police wrote it down as his heart. ¶ I pointed Mrs. Greco at the chair. She took it, and held her hat on her knees. ¶ “When did it happen, as near as anybody can say?” ¶ “The police can call it what they like,” she said. “The woman across the landing heard him laugh with somebody and then go quiet at nine or ten o’clock; she’d dozed off over the radio and can’t say which.” ¶ “He’d been at the Peacock earlier in the evening,” she said. “His usual.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad he’s gone?” ¶ “There’s a letter from Doyle in his desk,” Mrs. Greco said. “It was on top, and I didn’t look any further. He owed Doyle’s old flame, and wasn’t paying.” ¶ She opened her bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.

I went over Belkin’s table slowly, touching nothing I didn’t have to. ¶ I worked slowly. Mrs. Greco waited in the hall, and the stairs creaked every time she shifted her weight. ¶ A cup of cocoa gone cold, bitter at the bottom. Beside it a tin with a skull on the label, from the cellar shelf at the flats over Lipsky’s. Somebody made him cocoa. ¶ So the rat poison came from the flats over Lipsky’s, and rat poison takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Belkin had been at the flats over Lipsky’s earlier, to get it. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

It was a few blocks to the flats over Lipsky’s, uptown. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The fire escapes over Lipsky’s were letting the rain down in strings into the yard by the cellar steps, where the janitor had laid a plank across the puddle to his door. Up the stoop, the hall had a row of tin mailboxes with names in five different hands, two of them crossed out, and a wet umbrella dripping on every landing. There was the roof door at the top of the stairs, propped open with a brick summer and winter, because nobody has told the brick it’s winter. ¶ Wojcik was sitting on the cellar steps with his pipe. He had a ring of keys on a bootlace round his neck, worn under his undershirt where nobody can borrow them. Mrs. Krantz, in a grey fedora, was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. Russo, in a camel coat, was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ The rat poison had come from here. Russo had found Belkin. That was reason enough. From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe from supper till bed, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ The stairs had opinions about my weight and shared them all the way up.

Doyle’s flat lay a few blocks downtown. East Houston Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ Behind its own front door the Excelsior was asleep: a good door, with a brass knob and a wooden wedge holding it open an inch for some tenant who keeps losing his key. The lobby mirror gave me back a man who needed a shave and a better coat. Nobody watches this door; that’s what the tenants pay for. There was a dumbwaiter in the back hall for coal and parcels, with a bell on every floor that nobody answers. ¶ Doyle, in a green hat, was writing a name in a little black book. He was a florid man in a derby and a checked waistcoat, with a carnation in his buttonhole that the alderman pays for. ¶ Wojcik’s list had Doyle at the flats over Lipsky’s at seven and nine. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ I looked the place over the way you read a bill: twice, and slowly.

The Peacock was a fair few blocks uptown and west. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ With the band gone home, the Peacock looked like what it was: a low cellar with a damp ceiling and the chairs upside down on the tables, smelling of gin and of lilies, the lilies coming down through the floorboards from the undertaker’s. The steel door was bolted. The slot opened anyway when I knocked, which told me the doorkeeper didn’t go home either. There was a coffin on display in the undertaker’s window beside the stair, lid up, with the price folded on the pillow. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was looking through the slot in the steel door. She had a nose that was broken once and set by somebody in a hurry, and a pair of pearl earrings to make up for it. Amato, in a fur collar, had a table near the empty dance floor and was turning a glass slowly round and round by its stem. ¶ Belkin had been here earlier in the evening. Doyle had said Amato was with him at the flats over Lipsky’s at nine. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “Every face comes to my slot first. I don’t like most of them, so the ones I let in, I remember.” ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Amato had a fresh glass in front of him and the look of somebody who’d meant to stop at the last one. I leaned on the bar next to him and ordered nothing, which got noticed. He had a St. Christopher medal on a chain round his neck and another on the dashboard of his cab, in case one of them is off duty. ¶ I asked him where he’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ He didn’t seem to mind being asked, which is how most people seem. ¶ “Where to? Ha. Sorry. Habit. Go ahead, ask. I was home at the flats over Lipsky’s from seven through nine. Seven’s the worst hour for a cab. Everybody’s late, and everybody thinks it’s my fault. I take seven off when I can. Miss Moskin and Doyle were there at seven; Miss Moskin and Mrs. Krantz were there at eight; Miss Moskin, Doyle and Mrs. Krantz were there at nine. Come ten, I went round to Doyle’s for a game of gin.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Amato said Doyle’s flat. I didn’t believe it or disbelieve it. I wrote it down. ¶ There was a stuffed peacock by the bar, molting, with one glass eye; the other was lost in a bet in 1924, and nobody will say who won it. ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. Mrs. Greco had said nine or ten o’clock. The rat poison had come from the flats over Lipsky’s. I had evenings from Doyle and Amato, and lists from Wojcik and Mrs. Szabo. I didn’t have Miss Moskin’s, Mrs. Krantz’s or Russo’s evenings yet. ¶ It was the middle of the night and the middle of the job, and neither one felt like an end.

I sat down near Miss Moskin, in a corner nobody else was using. “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” ¶ She answered straight off, the way people do with an evening they’ve only just finished. ¶ “Sure, ask me anything. I’m rehearsing for being famous, so I might as well practice my interviews. I was home at the flats over Lipsky’s from seven through nine. Amato and Doyle were there at seven; Amato and Mrs. Krantz were there at eight; Amato, Doyle and Mrs. Krantz were there at nine. Eight, I’m always hungry, and I never eat. You can’t, at eight. You might need to look tragic later. At ten I went round to the bakery cellar at Sokol’s to see a man about a horse, with Fishel.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Miss Moskin said the bakery cellar at Sokol’s. That was her word for it, and I took it down as said. ¶ It turned out Fishel was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ I put it in the notebook with the rest. Every evening sounds like an evening until you set it next to another one.

Midnight. My office was a desk, two chairs and a window on Mulberry Street, and the window was the only one of them with a view. I gave up on bed around eleven and made my peace with the desk chair, which had never once let me sleep. The stairs outside creaked twice, some tenant getting home. ¶ There was a knock, and then the door opened before I’d said anything, which is how people knock when they’ve made up their minds. My visitor was already diagnosing the room, the stairs and my lack of a secretary before he sat down. ¶ “It’s a silver cigarette case,” Doyle said. “It was on the sideboard, where it always is, and now it isn’t.” ¶ “I was at the pictures all evening, and the flat was locked,” he said. “The spare key lives in the sugar tin on the kitchen shelf at Kowalski’s. Mrs. Kowalski keeps it there, and everybody who drops in knows it.” ¶ “When did this happen, as near as you can say?” ¶ “I can tell you when, near enough,” he said. “The man below heard the door go just after the ten o’clock el went by; he sets his watch by it.” ¶ “Who’d want it badly enough to take it?” ¶ “Look at Marchetti,” he said. “He was in at Kowalski’s this evening, where the spare key is kept. Who does that? And he lost his job on Friday, and asked me what the cigarette case was worth.” ¶ Then he went quieter, though there was nobody else in the room. “Wehrle, a cafeteria cashier, says the cigarette case was promised to her by my late father. And Ellery, an insurance agent, is three weeks behind on the rent, and once asked what the cigarette case would pawn for.” ¶ “Ten dollars,” Doyle said. “It’s what I have. Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

I asked Doyle to wait in the hall, and went over the parlor by myself. ¶ Doyle kept out of my way, the way people keep out of the way of a doctor. ¶ There was a clean square in the dust on the sideboard. The door had been locked again behind whoever it was, and there wasn’t a mark on it.
