Whoever it was had a key. ¶ So the key that let them in was the spare, and the spare lived in the sugar tin at Kowalski’s. ¶ Marchetti hadn’t told me his evening yet, and he was at the Blue Lantern. ¶ The aspidistra in the corner hadn’t moved, which is the great thing about aspidistras.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Kowalski. ¶ I went over to her and waited until she had a moment, which took a moment. I asked Mrs. Kowalski to give me the night the way only the landlady could: every face, every hour. ¶ She started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Wehrle, Ellery and Shapiro. Nobody else. Nine, Marchetti, Wehrle, Ellery and Shapiro. Nobody else at all. Ten, Ellery and Shapiro. Nobody else, that hour. The spare key for the Doyle flat was in its tin at eight. I didn’t look again.” ¶ That put Ellery here at ten, by her count. ¶ It turned out Shapiro was in the front room, in the good chair. ¶ Marchetti could tell me his own evening, and he was at the Blue Lantern. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

I got as near to Marchetti as manners allowed and said my name. “Mrs. Kowalski has you at Kowalski’s at nine. That’s one hour. Tell me about the others.” ¶ Marchetti put down what he was holding and gave me his attention. ¶ “I was at the Blue Lantern at eight, with Lefkowitz. Then at nine I went round to Kowalski’s to borrow a collar stud, with Wehrle, Ellery and Shapiro. Come ten, I had a table at the Blue Lantern, alone.” ¶ So Kowalski’s at nine, with Wehrle, Ellery and Shapiro, which was what Mrs. Kowalski had. That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for. For ten, the hour that mattered, he said the Blue Lantern. I didn’t believe it or disbelieve it. I wrote it down. ¶ It turned out Lefkowitz was at the far end of the bar, nursing something. ¶ Winslow had been there all evening with nothing to do but notice. ¶ The globe was still turning overhead, throwing light at a dance floor that had stopped asking for it.

I sat down with the form and a pencil. Every question on it had an answer, and every answer had a name and an hour behind it. ¶ The office stairs had done their bit for the night. They’d brought me the case.

Getting to the Shapiro flat meant a couple of blocks east. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ I went up to the Shapiro flat over the delicatessen on Second Avenue. A narrow stair, a landing with one door on it, and on the door a nameplate that somebody had polished thin. A china shepherdess stood on a doily, looking at the room with painted patience. ¶ Shapiro showed me where the cigarette case had been kept and touched the place once, lightly, the way you touch a sore tooth. ¶ There was no one to notice who passed through. ¶ If it went at ten, the flat had been empty, and anybody who’d heard Shapiro at the Bijou had known the way in. That was a room, more or less. It was a big room. ¶ I stood in the doorway a while before I went in. Rooms like that don’t like to be rushed.

A few blocks downtown and east, and I was at the Bijou. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ I went to the Bijou, a picture house on Clinton Street. It was a narrow little house with a ticket window the size of a mail slot and a smell of floor polish and oranges. A life-size cardboard cowboy stood in the lobby, fading, and tipping his hat at the box office. ¶ Ruggiero stood at the back of the house with a flashlight, pointed at the floor, ready. She had a roll of tickets on a spindle and a coin changer on her belt, and a callus on one thumb from tearing stubs, the only part of the job that showed. Stannard was in the lobby, reading the bills for next week as if they might change. ¶ An usher with a flashlight sees every face that comes in out of the street, and most of them twice. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

Ruggiero’s list had Stannard here at nine, and I wanted the rest of that evening. I sat down in the row behind him and leaned forward, like a man with a question about the seats. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, he wore clothes too good to have been bought. He’d made every stitch. ¶ I asked him to walk me through his night, every stop of it. He had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “I was at Moskowitz’s at eight, with Quill. At nine I went to the second show at the Bijou, and stayed the rest of the evening. Grasso was there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ Stannard said the Bijou at ten. She had Benny here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. They couldn’t both be true, and Ruggiero had no reason to be the wrong one. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it. ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at ten o’clock. Grasso and Stannard were at the Bijou while Shapiro told the room; Mulcahy wasn’t. Stannard had told me the Bijou at ten, and Ruggiero’s list said otherwise. Grasso and Mulcahy hadn’t told me where they were at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Benny at the Bijou at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Stannard now. Or I could find out first from the head waiter at Moskowitz’s who’d been in. ¶ That was everything I had, and it wasn’t enough yet.

I went over to where Vogel could see the whole room, which was where he always was. “You’ve been here all night,” I said. “Who came in, and when?” ¶ He seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Stannard and Quill. Nobody else. Nine, Quill. Nobody else at all. Ten, Grasso and Quill. Nobody else, that hour.” ¶ Vogel had Stannard here at eight, same as he said. That put Grasso here at ten, by his count. ¶ The samovar went on steaming at the end of the counter, the only thing in the room in no hurry at all.

Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants. The landlady’s bill was folded under the telephone. I’d see it every time the thing didn’t ring. I decided not to open it until it did. ¶ Somebody was coming up. At this hour it’s either trouble or a client, and in my experience they climb at the same speed. My visitor came in unhurried, as if the hour happened to other people. ¶ “Somebody has taken a silver cigarette case,” Broadnax said. “It was on the sideboard. It isn’t.” ¶ I offered him the chair and turned the lamp away from him. ¶ “I was at the pictures all evening, and the flat was locked,” he said. “The spare key lives in the sugar tin on the kitchen shelf at Rafferty’s. Mrs. Rafferty keeps it there, and everybody who drops in knows it.” ¶ “And when did the cigarette case go?” ¶ He had worked it out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “St. Teresa’s was striking ten when the woman across the hall heard the door.” ¶ “Who’d want to take it?” ¶ “Look at Weisglass,” he said. “She was in at Rafferty’s this evening, where the spare key is kept. Who does that? And she owes Lou the bookmaker forty dollars, and Lou takes things in kind.” ¶ Broadnax said the next part to the desk rather than to me. “Rosenbaum, an insurance agent, is three weeks behind on the rent, and once asked what the cigarette case would pawn for. And Zeldin, a bus conductor, says the cigarette case was promised to her by my late father.” ¶ He took a breath, the way people do before the part they’d rather not say. “Margolis, a bookmaker, always said the cigarette case was wasted on me.” ¶ He put ten dollars on the desk and smoothed it flat with his palm. “Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

I went over Broadnax’s parlor from the door to the far wall, slowly. ¶ Broadnax stood in the hall with his hands in his pockets, so as not to touch anything, which was more than whoever came before me had managed. ¶ There was a clean square in the dust on the sideboard. The door had been locked again behind whoever it was, and there wasn’t a mark on it. Whoever it was had a key. ¶ So the key that let them in was the spare, and the spare lived in the sugar tin at Rafferty’s. ¶ Somebody at Rafferty’s would have kept count of faces, and that would be the landlady. ¶ The china shepherdess had kept her painted patience through all of it. I was running low on mine.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Rafferty. I went over to her and waited until she had a moment, which took a moment. ¶ I asked her who’d been in tonight, everybody, hour by hour. She went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Rosenbaum and Zeldin. Nobody else. Nine, Weisglass and Rosenbaum. Nobody else at all. Ten and eleven, nobody but me. The spare key for the Broadnax flat was in its tin at eight. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Weisglass, Rosenbaum and Zeldin had been in here earlier, when the spare key was there for the taking. Margolis hadn’t been in here while it was there to take. For ten, the hour that mattered, Mrs. Rafferty had nobody. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

I said who I was, and Zeldin took it about as well as people do. “Mrs. Rafferty has you at Rafferty’s at eight. Where were you the rest of the evening? All of it, in order.” ¶ She answered straight off, the way people do with an evening they’ve only just finished. ¶ “I was home at Rafferty’s at eight, with Rosenbaum. Then at nine I went to the Kit Kat to dance, with Margolis. Come ten, I went home to listen to the radio. Around eleven I went to the Automat for coffee and a newspaper. At ten and eleven I was on my own.” ¶ Zeldin said home at ten. Mrs. Rafferty had nobody at Rafferty’s at ten o’clock. One of them was wrong. ¶ Somebody leaned on the chair with the short leg, and it told the whole room about it. ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at ten o’clock. Weisglass, Rosenbaum and Zeldin had been in at Rafferty’s earlier, when the spare key was there for the taking; Margolis hadn’t. Zeldin had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Rafferty’s list said otherwise. Weisglass, Rosenbaum and Margolis hadn’t told me where they were at ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the doorkeeper at the Kit Kat who’d been in. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

Zeldin had named Kreuzer: the Automat at ten, the two of them, and that wanted checking. I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. ¶ I asked him where he’d spent the night, plainly, the way you’d ask anybody. ¶ Kreuzer took a moment to put the evening in order before he handed it over. ¶ “I was home from eight through nine. Around ten I went to the Automat to meet Zeldin. At eleven I went home to change. Nobody was with me at eight, nine or eleven.” ¶ That put Zeldin here at ten, and he would swear to it. ¶ The doorkeeper at the Kit Kat would have seen everybody who came in. ¶ I wrote it all down. My handwriting at that hour looks like a spider fell in the ink, but I can read it, mostly.

I waited for a gap in Mosley’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. ¶ I asked him to count the night for me, face by face. He started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Lou the bookmaker was in his back booth all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Weisglass and Margolis. Nobody else. Nine, Zeldin and Margolis. Nobody else at all. Ten, Rosenbaum and Margolis. Nobody else, that hour. Eleven, Weisglass, Rosenbaum and Margolis. Nobody else. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Lou, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “Did you see what was under the coat?” ¶ “Something small. I didn’t ask it its name.” ¶ Mosley had Zeldin here at nine, same as she said. That put Rosenbaum and Margolis here at ten, by his count. Whatever went out of the Broadnax flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Lou. ¶ I could feel the door behind me, ready to swing wide the moment I turned. It’s nice to be wanted gone that efficiently.

I sat down at a table at the back of the Kit Kat with the form and a glass of water I hadn’t asked for. A name wants a line under it, and a line wants somebody’s word under that. I went down the form one line at a time. ¶ The office telephone never had rung tonight. It hadn’t needed to. The trouble had taken the stairs.

Tillman’s place lay a few blocks east. My knees had the temperature a block before any thermometer did. They’ve had more practice. ¶ I climbed to Tillman’s flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street. Each flight was a little darker than the one under it, and at the top there was a door with the light still on behind it. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Tillman was in the chair with his head back and his mouth a little open, the way a man sleeps when he’s too tired to care how he looks. ¶ My client, Feeney, had beaten me there and stood just inside the door, gloves in his hand. ¶ Nobody minded who came and went. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I wanted to read them properly. I went through Tillman’s papers, one folder at a time. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge against him, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and he’d written every one down. ¶ Wehrle: a wedding invitation nobody ever used; he jilted her sister a week before the wedding. Bidwell: a column of payments, every month for years, and his name at the top. Winslow: one line, where he was in 1921, and an address. Quill: an IOU for four hundred dollars, in his hand. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Kowalski’s and the chloral. ¶ Quill was at the Odessa, and I didn’t have a word of his evening yet. ¶ The empty birdcage hung in its corner. It had been empty a long time and was used to it.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Kowalski. ¶ She saw me coming before I’d decided to come. That’s the job. I asked Mrs. Kowalski to give me the night the way only the landlady could: every face, every hour. ¶ She started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Winslow and Bidwell. Nobody else. Eight, Quill and Bidwell. Nobody else at all. Nine, Bidwell. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, nobody but me. The chloral on my hall shelf was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Quill, Winslow and Bidwell had been here earlier, when the chloral was there for the taking. Wehrle hadn’t been here while it was there to take. That put Bidwell here at nine, by her count. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

The Odessa was round the corner. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ I went to the Odessa, a café where the actors eat after the show. The tables were marble, the tea came in glasses, and the mirrors on every wall made the room look three times the size it was. The day’s specials were chalked on a slate by the door, and the soup had been crossed out. ¶ Moretti was behind the register, doing the crossword in pencil and the day’s takings in ink. Quill had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. Round and pleasant and dressed a little too well for a cigar store, he kept his eyes on the door, in case it was the police or a winner. Wehrle was at a corner table with a plate of toast, eating it slowly, a corner at a time, like somebody paying by the bite. Bidwell was finishing a plate of something with the care of somebody who had paid for it. ¶ Winslow had said he was here at eight. Mrs. Kowalski’s list had Quill at Kowalski’s at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. Nobody leaves a place like that without paying Moretti, and he looks at every face that pays. ¶ The room had the late quiet of a place that stays open because nobody ever told it to close.

Moretti’s list had Quill here at seven and nine, so I went over. I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. ¶ I asked him where he’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ He thought for a second, the way anybody does, and started at the beginning. ¶ “I was at the Odessa at seven, with Wehrle and Tillman. Then at eight I took a letter round to Kowalski’s, with Bidwell. Come nine, I went to the Odessa to read the late paper over a plate of soup, and stayed the rest of the evening. Wehrle and Tillman were there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ Quill said the Odessa at ten. The cashier had Wehrle and Bidwell here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. They couldn’t both be true, and Moretti had no reason to be the wrong one. ¶ The cashier in the change booth at the Automat would have seen everybody who came in. ¶ The door opened. It was neither. It hardly ever is, which is how bookmakers stay in business.

I went over to Colquitt and waited until she had a moment, which took a moment. “Who was in tonight?” I said. “You’d know. Knowing is most of your job.” ¶ She looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶ “Ten o’clock, Winslow and somebody at the same table I didn’t know. I came on at ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ That put Winslow here at ten, by her count. ¶ The tin sign was still promising relief. It had been promising it for years.

Midnight. My office was a desk, two chairs and a window on Mulberry Street, and the window was the only one of them with a view. The coffee I’d made was cold by the time I remembered it. I drank it anyway; it was lighter than holding my head. ¶ I heard steps on the stairs, stopping on every landing to think it over. My visitor knocked twice and waited to be asked in, as if somebody’s mother was listening. ¶ He didn’t wait to be asked. “Martin Brennan. James Sweeney’s cousin. He’s dead, and nobody is doing anything about it.” ¶ Sweeney had been a pawnbroker. He was found in his own two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street at half past eleven. The one who found him was Reinhardt, who heard his radio still going and knocked. The police wrote it down as his heart. ¶ I offered my client the chair, and dusted it first, which I don’t do for everybody. ¶ “When did it happen, as near as anybody can say?” ¶ “I’ll tell you what the police didn’t ask,” he said. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “He’d been at Moskowitz’s earlier in the evening,” my client said. “His usual.” ¶ “Who’d want him dead badly enough to see to it?” ¶ “Ask Ashby,” he said. “She swore at him in the street on Monday, in front of the fruit man. He had been squeezing her for years.” ¶ “Fifty dollars,” Brennan said, and put it on the desk. “Find out who did this to him, and tell me before you tell anybody else.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

I went over the table. ¶ Brennan didn’t come in. I didn’t ask him to. ¶ There were two glasses on the table, and one of them smelled sweet and chemical. Under the table was an empty bottle with a Weiss’s pharmacy label, the kind that comes off the dispensary shelf. ¶ So the chloral came from Weiss’s pharmacy, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Sweeney had been at Weiss’s pharmacy earlier, to get it. ¶ The radiator was still knocking. It was the only thing in the room with anything to say.

It was a good walk from there to Moskowitz’s, uptown and west, with my collar up. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went down to Moskowitz’s, a Romanian restaurant four steps down on Second Avenue. The place smelled of garlic and grilled meat, there was a basket of bread on every table, and the piano in the corner had a cloth over it for the night. The day’s specials were chalked on a slate by the door, and the soup had been crossed out. ¶ Kavanagh stood by the reservation book at the door with a pencil, crossing out tables nobody would want now. Salerno was finishing a plate of something with the care of somebody who had paid for it. Young and tidy and a little tired, she still had the mark of the headset band pressed into her hair. Ashby had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. ¶ A head waiter shows everybody to a table, so Kavanagh would know who had come in tonight and where they’d been put. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Ashby had said Salerno was with her here at ten, so that was where I went next. I got as near to her as manners allowed and said my name. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” Salerno answered without looking at me, which is a way of answering. ¶ “I was at Moskowitz’s from seven through eight. At seven it was just me; Reinhardt and Sweeney were there at eight. Nine o’clock I went to the Eagle club office to pay my dues, with Reinhardt. Then at ten I went to Moskowitz’s for a glass of tea, with Ashby. Walking over to Moskowitz’s at ten I passed Prentiss on Hester Street, going fast, no hat.” ¶ So here at ten, which was what Ashby had said. That much of it stood up, and it stood up where I could check it. The part worth keeping came last. Hester Street was where Sweeney lived. ¶ Reinhardt had walked from Moskowitz’s to the Eagle club office at nine. I wanted to know what she’d passed on the way. ¶ My hat had left a mark in my hair too. Nobody was paying me by the hour for mine.

I found Reinhardt at the far end, where the light gave up, and stood where she could see me without having to want to. I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ She counted back through the evening under her breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “At seven I went to Weiss’s pharmacy to have a prescription made up, with Ashby. Come eight, I went to Moskowitz’s for coffee and pie, with Salerno and Sweeney. Around nine I went to the Eagle club office to write letters, with Salerno. At ten I went to Moskowitz’s for coffee, on my own.” ¶ Reinhardt said Moskowitz’s at ten. Ashby says she was at Moskowitz’s at ten o’clock, with Salerno. They couldn’t both be true, and I knew which one I’d bet on. ¶ The door opened. It was neither. It hardly ever is, which is how bookmakers stay in business. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. It happened at nine or ten o’clock, and I didn’t know which yet. The chloral came from Weiss’s pharmacy, so whoever used it had been there first. Reinhardt and Ashby had been at Weiss’s pharmacy earlier, when the chloral was there for the taking; Salerno hadn’t. Reinhardt had told me Moskowitz’s at ten, and Ashby’s story said otherwise. Salerno was at the Eagle club office at nine and Moskowitz’s at ten; Reinhardt and Ashby said so. Ashby was at Moskowitz’s at ten; Salerno said so. Prentiss hadn’t told me where she was at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to know what Prentiss had passed on the way to Moskowitz’s at nine. ¶ That was everything I had, and it wasn’t enough yet.

Reinhardt had named Steinbach: the Eagle club office at ten, the two of them. Whether that held was the next question. I kept my voice down. She kept her eyes on me. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said to her. “The whole evening, in order.” ¶ Steinbach thought about it the way you’d think about a step in the dark, and then took it. ¶ “I was home from seven through nine, alone. Come ten, I went to the Eagle club office to meet Reinhardt.” ¶ That put Reinhardt here at ten, and she would swear to it. ¶ Prentiss had walked from Weiss’s pharmacy to Moskowitz’s at nine. I wanted to know what she’d passed on the way. ¶ Nobody had fixed the chair with the short leg. In a room like that, a folded matchbook under the leg counts as a carpenter.

Prentiss kept me standing in the hall, which told me how long the visit was going to be. ¶ I asked her to walk me through her night, every stop of it. ¶ She kept it short. Some people do with everybody. ¶ “I was home at seven. Then at eight I went to Weiss’s pharmacy for a powder for my nerves, with Ashby. Come nine, I couldn’t settle, so I went to Moskowitz’s for coffee, with Ashby and Sweeney. Around ten I went home to listen to the radio. Nobody was with me at seven or ten.” ¶ Prentiss said home at ten. Salerno passed her on Hester Street at ten. Two stories about her at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. The rest held where I could check it: Ashby had her at Moskowitz’s at nine, with Sweeney, and at Weiss’s pharmacy at eight, same as she said. Brennan had said nine or ten. Sweeney was at Moskowitz’s at nine, alive. ¶ The gramophone’s big tin horn was pointed at me, as if it had something to add.

Midnight. My office was two rooms at the top of a walk-up on Mulberry Street, and the second room was mostly for show. The mirror over the washbasin showed more of the night before than I wanted explained. I turned the lamp away from it. ¶ Somebody was coming up. At this hour it’s either trouble or a client, and in my experience they climb at the same speed. My visitor came in with an apology for the hour and a second one for the first, and was well into a third before sitting down. ¶ He didn’t wait to be asked. “Louis Abramowitz. Albrecht Lindemann’s brother-in-law. He’s dead, and nobody is doing anything about it.” ¶ Lindemann was an alderman’s clerk. Pickering, who’d come to return a borrowed book, found him in his own flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street at half past eleven. The police called it his heart and went home. ¶ “When did he die?” ¶ “I’ll tell you what the police didn’t ask,” he said. “The coroner says chloral in a drink, taken at nine or ten o’clock; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “He was at Moe’s earlier in the evening,” my client said. “His usual. He liked his usual.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad he’s gone?” ¶ “There’s Kreuzer,” Abramowitz said. “I don’t like gossip, but He threw him out of a lease. The woman downstairs told me.” ¶ He counted fifty dollars onto the blotter and kept a finger on the last bill. “Find out who did it. Then tell me first.” ¶ I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.

I went over Lindemann’s table slowly, touching nothing I didn’t have to. ¶ I worked slowly. Abramowitz waited in the hall, and the stairs creaked every time he shifted his weight. ¶ There were two glasses on the table. One smelled of rye and nothing else. The other smelled of rye and something sweet and chemical, like a hospital left out in the sun. Under the table, where it had rolled, was an empty brown bottle with a paper label from Mrs. Nagy’s. The lodgers there keep it on the hall shelf. The dead man had been drinking with somebody he knew. ¶ So the chloral came from Mrs. Nagy’s, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Lindemann had been at Mrs. Nagy’s earlier, to get it. ¶ I had what there was. A room can’t lie to you, but it can keep quiet.

A good walk uptown and east, and I was at Mrs. Nagy’s. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ Mrs. Nagy’s, on East Fourth Street, was quiet at this hour. The hall smelled of paprika and floor wax, and a lamp had been left on at the turn of the stair. A holy picture hung in the hall, with a little lamp in a red glass under it. ¶ Mrs. Nagy was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Hurwitz, with a bandaged hand, was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. Pickering, in a green hat, was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into his collar. ¶ The chloral had come from here. Pickering had found Lindemann. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them. ¶ The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

I walked downtown and west to Moe’s. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ Moe’s, a back-room bar behind a cigar store, was one room with no windows, a curtain for a door and a bar along one wall. After midnight it had the quiet of a place that expects to be quiet and is paid to be. A brass spittoon stood at the foot of the bar, polished brighter than anything else in the room. ¶ Mulcahy stood at the register end of the bar with her arms folded, as if the till might try something. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Petrosino, in a grey fedora, was at the bar with a drink he wasn’t drinking. ¶ Lindemann had been here earlier in the evening. Mrs. Nagy’s list had Petrosino at Mrs. Nagy’s at seven, eight and nine, and that was worth the walk. ¶ From behind a bar you can see the whole room and the door, and that side of the bar belonged to Mulcahy. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Petrosino was still there, which at that hour in that room is most of what you can ask of anybody. I leaned on the bar next to him and ordered nothing, which got noticed. He smelled of gasoline and cold coffee and kept his gloves on indoors, the fingertips cut out of them. ¶ “Mrs. Nagy has you at Mrs. Nagy’s at seven and eight. Where were you the rest of the evening? All of it, in order.” ¶ He didn’t seem to mind being asked, which is how most people seem. ¶ “At seven I went to Mrs. Nagy’s to help write letters home, and stayed through nine. Shapiro was there at seven; Kreuzer and Pickering were there at eight and nine. Around ten I went round to Shapiro’s for a game of gin.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Petrosino said Shapiro’s flat. I put it with the rest and didn’t argue with it yet. ¶ I could have used gloves like that. Mine have all ten fingertips, and they still let the cold in. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. Abramowitz had said nine or ten o’clock. The chloral had come from Mrs. Nagy’s. I had an evening from Petrosino, and lists from Mrs. Nagy and Mulcahy. I didn’t have Hurwitz’s, Kreuzer’s, Shapiro’s or Pickering’s evenings yet. ¶ It was the middle of the night and the middle of the job, and neither one felt like an end.

I sat down near Kreuzer, in a corner nobody else was using. ¶ I asked him for his evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. He had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “I was at Moe’s at seven, with Hurwitz, Pickering and Lindemann. At eight I went to Mrs. Nagy’s for the company, and stayed through nine, with Petrosino and Pickering. Ten o’clock I went in to the print shop to set type for the morning, with Rafferty.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Kreuzer said the print shop. Whether anything else I held touched it, I’d have to see. ¶ It turned out Rafferty was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ The door opened. It was neither. It hardly ever is, which is how bookmakers stay in business.

It was a good walk from there to Shapiro’s flat, east, with my collar up. Cannon Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ I went round to Shapiro’s flat on Cannon Street. It was a walk-up like every walk-up on Cannon Street: a hall that smelled of other people’s suppers and a stair with a bend in it. A kettle sat on a gas ring on the shelf, gone cold. ¶ Shapiro, in a fur collar, was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. She was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until she needed one, and then only the one. ¶ Petrosino had said Shapiro was with him here at ten. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ There was no one to notice who passed through. ¶ I took it all in, which didn’t take long, and then took it in again.

I sat down on the stairs with the form, which is where I do my best paperwork. Whatever I wrote down, I’d have to be able to say whose word it stood on. ¶ The mirror over my washbasin could wait for morning. One of us had had a long night, and it wasn’t the mirror.

From there to the Doyle flat was a few blocks. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There were brass mailboxes with little windows, so the whole building can see who gets letters and who gets bills. ¶ Doyle showed me where the spoons had been kept and touched the place once, lightly, the way you touch a sore tooth. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶ If it went at ten, the flat had been empty, and anybody who’d heard Doyle at the Peacock had known the way in. That was a room, more or less. It was a big room. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

It was a fair few blocks to the Peacock, uptown and west. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A trolley went by, with the same people asleep on it for all I knew, going round again for the company. ¶ Down in the cellar club it was the last set, for the serious drinkers, and the band had slowed to match them. Smoke hung under the low ceiling like a second ceiling. Through the velvet curtain at the foot of the stairs, four couples on the dance floor were holding each other up. When there’s a wake upstairs a card goes up on the steel door, QUIET PLEASE, and the band plays the slow numbers, louder. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was looking through the slot in the steel door. She had a nose that was broken once and set by somebody in a hurry, and a pair of pearl earrings to make up for it. Teitel had a table near the empty bandstand and was tapping the time of a song nobody was playing. Mrs. Krantz had a table near the empty dance floor and was turning a glass slowly round and round by its stem. ¶ From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “Every face comes to my slot first. I don’t like most of them, so the ones I let in, I remember.” ¶ The glasses behind the bar caught the light and did nothing else with it.

Teitel watched me come over the way you watch weather. ¶ I took the stool beside him and let him finish his drink before I spoiled it. He had a necktie of his own so loud it seems to be shouting for the others. ¶ “Mrs. Szabo has you here at nine. Now tell me the rest of it, from the beginning.” ¶ He told it the way you give somebody directions, landmark by landmark. ¶ “For you, a special price: the whole evening, free. Nobody gets that from Teitel. Listen. I was at the Lyric at eight, with Amato and Belkin. Around nine I went to the Peacock, because a friend was on the door, and stayed the rest of the evening. Nine, business. I think about it; it doesn’t think about me. Mrs. Krantz, Amato and Mabry were there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ Teitel said the Peacock at ten. Mrs. Szabo had Mrs. Krantz, Mabry and Miss Marsh here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ There was a stuffed peacock by the bar, molting, with one glass eye; the other was lost in a bet in 1924, and nobody will say who won it. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at ten o’clock. Teitel had told me the Peacock at ten, and Mrs. Szabo’s list said otherwise. Mrs. Krantz was at the Peacock at ten; Mrs. Szabo said so. Amato hadn’t told me where he was at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Marsh, the cigarette girl at the Peacock at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Teitel now. Or I could find out first from the usher at the Lyric who’d been in. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

There were sunflower-seed shells in the gallery aisles, swept up every night and back by the second act. ¶ I asked Pinsky who’d been in tonight, everybody, hour by hour. He started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Eight, the curtain goes up, and I go to the back of the house, where an usher belongs and an actor once didn’t. Eight o’clock, Teitel, Amato and Belkin. Nobody else. Nine, Belkin. Nobody else at all. Ten, Amato and Belkin. And nobody else. Every cross on the chart has a face, and I’ve given you every face.” ¶ Pinsky had Teitel here at eight, same as he said. That put Amato here at ten, by his count. ¶ Mouthing the third act from the back of the house: that was the last I saw of him.

Midnight. My office was a desk, two chairs and a window on Mulberry Street, and the window was the only one of them with a view. I’d paid the landlady on my way up, and she’d counted it on the landing in front of me. The stairs felt shorter for it. The office looked the same as always, which was its own kind of relief. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. A woman came in, coat buttoned against the cold, and asked straight off what it would cost. I liked her. ¶ “It’s a set of silver spoons,” Dr. Hirsch said. “It was in the velvet box in the sideboard drawer, where it always is, and now it isn’t.” ¶ I offered her the chair. She sat on the front half of it, which is the half I keep for clients. ¶ “I sat in Steinmetz’s from eight until ten,” she said, “complaining to anybody who’d listen that my parlor window won’t latch, and that I was off to my sister’s for the night.” ¶ “What time are we talking about?” ¶ “And I know when,” she said. “The dog next door went off at ten o’clock, the way it does when somebody’s on the stairs.” ¶ “Who’d want it?” ¶ “There’s Russo,” she said. “I don’t like gossip, but he says my IOU to him is overdue, and that the spoons would square it. The woman downstairs told me.” ¶ Then, smaller: “Miss Lowenthal, the piano teacher, has always wanted the spoons, and asked me the price. And Belkin, the leading man, owes Wexler money, and he has started asking for it.” ¶ “I’ll pay,” Dr. Hirsch said, and did: ten dollars, folded small. “Who, and where the spoons is now. That’s all I want.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

I went over the parlor, and then the door, and then the parlor again. ¶ Dr. Hirsch told me twice where everything usually was. I let her. It was her flat, and it was the only thing she could do. ¶ The velvet box in the sideboard drawer was empty. The parlor window was up six inches, and there was soot on the sill from the fire escape. Whoever it was had known which window. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Dr. Hirsch at Steinmetz’s between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made Steinmetz’s the place to start counting. ¶ The head waiter at Steinmetz’s would have seen everybody who came in. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Demos. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. ¶ I asked him who’d been here tonight, and said I’d take it untidy, the way it happened. He counted it off on his fingers, and ran out of fingers before he ran out of night. ¶ “Eight, the full room, and one stands at the stand like a traffic policeman in a tailcoat. Benny the pawnbroker’s runner was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Russo and Dr. Hirsch telling the room about her window. Nobody else. Nine, Miss Lowenthal and Dr. Hirsch, still telling it. Nobody else at all. Ten, just Benny. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Benny, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “Under the coat,” I said. “What was it?” ¶ “Something small. I didn’t see what.” ¶ Whatever went out of the Hirsch flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Benny. At ten, when it counted, Demos had Benny. ¶ Seating a man who would rather have stood: that was the last I saw of him.

The flats over Lipsky’s were only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. A cab sat at the curb with its engine running and its driver asleep, waiting for somebody who wasn’t coming out in this. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s were waking from the top down, a light on the fifth floor, then the fourth. In the street the first pushcart man was already untying his tarpaulin. In the cloth shop’s window a dressmaker’s dummy wore a hat it had been wearing since spring, and wore it well. The janitor knocks his pipe out on the stoop rail so often the rail has a dent in it the shape of the bowl. ¶ Wojcik was sitting on the cellar steps with his pipe. He had a ring of keys on a bootlace round his neck, worn under his undershirt where nobody can borrow them. Miss Lowenthal was correcting an exercise book in red pencil. Teitel was eating a baked potato from a street stove. ¶ Russo had said he was here at nine. Demos’s list had Miss Lowenthal at Steinmetz’s at nine. That settled where I was going. From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe from supper till bed, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ I wiped my feet, because somebody in that house would notice if I didn’t.

Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants. The landlady’s bill was folded under the telephone. I’d see it every time the thing didn’t ring. I decided not to open it until it did. ¶ Somebody was coming up. At this hour it’s either trouble or a client, and in my experience they climb at the same speed. My visitor came in unhurried, as if the hour happened to other people. ¶ “Somebody has taken a pearl brooch,” Doyle said. “It was in the dish on the dresser. It isn’t.” ¶ I offered him the chair and turned the lamp away from him. ¶ “I sat in Sokol’s from eight until ten,” he said, “telling anybody who’d listen that I was off to my sister’s for the night, and the key was under the mat.” ¶ “And when did the brooch go?” ¶ He had worked it out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “The boy from the delicatessen came up with an order at a quarter past ten and passed somebody on the dark stairs, going down in a hurry.” ¶ “Who’d want to take it?” ¶ “You might ask about Teitel,” he said. “He has had my money since Easter, and asked me for more on Friday. That’s from the woman downstairs, and she hears most things.” ¶ Doyle said the next part to the desk rather than to me. “Mrs. Krantz, the rent collector, says the brooch was promised to her, back in my courting days. And Lieb, the pawnbroker’s clerk, hasn’t forgotten what my family did to Amato, his friend.” ¶ He took a breath, the way people do before the part they’d rather not say. “Belkin, the leading man, owes Wexler money, and he has started asking for it.” ¶ He put ten dollars on the desk and smoothed it flat with his palm. “Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

I went over Doyle’s parlor from the door to the far wall, slowly. ¶ Doyle stood in the hall with his hands in his pockets, so as not to touch anything, which was more than whoever came before me had managed. ¶ The dish on the dresser was empty. The key was back under the mat, and there wasn’t a mark on the door. Whoever it was had known exactly where to look. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Doyle at Sokol’s between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made Sokol’s the place to start counting. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Sokol. He was counting glasses onto a towel. ¶ “I need the whole night,” I said. “Everybody who was here, hour by hour, and anybody you didn’t know.” Sokol went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Eight’s the regulars. I pour before they ask. It saves them the strain. Fishel the bookmaker was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Teitel, Mrs. Krantz and Mr. Doyle telling the room about his key. Nobody else. Nine, Mrs. Krantz, Lieb and Mr. Doyle, still telling it. Nobody else at all. Ten, Mrs. Krantz and Belkin. Nobody else, that hour. Eleven, Teitel, Mrs. Krantz and Belkin. Nobody else. If there was, there’s a glass I can’t account for, and there isn’t. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Fishel, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “What was it?” I said. “Under the coat.” ¶ “Something small. I didn’t see what.” ¶ Teitel and Mrs. Krantz heard about the key at eight, and Lieb at nine. Belkin never heard Doyle tell the room. That put Mrs. Krantz and Belkin here at ten, by his count. Whatever went out of the Doyle flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Fishel. ¶ Slicing rye for a free lunch nobody eats: that was the last I saw of him.

The undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock was a couple of blocks east. The fog was still at the end of whatever street I was on. It followed me better than I follow people. ¶ I found the undertaker’s cellar, through the coal hole at the Peacock. It was the kind of place people go to so they can say they were somewhere else. There was a coffin on display in the undertaker’s window beside the stair, lid up, with the price folded on the pillow. ¶ Lieb was on a hard chair by the wall, turning his hat round and round in his hands. Lieb had a silk scarf with somebody else’s monogram on it, worn with the monogram tucked in. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Lieb had told me Sokol’s at ten, and Sokol’s list said otherwise. I wanted to hear what he would say to that. I turned back to him with my notebook open, which is never good news for anybody. ¶ “Let me read you something back,” I said. “You told me Sokol’s at ten. Sokol had Mrs. Krantz, Belkin and Fishel at Sokol’s at ten o’clock, and nobody else.” ¶ He rubbed his face with both hands and came out from behind them looking a little older. “Look, don’t tell my uncle. Here’s the honest version. It’s shorter. I wasn’t at Sokol’s. I was at the undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock, with Miss Nowak. Ask her.” ¶ That was a hole in Lieb’s story, all right. I wasn’t sure yet it was the one I was looking for. An owned-up story is only as good as whoever’s in it with you. If it held, he had been at the undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock at ten, not at Sokol’s. ¶ It turned out Miss Nowak had come back in and was in the corner, out of the light.

The flats over Lipsky’s were a couple of blocks east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The flats over Lipsky’s were waking from the top down, a light on the fifth floor, then the fourth. In the street the first pushcart man was already untying his tarpaulin. In the cloth shop’s window a dressmaker’s dummy wore a hat it had been wearing since spring, and wore it well. There was a tin of rat poison on the cellar shelf, with a skull on the label and a coffee ring on the skull. ¶ Wojcik was answering the fourth floor by banging a pipe with a wrench. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe from supper till bed, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ There was the boiler in the cellar, which the janitor speaks of as a difficult woman, and which knocks on the pipes whenever her name comes up.

I sat on a hard chair in the hall with the form on my knee. A name wants a line under it, and a line wants somebody’s word under that. I went down the form one line at a time. ¶ The office telephone never had rung tonight. It hadn’t needed to. The trouble had taken the stairs.

Russo’s place lay a few blocks east. My knees had the temperature a block before any thermometer did. They’ve had more practice. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There was a gas ring in every kitchen, and on the third floor a smell of gas the tenants have been mentioning to each other since spring. ¶ Russo was in the chair with his head to one side, like a man dozing over the evening paper, except that nobody dozes that still. He had a fresh deck in his breast pocket, still in its band, and his green eyeshade in his hand. ¶ My client, Mrs. Krantz, had beaten me there and stood just inside the door, gloves in her hand. ¶ Nobody minded who came and went. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I wanted to read them properly. I went through Russo’s papers, one folder at a time. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge against him, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and he’d written every one down. ¶ Miss Lowenthal: an IOU from her friend, with her name pencilled beside it. Mrs. Greco: a copy of the family will, with her name underlined. Dr. Hirsch: an IOU in her hand, and a note of what was still owing. Mrs. Sobel: a note about her and Sokol’s, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from the flats over Lipsky’s and the rat poison. ¶ The one to ask was the doorkeeper at the Peacock, who’d been there all night. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Szabo. She saw me coming before I’d decided to come. That’s the job. ¶ I asked Mrs. Szabo who she’d seen come and go since the evening started. She answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Dr. Hirsch, Mrs. Greco and Russo. Nobody else. Eight, Mrs. Greco, Mrs. Sobel and Russo. Nobody else at all. Nine, Mrs. Greco and Russo. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Miss Lowenthal and Mrs. Greco. Nobody else. I’d remember. I don’t like enough faces to forget any.” ¶ Mrs. Greco hadn’t been at the flats over Lipsky’s while it was there to take. That put Miss Lowenthal and Mrs. Greco here at ten, by her count. Mrs. Krantz had said nine or ten. Russo was at the Peacock at nine, alive. ¶ The janitor at the flats over Lipsky’s would know who’d been in. ¶ Eating a pickle out of a paper bag on her stool: that was the last I saw of her.

Wojcik was shoveling coal into the boiler. “Who was in tonight?” I said. “All of them, hour by hour, and who you didn’t know.” ¶ He counted it off on his fingers, and ran out of fingers before he ran out of night. ¶ “Seven, I bank the boiler for the night. She sulks. Then she settles. Seven o’clock, Miss Lowenthal and Mrs. Sobel. Nobody else. Eight, Dr. Hirsch and Miss Lowenthal. Nobody else at all. Nine, Miss Lowenthal and Mrs. Sobel. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, nobody. The rat poison on the cellar shelf was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Dr. Hirsch, Miss Lowenthal and Mrs. Sobel had been here earlier, when the rat poison was there for the taking. At ten, when it counted, Wojcik had nobody. ¶ Sweeping a stoop he had swept an hour ago: that was the last I saw of him.

The back room at Wexler’s was a couple of blocks west, and I took it at a good clip. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The back room among the unredeemed coats at Wexler’s didn’t have a sign, which was the sign. Somebody let me in and then looked at me as if they’d made a mistake. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Dr. Hirsch was in the corner with a cup of coffee, holding it in both hands for the warmth. She had steel-rimmed spectacles that she looks over, not through, when she doesn’t believe you. ¶ Wojcik’s list had Dr. Hirsch at the flats over Lipsky’s at eight, and that was worth the walk. Nobody kept watch there. It wasn’t that kind of place. ¶ The room had been arranged so that nobody in it was ever quite facing anybody else.

Dr. Hirsch had told me the Peacock at ten, and Mrs. Szabo’s list said otherwise. I wanted to hear what she made of the pair of them. She saw the notebook in my hand and knew what it meant before I opened my mouth. ¶ I looked at her over the notebook. “You said the Peacock at ten. Mrs. Szabo had Miss Lowenthal and Mrs. Greco at the Peacock at ten o’clock, and nobody else.” ¶ She let out a breath she’d been keeping since I sat down. “I suppose it’s better out than in. That’s what I tell everybody. I wasn’t at the Peacock. I was at the back room at Wexler’s, with Miss Nowak. Ask her.” ¶ That was a hole in Dr. Hirsch’s story, all right. I wasn’t sure yet it was the one I was looking for. An owned-up story is only as good as whoever’s in it with you. If it held, she had been at the back room at Wexler’s at ten, not at the Peacock. ¶ It turned out Miss Nowak was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ The tin sign on the wall had outlasted the company and would outlast me.

I sat at the end of the table with the form, where the light was worst. It was my name at the bottom, so it had better be my reasons above it. ¶ The office radiator always knows when there’s money about. It would be knocking till morning, pleased with itself.

Getting to Russo’s place meant a few blocks east. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There were marble stairs to the second floor and plain wood after that, where the builder ran out of marble or interest. ¶ Russo was in his chair, sitting very still, the way nobody living ever sits for long. He had a fresh deck in his breast pocket, still in its band, and his green eyeshade in his hand. ¶ Lieb was there, with a cup of something he hadn’t touched and his coat still buttoned. ¶ Nobody kept watch there. It wasn’t that kind of place. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I stood in the doorway a while before I went in. Rooms like that don’t like to be rushed.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. I went through his papers with the lamp pulled close, the way you read a will you aren’t in. ¶ He had a page on everybody who held something against him, typed and clipped together, and every page said what the grudge was. He’d kept them square, so that nobody got top billing. ¶ Teitel: a note about him and the card room over Feingold’s garage, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. Dr. Hirsch: an IOU in her hand, and a note of what was still owing. Miss Lowenthal: an IOU from her friend, with her name pencilled beside it. Mrs. Greco: a copy of the family will, with her name underlined. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from the flats over Lipsky’s and the rat poison. ¶ I dusted off my knees. They’d done more work tonight than the rest of me.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Pinsky. ¶ There were sunflower-seed shells in the gallery aisles, swept up every night and back by the second act. “You’ve been here all night,” I said. “Who came in, and when?” ¶ Pinsky went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Seven, I open the doors and take up the chart. Every seat sold, a cross. I’m very good at crosses. Seven o’clock, nobody. Eight, Miss Lowenthal. Nobody else at all. Nine, Mrs. Greco and Russo. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Dr. Hirsch and Teitel. And nobody else. Every cross on the chart has a face, and I’ve given you every face.” ¶ That put Dr. Hirsch and Teitel here at ten, by his count. Lieb had said nine or ten. Russo was at the Lyric at nine, alive. ¶ Pointing his flashlight at a man who was talking: that was the last I saw of him.

I headed east for the flats over Lipsky’s, a few blocks away. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ The tenement over Lipsky’s was dark from the stoop to the roof, except one kitchen on the third floor where somebody was ironing a shirt for the morning. The shop window below had a card in it, EVERYTHING MUST GO, which had been saying so since the war. There was the roof door at the top of the stairs, propped open with a brick summer and winter, because nobody has told the brick it’s winter. ¶ Wojcik was sweeping a stoop he had swept an hour ago. He had a ring of keys on a bootlace round his neck, worn under his undershirt where nobody can borrow them. ¶ Dr. Hirsch had said she was here at nine. It was reason enough to look. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe from supper till bed, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

I walked downtown to Mrs. Greco’s flat. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ The milkman had been to the Excelsior and left a bottle outside every door on every floor, and nobody in the building had seen him come or go. That’s the kind of building it is: no doorman, no janitor in sight, and a landlord who lives uptown and sends a man on the first of the month. There was a wooden wedge holding the front door open an inch for whichever tenant has lost his key this week. ¶ Mrs. Greco was scrubbing a pot as if it had insulted her. She had a gold crucifix on a chain, and a burn on the inside of her wrist the shape of a ladle’s rim. ¶ Wojcik’s list had Mrs. Greco at the flats over Lipsky’s at eight. That settled where I was going. It was the kind of place nobody kept an eye on. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

A fair few blocks uptown and west, and I was at the undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ The undertaker’s cellar, through the coal hole at the Peacock, didn’t have a sign, which was the sign. Somebody let me in and then looked at me as if they’d made a mistake. There was a coffin on display in the undertaker’s window beside the stair, lid up, with the price folded on the pillow. ¶ Miss Lowenthal was on a hard chair by the wall, turning her hat round and round in her hands. She had long fingers that tap out scales on whatever’s in front of them: a table, a banister, your sleeve. ¶ Wojcik’s list had Miss Lowenthal at the flats over Lipsky’s at seven. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. There was nobody on duty, and nobody to ask who had been by. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Miss Lowenthal had told me home at ten, and Wojcik’s list said otherwise. That wanted putting to her before it went any further. I took the chair beside her without asking. I’d stopped being company. ¶ “You told me home at ten,” I said to her. “Wojcik had nobody at the flats over Lipsky’s at ten o’clock.” ¶ She looked round to see who was listening, and lowered her voice. “Since we are being honest, and apparently we are, I shall play it as written. I wasn’t at the flats over Lipsky’s. I was at the undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock, with Mrs. Krantz. Ask her.” ¶ That was a hole in Miss Lowenthal’s story, all right. I wasn’t sure yet it was the one I was looking for. An owned-up story is only as good as whoever’s in it with you. If it held, she had been at the undertaker’s cellar at the Peacock at ten, not home. ¶ It turned out Mrs. Krantz was in the corner, out of the light.

I pulled up a chair nobody else wanted and took out the form. I read the night back to myself, from the office to here, and started at the top of the form. ¶ The coffee on my desk would have gone the rest of the way cold by now. I’d finish it anyway. I’d started it, and I’m a professional.

I headed east for Doyle’s place, a few blocks away. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There was a gas ring in every kitchen, and on the third floor a smell of gas the tenants have been mentioning to each other since spring. ¶ Doyle was where they’d found him, in the chair by the table, as if he’d sat down to wait for something and it had come. He had a carnation in his buttonhole and his little black book in his waistcoat, the rubber band still round it. ¶ Lieb was there ahead of me, hat in his hands, turning the brim. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ If it happened at eight or nine, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I kept my hands in my pockets for the first minute. A room should be looked at before it’s touched.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. His papers were in a box under the bed, the kind of box a man keeps for the things he’d rather not file. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge against him, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and he’d written every one down. ¶ Miss Lowenthal: a note about her and the Peacock, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. Mrs. Krantz: a bundle of her letters, tied with string and never given back. Teitel: an IOU in his hand, and a note of what was still owing. Mabry: an IOU from his friend, with his name pencilled beside it. Amato: a complaint he’d made against him, in triplicate. ¶ A reason is the easy half. Everybody in Doyle’s box had one. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Amato. ¶ I found him at the far end, where the light gave up, and stood where he could see me without having to want to. “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” ¶ He thought for a second, the way anybody does, and started at the beginning. ¶ “My night? I’ll give it to you like a fare: the long way, and you don’t argue with the meter. At seven I went to Rafferty’s to help write letters home, and stayed through eight. Eight, I eat. Most men eat sitting at a table. I’m not most men. Mrs. Krantz, Mabry and Teitel were there at seven; Mabry and Teitel were there at eight. Nine o’clock I went round to the bakery cellar at Sokol’s to see a man about a horse, and stayed the rest of the evening, with Fishel.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Amato said the bakery cellar at Sokol’s. I put it with the rest and didn’t argue with it yet. ¶ It turned out Fishel was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ I wrote it down, word for word. I’m a fast writer when people talk slowly.

I set off east for Rafferty’s. It was a couple of blocks. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ The milk wagon was two streets off and I could hear every bottle on it, which tells you how quiet the rooming house had got. The hall smelled of soda bread and floor polish; the landlady polishes before she sleeps, so the morning finds it done. Every door upstairs had a brass number on it, and every number shone. There was a row of umbrella hooks in the hall, each with a lodger’s name inked over it, and one with no name that nobody will explain. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was writing in the rent book in pencil and going over it in ink. She had reading glasses pushed up into her gray hair, where she forgets them, and finds them, and forgets them again. Mabry, in a sailor’s pea coat, was eating pie at four in the morning. Miss Lowenthal, in a green hat, was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. ¶ Amato had said he was here at seven and eight, and that Mabry was with him here at eight, and that was worth the walk. ¶ From her post Mrs. Rafferty could see the front door, the stairs and every landing to the top. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

I walked downtown and east to Mrs. Krantz’s flat. It was a fair few blocks, and I took all of it. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ Rain on East Houston Street, which is wide enough to rain on properly. The lobby of the Excelsior had a rubber mat inside the door and a sign above it asking tenants please to use it, with the please underlined twice, which tells you how that was going. There was a dumbwaiter in the back hall for coal and parcels, with a bell on every floor that nobody answers. ¶ Mrs. Krantz, with a cane, was looking at a banister as if it owed her money. She had a pince-nez on a black ribbon, which she puts on to read a rent book and takes off to read a face. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty’s list had Mrs. Krantz at Rafferty’s at seven. That settled where I was going. ¶ It was the kind of place nobody kept an eye on. ¶ The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

The Lyric was a few blocks uptown and west, and I took it at a good clip. The rain was letting up as the sky went gray, as if it had only come out to keep the night company. ¶ The Lyric had emptied as far as a theater ever empties, which isn’t far: programs on the seats, somebody’s glove, a bag of sunflower seeds spilled in the twelfth row. Up in the ventilator over the gallery, the pigeons were rehearsing. There was the usher’s flashlight, pointed at the floor and never at a face, unless the face is talking. ¶ Pinsky was marking crosses on his seating chart. He had a white mustache waxed to points so fine they quiver when he disapproves. Teitel, in a camel coat, was in the back row with a bag of peanuts, shelling them one at a time and not eating them. ¶ Doyle had been here earlier in the evening. Mrs. Krantz had said Teitel was with her at her place at nine. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “I seat by the chart. Every seat sold is a cross, every cross has a face, and I could draw you the face.” ¶ The seats were all turned the same way, waiting for something, and I knew how they felt.

Pinsky’s list had Teitel here at ten. That was reason enough to ask. ¶ I sat one seat over. He had a necktie of his own so loud it seems to be shouting for the others. I asked him to tell me his evening, from the beginning, and not to leave out the dull parts. ¶ He put down what he was holding and gave me his attention. ¶ “For you, a special price: the whole evening, free. Nobody gets that from Teitel. Listen. At seven I went up to Rafferty’s to pay a call, and stayed through eight. Seven, I count the day. It never takes long. Amato, Mrs. Krantz and Mabry were there at seven; Amato and Mabry were there at eight. At nine I went round to Mrs. Krantz’s for a game of gin. Ten o’clock I went to the second show at the Lyric, by myself.” ¶ For nine, the hour that mattered, Teitel said Mrs. Krantz’s flat. I wrote it down and left it standing, for now. ¶ There was the daughter’s death scene in the third act, eleven minutes long, which the usher mouths along with from the back of the house, every word. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. Lieb had said eight or nine o’clock. The chloral had come from Rafferty’s. I had evenings from Amato, Fishel, Mrs. Krantz and Teitel, and lists from Mrs. Rafferty and Pinsky. I didn’t have Mabry’s or Miss Lowenthal’s evenings yet. ¶ That was the night so far: a lot of people who were somewhere, and one hour nobody wanted to talk about.

Midnight. I was in the office on Mulberry Street with my feet on the desk and the radio turned down low. The rent was two weeks late, and the landlady had stopped knocking about it, which was worse. Outside the window the night was clear, the street lamps sharp as far as the corner. ¶ Somebody knocked twice, politely, and then a third time, less politely. My visitor came in unhurried, as if the hour happened to other people. ¶ “My name is Ida Rosenbaum,” she said. “I’m Booker Mosley’s business partner. He’s dead.” ¶ Mosley was a moneylender. At half past eleven, Margolis, who’d come round to collect a debt, found him in his own walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street. The police had a look and called it his heart. ¶ I offered my client the chair. She looked at it the way you’d look at a dog that might bite, and sat anyway. ¶ “When did he die?” ¶ “The police can call it what they like,” she said. “The woman across the hall heard him laughing with somebody all through the Eveready Hour, which runs from ten o’clock. The coroner says laudanum, taken then; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “He was at the Kit Kat earlier in the evening,” she said. “His usual. He liked his usual.” ¶ “Who had a reason?” ¶ “Ask about Schilling,” Rosenbaum said. “He knew where he was in 1921. I had that from the woman downstairs.” ¶ She opened her bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

I went over the table. ¶ Rosenbaum watched from the landing with her coat buttoned to the neck, as if the cold were in the room. ¶ A cup of cocoa sat on the table, gone cold and bitter at the bottom. Beside it was a brown bottle with a druggist’s label made out to the Delmonico rooms. Somebody had made Mosley cocoa, which is a kind thing to do, and then made sure it was the last. ¶ So the laudanum came from the Delmonico rooms, and laudanum takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Mosley had been at the Delmonico rooms earlier, to get it. ¶ Schilling could tell me his own evening, and he was at the Kit Kat. ¶ That was all the room had to tell me, and it had told it without being asked twice.

The Delmonico rooms were a few blocks downtown and west, near enough for anybody to walk it there and back inside the hour. I made a note of that. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. A framed sign in the hall said that baths were on Saturdays and the hot water was by arrangement. ¶ Mrs. Broadnax had the parlor door open and the parlor lamp on, so that nothing in the hall could happen without an audience. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Stannard was at the sink with his sleeves rolled up, and dried his hands slowly before he turned round. ¶ The laudanum had come from here. That was reason enough for the walk. A landlady who sits on her stairs knows who used them. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

A few blocks downtown and west, and I was at the Delmonico rooms. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. The street was empty and clear and very quiet, and my heels were the loudest thing on it. ¶ The Delmonico rooms again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Mrs. Broadnax sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. Stannard was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. ¶ The laudanum had come from here. That was reason enough. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

The Kit Kat was a fair few blocks uptown and west. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went up the outside stair to the Kit Kat, a speakeasy over a garage. The garage underneath was shut for the night, but the room still smelled of motor oil under the perfume and the cigarettes. A row of paper lanterns was strung across the room, faded from red to pink by years of smoke. ¶ Donnelly was on a chair tipped back against the door frame, chewing a toothpick down to splinters. Heavy in the coat and light on her feet, she had the door swung wide before I’d reached for it, and shut again before I’d decided anything. Margolis sat at the end of the long bench by the wall, with a glass of ginger ale and a very straight back. Schilling was at the bar with his back to the room, watching the room in the mirror. ¶ Mosley had been here earlier in the evening. It was reason enough to look. ¶ Everybody who came in tonight had to get past Donnelly first, and she has the kind of face that remembers who tried. ¶ I found a place at the bar and let the room settle around me.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, downtown and west to the Delmonico rooms, a few blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Back at the Delmonico rooms, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ Mrs. Broadnax sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. Stannard was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into his collar. ¶ The laudanum had come from here, and that was worth the walk. ¶ I read the sign about the bath again. Saturday seemed a long way off.

Midnight. The office on Mulberry Street had one lamp, one chair worth sitting in and one detective, and the detective was in the worst repair of the three. I had money in the desk drawer for once. I’d opened the drawer twice to make sure, and once more just to visit. ¶ There was a knock, and then the door opened before I’d said anything, which is how people knock when they’ve made up their minds. My visitor knocked twice and waited to be asked in, as if somebody’s mother was listening. ¶ “My name is Rocco Tramonti,” he said. “I’m Michael Quill’s business partner. He’s dead.” ¶ Quill was an alderman’s clerk. At half past eleven, Kreuzer, who heard his radio still going and knocked, found him in his own two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street. The police had a look and called it his heart. ¶ I offered my client the chair. He looked at it the way you’d look at a dog that might bite, and sat anyway. ¶ “When was this?” ¶ “Here’s what they don’t want to hear,” he said. “He telephoned me at nine o’clock, cheerful, to say he had company. The coroner says chloral, taken then; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “He’d been at Hanley’s earlier in the evening,” my client said. “His usual.” ¶ “Who didn’t like him?” ¶ “Bidwell swore at him in the street on Monday, in front of the fruit man,” my client said. “I’d start there. He threw her out of a lease.” ¶ “The police have their answer,” Tramonti said, and put fifty dollars on my desk. “I want the right one.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

I bent over the table and took it a piece at a time, from one edge to the other. ¶ Tramonti didn’t come in. I didn’t ask him to. ¶ There were two glasses on the table, and one of them smelled sweet and chemical. Under the table was an empty bottle with a Weiss’s pharmacy label, the kind that comes off the dispensary shelf. ¶ So the chloral came from Weiss’s pharmacy, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Quill had been at Weiss’s pharmacy earlier, to get it. ¶ Somebody at Hanley’s would have kept count of faces, and that would be the bartender. ¶ The little swing in the empty birdcage moved when the door went. That was all that moved.

It was a couple of blocks to Sokol’s back room, uptown and east. The doorways along here were full of people waiting out the rain. Nobody offered to share. ¶ I went round to the back of Sokol’s bakery on Rivington Street, where the numbers are taken. It was warm from the ovens, with sacks of flour along one wall and a table by the other where a nickel bet on a three-figure number bought you a reason to get up tomorrow. A wooden chair with one short leg stood by the wall, and rocked whenever anything touched it. ¶ Kreuzer looked up when I came in, and then looked as if he wished he hadn’t. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, he wore clothes too good to have been bought. He’d made every stitch. ¶ Kreuzer had found Quill. That was reason enough. ¶ Nobody there was paid to keep track of anybody. ¶ It was the sort of room people say they were never in. I made a note that I was.

Quill’s place was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down.
