Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ Quill’s place looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Tramonti was there, with a cup of something he hadn’t touched and his coat still buttoned. ¶ The night had started here, with Quill, and I wanted to see it again with what I knew now. ¶ I wiped my feet, because somebody in that house would notice if I didn’t.

Quill’s place was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. The rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ Back at Quill’s place, I had my hands in my pockets and my questions in order. ¶ Tramonti, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ This was where Quill had died. Everything else would be somebody’s story, and the room wouldn’t. ¶ I took it all in, which didn’t take long, and then took it in again.

I found a chair at Sokol’s back room and sat down with the form. A name wants a line under it, and a line wants somebody’s word under that. I went down the form one line at a time. ¶ The new money would go in the desk drawer with the old. The drawer had never had company before.

I walked east to Doyle’s place. It was a couple of blocks, and I took all of it. The fog had swallowed the far end of the street and was in no hurry to give it back. ¶ I went up to Doyle’s two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street. The bakery downstairs had its ovens going, and the warm smell of bread came up through the floorboards, which didn’t seem right, and wasn’t anybody’s fault. A coal merchant’s calendar hung by the stove, still turned to last month. ¶ Doyle was on the floor on his back, with one arm flung out and his eyes on the ceiling. ¶ Petrosino, my client, had beaten me there and was waiting on the landing, with her coat on and her hands in her pockets. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶ If it happened at ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. I went through Doyle’s papers, one folder at a time. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge against him, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and he’d written every one down. ¶ Mosley: a notice to quit, from when he threw her out of a lease. Kessler: the lease on a shop, the rent owing, and a carbon of his letter calling it in. Grasso: one line, where she was in 1921, and an address. Mulcahy: a column of payments, every month for years, and his name at the top. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Rafferty’s and the revolver. ¶ The usher at the Orpheum sees every face that comes through the door. I wanted all of them. ¶ The calendar went on saying last month. In that room, it might as well.

A couple of blocks downtown and east, and I was at the Orpheum. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ I went in at the Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight. The last show had let out, the screen was a big gray blank, and the rows were full of peanut shells and dropped programs. A big brass ashtray full of sand stood by the inner doors, with a neat pattern raked into the sand. ¶ Weisglass was in the lobby, counting the evening’s ticket stubs into bundles and putting a rubber band round each one. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. Kessler was in the lobby, reading the bills for next week as if they might change. Grasso sat in the back row with her hat on her knee, watching the picture without looking at it. ¶ Doyle had been here earlier in the evening. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Weisglass. ¶ I put my cigarette out in the brass ashtray and spoiled the pattern. It was that kind of night.

Grasso had found Doyle. I knew a little of her evening and nothing of her reasons, and I wanted both. I sat one seat over. ¶ I said his name and watched what her face did with it. She took a long moment over it, the way anybody does who knows the answer will be written down. ¶ “Doyle knew where I was in 1921,” she said. “I’ve spent a lot of years making sure nobody else does, so you’ll understand if I stop there.” ¶ That was Grasso’s reason, in her own words. Petrosino hadn’t mentioned it. A reason isn’t an hour, though. For ten, she had told me the Orpheum at ten. ¶ The sand in the brass ashtray had been raked smooth again. Order gets kept where it can be.

A fair few blocks uptown and west, and I was at Rafferty’s. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ I went back to Rafferty’s, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. Mosley was at the sink with her sleeves rolled up, and dried her hands slowly before she turned round. ¶ Grasso had said she was here at seven, eight and nine, and that Mosley was with her at her place at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

It was a fair few blocks to Rafferty’s, uptown and west. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The fog was going gray at the top, which was how I knew the morning had started without me. ¶ Rafferty’s again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty had the parlor door open and the parlor lamp on, so that nothing in the hall could happen without an audience. Mosley answered the door in her stocking feet, with the lamp behind her. ¶ Grasso had said she was here at seven, eight and nine, and that Mosley was with her at her place at eight. That settled where I was going. ¶ The red lamp under the holy picture was still burning, for whoever needed it most.

The Orpheum lay a couple of blocks downtown and east. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The Orpheum looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Weisglass was by the inner doors, sorting a stack of programs into the ones that could be used again and the ones that couldn’t. Kessler was in the back row with a bag of peanuts, shelling them one at a time and not eating them. Grasso was sitting near the front, very upright, with both hands on the back of the seat in front. ¶ Mosley had said she was here at seven. Grasso had said Kessler was with her here at ten. It was reason enough to look. ¶ My own hat had been reshaped by a few nights too. Not hot ones.

I asked for the use of a table and got one, and took out the form. It was my name at the bottom, so it had better be my reasons above it. ¶ My head was still keeping time with the clock over the office safe, a little behind and a lot louder.

Carbone’s place was a few blocks east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ I went up to Carbone’s flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street. By the top floor I had a stitch in my side and an opinion about stairs, and the opinion was not kind. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Carbone was face down by the door, where he’d turned his back on somebody. It’s the one thing in this city you never do. ¶ Brennan, my client, had beaten me there and was waiting on the landing, with his coat on and his hands in his pockets. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. I went through Carbone’s papers, one folder at a time. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge against him, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and he’d written every one down. ¶ Hauck: an IOU for four hundred dollars, in her hand. Hurwitz: a wedding invitation nobody ever used; he jilted her sister a week before the wedding. Abramowitz: the order that closed her business, with his signature on it. Lathrop: one line, where she was in 1921, and an address. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Mrs. Nagy’s and the carving knife. ¶ Somebody at the Velvet Room would have kept count of faces, and that would be the bartender. ¶ The empty birdcage hung in its corner. It had been empty a long time and was used to it.

The Velvet Room lay a good walk downtown and west. The cold was still out there doing its rounds. It’s the only thing in this city that works all night for nothing. ¶ I went down to the Velvet Room, six steps down under a hat shop. Upstairs the hat shop had gone dark, and down here the lamps were low and the talk was lower, the way it gets after midnight when the loud things have all been said. A brass spittoon stood at the foot of the bar, polished brighter than anything else in the room. ¶ Ruggiero was behind the bar with both hands spread on it, the way somebody stands who has been standing since the afternoon and has opinions about it. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Hauck was on a stool with her hat pushed back, turning a coin over and over on the bar. Lathrop sat at a little table by the wall, with a beer going flat in front of her. Abramowitz had a stool at the end of the bar and was looking at the mirror behind it, which looked back. ¶ Carbone had been here earlier in the evening. It was reason enough to look. ¶ Nobody gets a drink in a place like that without the one who pours it looking at them, and Ruggiero looks at everybody twice. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Lathrop was in the room, and I hadn’t heard from her yet, so I started there. ¶ I got as near to her as manners allowed and said my name. I asked her where she’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ She counted back through the evening under her breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “I was at the Velvet Room at seven, with Hauck and Carbone. Come eight, I went up to Mrs. Nagy’s to see about some money owed, with Abramowitz. Around nine I went up to the card room to do the books. At ten I wanted company, so I went to the Velvet Room. At nine and ten I was on my own.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Lathrop said the card room at nine and the Velvet Room at ten. I took it down the way it was given. ¶ Ruggiero would have seen everybody who came in. ¶ The spittoon still shone at the foot of the bar. That room had its priorities.

It was a couple of blocks to the card room, uptown and east. A night watchman stood over a fire in a barrel, warming one hand and then the other, like a man counting money. ¶ The card room over the Bowery garage had no sign and no name on the door, only a light under it. A gambling room doesn’t advertise. The people who need it always find it. A bare bulb hung on a cord, swinging a little whenever the door shut. ¶ Callahan sat by the door with the cash box, and nobody went near the table without going near her. Hands clasped in front, weight back on her heels, she stood as though poured there and left to set. ¶ Lathrop had said she was here at nine. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Whoever runs a game knows who sat down at it, and what they lost, too, but that wasn’t my business tonight. ¶ There was one light, and everybody had arranged to be just outside it.

From there to the card room was a couple of blocks. A coal cart was making its first round, and the man on it had a scarf wound up to his eyes and no intention of talking. ¶ The card room again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Callahan was shuffling a deck with one hand, not to play, just to keep the hand busy. ¶ Lathrop had said she was here at nine. That settled where I was going. ¶ Whatever had been poured there had set by then. I walked round it.

Getting to Mrs. Nagy’s meant a fair few blocks uptown and east. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ Mrs. Nagy’s looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Mrs. Nagy sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. Hurwitz answered the door in her stocking feet, with the lamp behind her. ¶ Lathrop had said she was here at eight. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

It was a fair few blocks from there to Ashby’s place, east, with my collar up. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ I climbed to Ashby’s walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street. The drugstore below was dark, and the only sound in the building was the stair under my feet. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Ashby sat in his chair with his hands in his lap. If you didn’t know, you’d have said he was asleep, and lowered your voice. ¶ Corrigan was there ahead of me, hat in her hands, turning the brim. ¶ No clerk, no doorman, nobody watching the stairs: nobody saw who came. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I took my hat off. It seemed like the thing to do.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. His papers were in a box under the bed, the kind of box a man keeps for the things he’d rather not file. ¶ He had a page on everybody who held something against him, typed and clipped together, and every page said what the grudge was. He’d kept them square, so that nobody got top billing. ¶ Tillman: a notice to quit, from when he threw him out of a lease. Cheatham: the order that closed his business, with his signature on it. Hurwitz: a court transcript, his own testimony against his brother. Quill: a file he’d kept on him, thick enough to matter. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Cheatham’s surgery and the chloral. ¶ I didn’t touch the empty birdcage. Some things in a room are only there to be sad.

Ashby’s place was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Ashby’s place again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Corrigan, my client, had beaten me there and was waiting on the landing, with her coat on and her hands in her pockets. ¶ Ashby had died here, and a room like that is worth a second look. ¶ The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

The Orpheum was a fair few blocks uptown and west, and I took it at a good clip. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ I went in at the Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight. The last show had let out, the screen was a big gray blank, and the rows were full of peanut shells and dropped programs. Above the lobby doors a painted plaster mask grinned down at everybody who came in, with the tip of its nose missing. ¶ Schilling was by the inner doors, sorting a stack of programs into the ones that could be used again and the ones that couldn’t. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. Cheatham sat in the back row with his hat on his knee, watching the picture without looking at it. Quill sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with his coat folded on his knees. ¶ Cheatham had found Ashby. That was reason enough for the walk. An usher with a flashlight sees every face that comes in out of the street, and most of them twice. ¶ Somebody had left a program on a seat. I didn’t read it. I had enough people to keep track of.

Tillman’s flat was a fair few blocks uptown and east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The street was empty and clear and very quiet, and my heels were the loudest thing on it. ¶ Tillman’s flat on Pitt Street was two rooms and a kitchen at the top of the stairs, behind a doormat that had given up saying welcome years ago. A gramophone with a big tin horn stood in the corner, with a record still on it. ¶ Tillman was at the sink with his sleeves rolled up, and dried his hands slowly before he turned round. He was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until he needed one, and then only the one. ¶ Quill had passed Tillman on Grand Street at ten. That was reason enough. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Tillman’s flat lay a fair few blocks uptown and east. The sky had gone gray along the bottom edge, and a milk wagon was working the next block. ¶ Tillman’s flat looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Tillman was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. ¶ Quill had passed Tillman on Grand Street at ten. It was reason enough to look. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully.

I set off downtown and west for Cheatham’s surgery. It was a few blocks. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ I went back to Cheatham’s surgery, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Mulcahy was at the front desk, writing tomorrow’s appointments into a book in very neat ink. ¶ The chloral had come from here. That settled where I was going. ¶ The crossed-off calendar behind the counter looked at me like a bill.

I took the form out and smoothed it flat on my knee. It was my name at the bottom, so it had better be my reasons above it. ¶ The quiet in my building would have moved back in the minute I left. It never did like company.

Salerno’s place lay a couple of blocks east. My shoes had let the rain in two blocks back, and now they were just carrying it around for me. ¶ Salerno’s two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street were up a stair the police had worn a path in tonight. The door was shut and the light was on, the way they leave things. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Salerno was on the floor in the middle of the room. A man looks smaller on the floor than he ever did standing up. ¶ Wehrle had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶ If it happened at eight or nine, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I wanted to read them properly. Salerno kept his papers in a box file, and I sat down with it under the lamp. ¶ The papers held a page on everybody who had it in for him, kept like a doctor’s files, one grudge to a page and every page full. ¶ Hanrahan: the order that closed her business, with his signature on it. Lathrop: a wedding invitation nobody ever used; he jilted his sister a week before the wedding. Havemeyer: an IOU for four hundred dollars, in his hand. Doyle: a file he’d kept on him, thick enough to matter. Carbone: a column of payments, every month for years, and her name at the top. ¶ A reason is the easy half. Everybody in Salerno’s box had one. ¶ I didn’t touch the empty birdcage. Some things in a room are only there to be sad.

It was a few blocks from there to Hanley’s, downtown and west, with my collar up. The rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ I went in at Hanley’s, a saloon with sawdust on the floor. It was an old high room with a tin ceiling and a long mahogany bar, and the sawdust on the floor had collected the whole day in it: ash, peanut shells and bottle caps. Over the bar hung a mirror gone cloudy at the corners, which is the kindest way to be looked at after midnight. ¶ Vitale was behind the bar with both hands spread on it, the way somebody stands who has been standing since the afternoon and has opinions about it. He had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Hanrahan, in a sailor’s pea coat, was in a booth by the wall, alone with a glass of beer and a newspaper. ¶ Salerno had been here earlier in the evening. That settled where I was going. ¶ Nobody gets a drink in a place like that without the one who pours it looking at them, and Vitale looks at everybody twice. ¶ The glasses behind the bar caught the light and did nothing else with it.

Hanrahan was in the room, and I hadn’t heard from her yet. That seemed worth putting right. ¶ I leaned on the bar next to her and ordered nothing, which got noticed. I asked her where she’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ She answered without looking at me, which is a way of answering. ¶ “At seven I went up to Mrs. Nagy’s to pay a call, and stayed through eight. Carbone, Doyle and Havemeyer were there at seven; Carbone and Havemeyer were there at eight. Around nine I went round to Doyle’s for a game of gin. At ten I stopped in at Hanley’s to get warm, on my own.” ¶ For eight and nine, the hours that mattered, Hanrahan said Mrs. Nagy’s at eight and Doyle’s flat at nine. I put it with the rest and didn’t argue with it yet. ¶ I caught myself in the cloudy mirror and decided not to ask.

I walked downtown and west to the Automat. It was a good walk, and I took all of it. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ I went into the Automat on Delancey Street, open all night. It was a long bright room of little glass doors, each with a sandwich or a slice of pie behind it, and a nickel would open any one of them. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Carbone, with a bandaged hand, was in the corner with a cup of coffee, holding it in both hands for the warmth. ¶ Hanrahan had said Carbone was with her at Mrs. Nagy’s at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Anybody could have come and gone, and nobody would have known it. ¶ The tin sign on the wall had outlasted the company and would outlast me.

A couple of blocks downtown and west, and I was at the Automat. Delancey Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ I went back to the Automat, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Carbone, with a bandaged hand, was at a table by the wall, watching the room the way people watch rooms they shouldn’t be in. ¶ Hanrahan had said Carbone was with her at Mrs. Nagy’s at eight. It was reason enough to look. ¶ I read the old cough syrup sign again. Relief guaranteed. I’d have settled for less.

It was a good walk to Mrs. Nagy’s, uptown and east. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ Mrs. Nagy’s again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Mrs. Nagy sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. Lathrop, in a camel coat, was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. Havemeyer, in a fur collar, was at the sink with his sleeves rolled up, and dried his hands slowly before he turned round. ¶ Hanrahan had said she was here at seven and eight. Lathrop had found Salerno. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ The holy picture had its eyes on me, with an expression I couldn’t afford.

I sat down at the kitchen table with the form, under the one good light. A name wants a line under it, and a line wants somebody’s word under that. I went down the form one line at a time. ¶ The office stairs would still be a little shorter when I climbed them next. Paid rent does that to a building.

I set off east for Doyle’s place. It was a few blocks. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There were brass mailboxes with little windows, so the whole building can see who gets letters and who gets bills. ¶ Doyle was slumped in the chair with one arm hanging down, as if sleep had come over him in the middle of a sentence. He had a carnation in his buttonhole and his little black book in his waistcoat, the rubber band still round it. ¶ Mrs. Greco was there ahead of me, hat in her hands, turning the brim. ¶ Nobody there was paid to keep track of anybody. ¶ If it happened at ten, it happened in this room, and whoever did it had walked in here with the rat poison already in hand. ¶ I stood a moment and let my eyes catch up with the rest of me.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, so I went through them. His papers were in a box under the bed, the kind of box a man keeps for the things he’d rather not file. ¶ He had a page on everybody who held something against him, typed and clipped together, and every page said what the grudge was. He’d kept them square, so that nobody got top billing. ¶ Teitel: an IOU in his hand, and a note of what was still owing. Amato: a complaint he’d made against him, in triplicate. Mrs. Krantz: a bundle of her letters, tied with string and never given back. ¶ Everybody in Doyle’s box had a reason. Fewer of them had been at the flats over Lipsky’s to get the rat poison. ¶ The doorkeeper at the Peacock sees every face that comes through the door. I wanted all of them. ¶ I dusted off my knees. They’d done more work tonight than the rest of me.

It was a few blocks to Doyle’s place, downtown. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ Doyle’s place again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Mrs. Greco had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ Doyle had died here. I wanted another look at the room before I asked anybody anything more. ¶ I wiped my feet, because somebody in that house would notice if I didn’t.

Amato had found Doyle. A where without a why is half an answer, and I wanted the other half from Amato. I got as near to him as manners allowed and said my name. He was a stocky man in a leather jacket and a chauffeur’s cap pushed back, moving a toothpick from one side of his mouth to the other to show he’s thinking. ¶ I mentioned Doyle to Amato and let the quiet do some of the asking. “Couldn’t say. My eyes were on the road, and the road was empty.” ¶ “Doyle had my cab license pulled for a week because I wouldn’t drive his cousin for nothing. A week is a lot of fares.” ¶ That was his reason, in his own words. Mrs. Greco hadn’t mentioned it. A reason is the easy half. ¶ Arguing with a horse cab about the right of way: that was the last I saw of him.

Doyle’s place lay a fair few blocks downtown and east. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ Doyle’s place looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Mrs. Greco, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ The night had started here, with Doyle, and I wanted to see it again with what I knew now. ¶ My feet were glad to stop, and said so.

A few blocks downtown, and I was at Doyle’s place. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. The sky had gone gray along the bottom edge, and a milk wagon was working the next block. ¶ I let myself back into Doyle’s place, and nobody made a fuss about it. ¶ Mrs. Greco, my client, had beaten me there and was waiting on the landing, with her coat on and her hands in her pockets. ¶ Doyle had died here, and a room like that is worth a second look. ¶ The stairs had opinions about my weight and shared them all the way up.

I walked east to Russo’s place. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. The rain had driven everybody into the doorways, where they stood smoking and watching it like a show nobody had paid for. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There was a dumbwaiter in the back hall for coal and parcels, with a bell on every floor that nobody answers. ¶ Russo was where they’d found him, in the chair by the table, as if he’d sat down to wait for something and it had come. He had a fresh deck in his breast pocket, still in its band, and his green eyeshade in his hand. ¶ Mrs. Krantz had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ Nobody minded who came and went. ¶ If it happened at nine, it happened in this room, and whoever did it had walked in here with the chloral already in hand. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I wanted to read them properly. Russo kept his papers in a box file, and I sat down with it under the lamp. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge against him, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and he’d written every one down. ¶ Dr. Hirsch: an IOU in her hand, and a note of what was still owing. Teitel: a note about him and the card room over Feingold’s garage, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. Doyle: a note about him and the Peacock, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Dr. Hirsch’s surgery and the chloral. ¶ The head waiter at Steinmetz’s sees every face that comes through the door. I wanted all of them. ¶ I put the room back the way I found it, which is more than whoever came before me had done.

From there to Dr. Hirsch’s surgery was a good walk. A cab sat at the curb with its engine running and its driver asleep, waiting for somebody who wasn’t coming out in this. ¶ The bank’s brass doors were shining wet, and up the side stair the dentist’s waiting room had an umbrella stand full of umbrellas nobody came back for: people with toothaches forget everything, and people without them don’t come back. There was a cylinder of laughing gas on a trolley, with a rubber mask that has seen a great many faces at their worst. ¶ Miss Gutman was writing appointment cards in her best hand. Teeth so perfect people assume the doctor did them; she was born with them, and she’ll tell you. ¶ The chloral had come from here, and that was worth the walk. From her post Miss Gutman could see the waiting room and the stairs up from the street. “Everybody signs the book and everybody rings the bell, and the bell’s louder than the book, so I go by the bell.” ¶ There was a stack of magazines in the waiting room old enough that the patients read them as history.

Dr. Hirsch’s surgery was only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ I let myself back into Dr. Hirsch’s surgery, and nobody made a fuss about it. ¶ Miss Gutman was telling a man with a toothache to sit down and be brave. ¶ The chloral had come from here. That settled where I was going. ¶ Adding up the day’s fees in the cash book: that was the last I saw of her.

The costume room at the Lyric lay a few blocks uptown and west. The rain was letting up as the sky went gray, as if it had only come out to keep the night company. ¶ Back at the costume room at the Lyric. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Teitel was on a hard chair by the wall, turning his hat round and round in his hands. ¶ Mrs. Krantz had pointed me at Teitel. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it, and I said it.

Midnight. My office was two rooms at the top of a walk-up on Mulberry Street, and the second room was mostly for show. My head kept its own time, behind the clock over the safe and louder. I put the lamp low and thanked it. ¶ The stairs creaked all the way up, and then somebody stood outside my door long enough to change their mind and change it back. My visitor came in with an apology for the hour and a second one for the first, and was well into a third before sitting down. ¶ He sat down in the good chair without being asked. “Solomon Teitel. I was Carmine Russo’s neighbor. Somebody has killed him.” ¶ Russo was the card-room keeper. At half past eleven, Mrs. Greco, who’d come to return a borrowed book, found him in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street. The police had a look and called it his heart. ¶ “When did it happen, as near as anybody can say?” ¶ He said it slowly, so that I’d get it right. “He telephoned me at nine o’clock, cheerful, to say he had company. The coroner says chloral, taken then; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “He ate at the Lyric most nights,” my client said. “He was there earlier tonight. His usual.” ¶ “Who didn’t like him?” ¶ “Talk to Mabry,” Teitel said, without having to think about it. “He knew what he got up to at Sokol’s, and let him know he knew.” ¶ He opened his bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I took the money. The case came with it, the way a cold comes with a wet night.

I went over Russo’s table slowly, touching nothing I didn’t have to. ¶ Teitel didn’t come in. I didn’t ask him to. ¶ There were two glasses on the table. One smelled of rye and nothing else. The other smelled of rye and something sweet and chemical, like a hospital left out in the sun. Under the table, where it had rolled, was an empty brown bottle with a paper label from Rafferty’s. The lodgers there keep it on the hall shelf. The dead man had been drinking with somebody he knew. ¶ So the chloral came from Rafferty’s, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Russo had been at Rafferty’s earlier, to get it. ¶ Who was only half of it. The papers at Russo’s place might know the why. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

Rafferty’s was a fair few blocks uptown and west, near enough for anybody to walk it there and back inside the hour. I made a note of that. The fog was still at the end of whatever street I was on. It followed me better than I follow people. ¶ Rafferty’s had gone to sleep the way rooming houses do: one radiator knocking, one lodger coughing, and a kettle somewhere at the back that never quite goes off the boil. The stair carpet was worn pale down the middle, a path laid by everybody who ever came home later than they said. There was the mending basket, set square across the top of the first flight, so that coming up the stairs means asking it to move. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was writing in the rent book in pencil and going over it in ink. She had a ring of keys at her belt the size of a saucer, and she knows each key by the sound it makes. Miss Nowak was saying ‘Number, please’ in her sleep. ¶ The chloral had come from here. That was reason enough. ¶ From her post Mrs. Rafferty could see the front door, the stairs and every landing to the top. ¶ I wiped my feet, because somebody in that house would notice if I didn’t.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Greco. ¶ There were sunflower-seed shells in the gallery aisles, swept up every night and back by the second act. She had a gold crucifix on a chain, and a burn on the inside of her wrist the shape of a ladle’s rim. I asked her where she’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ She kept it short. Some people do with everybody. ¶ “My night. I was on my feet. Write that down first. I was at the Lyric all evening. Miss Nowak was there at seven; Dr. Hirsch and Russo were there at eight; Mabry was there at nine and ten. Seven, my feet start to hurt. They hurt till Sunday.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Mrs. Greco said the Lyric. That was her word for it, and I took it down as said. ¶ Pinsky had been there all evening with nothing to do but notice. ¶ Everybody’s evening makes sense to the one who spent it.

Russo’s place was a few blocks downtown and east. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Back at Russo’s place. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Teitel was there, with a cup of something he hadn’t touched and his coat still buttoned. ¶ Russo died here, so I looked again. ¶ It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it, and I said it.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, downtown and east to Russo’s place, a fair few blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. The fog had come up off the river and was taking the streetlamps one at a time. ¶ Back at Russo’s place, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ Teitel, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ Russo had died here, and a room like that is worth a second look. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

There was a pot of tea stewing on the back of the stove at all hours, offered to everybody, and always too strong to refuse politely. Miss Nowak was pale under a cloche hat, with a red mark across the top of her head from the headset that her hair doesn’t quite hide. I asked her to walk me through her night, every stop of it. ¶ Miss Nowak asked why I wanted to know, and then told me before I could answer. ¶ “Number, please. Sorry. I mean, what would you like to know? I’ll put you through. I was at the Lyric at seven, with Mrs. Greco. Seven, I still hear the switchboard in my ears. It takes till eight to stop. Come eight, I went home to change, and stayed the rest of the evening. Mabry was there at eight; at nine and ten it was just me.” ¶ So the Lyric at seven, which was what Mrs. Greco had said. So far as it went, it stood up. For nine, the hour that mattered, she said home, here at Rafferty’s. I didn’t believe it or disbelieve it. I wrote it down. ¶ I wanted Mrs. Rafferty’s count of the night, everybody, hour by hour. ¶ Painting her nails a red her landlady disapproves of: that was the last I saw of her.

It was a few blocks from there to Russo’s place, downtown and east, with my collar up. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Back at Russo’s place, I had my hands in my pockets and my questions in order. ¶ Teitel let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ The night had started here, with Russo, and I wanted to see it again with what I knew now. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

Doyle’s place was a few blocks east, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Steam heat is the whole reason anybody pays what they pay to live in the Excelsior’s flats, and against the cold the lobby was warm enough to make your nose run. A row of brass mailboxes with little windows showed who had letters and who had bills. Upstairs a phonograph was playing the same record for the third time, to somebody who didn’t care for it. There was a gas ring in every kitchen, and on the third floor a smell of gas the tenants have been mentioning to each other since spring. ¶ Doyle was on the floor between the table and the door. Nobody had covered him yet, and nobody had closed his eyes. He had a carnation in his buttonhole and his little black book in his waistcoat, the rubber band still round it. ¶ Amato, my client, had beaten me there and was waiting on the landing, with his coat on and his hands in his pockets. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I looked the place over the way you read a bill: twice, and slowly.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. I went through Doyle’s papers, one folder at a time. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge against him, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and he’d written every one down. ¶ Miss Nowak: a note about her and the Peacock, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. Mrs. Krantz: a bundle of her letters, tied with string and never given back. Mrs. Sobel: an IOU from her in-law, with her name pencilled beside it. Teitel: an IOU in his hand, and a note of what was still owing. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Rafferty’s and the revolver. ¶ Somebody at the Lyric would have kept count of faces, and that would be the usher. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

The Lyric was only round the corner, and I was there before I’d finished a thought. The cold was still out there doing its rounds. It’s the only thing in this city that works all night for nothing. ¶ Only the lobby of the playhouse was lit, where the cleaners had started on the brass and stopped for a glass of tea. The poster by the doors still said THE RABBI’S DAUGHTER, ELEVENTH TRIUMPHANT WEEK, and under it somebody had written, in pencil, and twelfth. There was a pair of silver candlesticks for the Sabbath scene in the second act, real silver, counted by the stage manager before the curtain and after. ¶ Pinsky was marking crosses on his seating chart. He had his seating chart under one arm on a clipboard, the way other men carry a newspaper. Teitel was in the back row with a bag of peanuts, shelling them one at a time and not eating them. Mrs. Krantz stood at the back with her hat in her hand, as if she had just come in or was just going. Mrs. Sobel sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with her coat folded on her knees. ¶ Doyle had been here earlier in the evening. It was reason enough to look. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “I seat by the chart. Every seat sold is a cross, every cross has a face, and I could draw you the face.” ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Krantz. There were sunflower-seed shells in the gallery aisles, swept up every night and back by the second act. ¶ I asked her where she’d been tonight. All of it, in order. ¶ She counted back through the evening under her breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “I’ll answer you the way I answer everything: in writing, if you like, and in ink. I was at the Lyric all evening. Miss Nowak was there at seven; Teitel and Doyle were there at eight; Miss Nowak and Doyle were there at nine; Mrs. Sobel was there at ten. Nine is a good hour for rent: people are fed, and home, and feeling guilty.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Mrs. Krantz said the Lyric. It went in the notebook in her own words. ¶ Teitel was in the room, and I hadn’t had his evening yet. ¶ I wrote it all down. My handwriting at that hour looks like a spider fell in the ink, but I can read it, mostly.

I went round the corner to Rafferty’s. The cold was at its worst, the kind that finds the hole in your glove you didn’t know you had. ¶ Back at Rafferty’s, I had my hands in my pockets and my questions in order. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was pouring tea nobody asked for. Miss Nowak was painting her nails a red her landlady disapproves of. ¶ Mrs. Sobel had said she was here at seven, eight and nine, and that Miss Nowak was with her here at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Darning a lodger’s sock on the first landing: that was the last I saw of her.

Rafferty’s was a fair few blocks uptown and west, near enough for anybody to walk it there and back inside the hour. I made a note of that. A coal cart was making its first round, and the man on it had a scarf wound up to his eyes and no intention of talking. ¶ Rafferty’s again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was counting the umbrellas on their hooks. Miss Nowak was counting out change for a horse she likes. ¶ Mrs. Sobel had said she was here at seven, eight and nine, and that Miss Nowak was with her here at eight, and that was worth the walk. ¶ There was Parnell, a ginger cat, asleep on a different stair every time anybody comes in, as if he were keeping count for her.

A fair few blocks downtown and east, and I was at Doyle’s place. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ I went back to Doyle’s place, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Amato had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ The night had started here, with Doyle, and I wanted to see it again with what I knew now. ¶ Somebody’s radio was going behind a door, low, so as not to wake anybody who was already awake.

It was a few blocks from there to Doyle’s place, east, with my collar up. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There was a gas ring in every kitchen, and on the third floor a smell of gas the tenants have been mentioning to each other since spring. ¶ Doyle lay on the floor where he’d fallen, on his side, with his knees drawn up a little. He had a carnation in his buttonhole and his little black book in his waistcoat, the rubber band still round it. ¶ Amato was there ahead of me, hat in his hands, turning the brim. ¶ No clerk, no doorman, nobody watching the stairs: nobody saw who came. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I took my hat off. It seemed like the thing to do.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. His papers were in a box under the bed, the kind of box a man keeps for the things he’d rather not file. ¶ He had a page on everybody who held something against him, typed and clipped together, and every page said what the grudge was. He’d kept them square, so that nobody got top billing. ¶ Russo: a note about him and the card room over Feingold’s garage, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. Teitel: an IOU in his hand, and a note of what was still owing. Mabry: an IOU from his friend, with his name pencilled beside it. Mrs. Krantz: a bundle of her letters, tied with string and never given back. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Rafferty’s and the revolver. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

Steinmetz’s was a couple of blocks downtown, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ Closing a chop house of the old kind takes an hour, and Steinmetz’s was in the middle of it: the chairs going up table by table, slowly, so as not to hurry anybody who might still order pie. The head waiter stood at his stand by the door, writing the last covers in his book in ink. The sawdust had been swept into the corners to think over what it had heard. There was a rack of bone-handled steak knives by the kitchen door, counted out at noon and counted back at closing, more or less. ¶ Demos was folding napkins into shapes nobody asked for. He had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty; he says he feels undressed without it. Teitel sat at a table by the mirror with a glass of tea, drinking it the old way, through a lump of sugar held in his teeth. Russo was at a corner table with a plate of toast, eating it slowly, a corner at a time, like somebody paying by the bite. Mabry was finishing a plate of something with the care of somebody who had paid for it. ¶ Doyle had been here earlier in the evening. It was reason enough to look. From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “I seat every table myself, and I write the covers in the book with the time beside them. Nobody sits in my room without my say-so.” ¶ The coffee smelled better than it was going to taste. Most coffee does.

Russo was in the room, and I hadn’t heard from him yet, and there was no time like now. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. ¶ I asked him where he’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ Russo gave it to me in as few words as the evening would go into. ¶ “Sure. Cut the deck. I’ll deal you the evening. I was at Steinmetz’s from seven through eight. Teitel and Mabry were there at seven; Mrs. Krantz and Doyle were there at eight. Then at nine I took a letter round to Rafferty’s, with Teitel. Nine, I watch. I always watch at nine. It’s when people get brave. Come ten, I couldn’t settle, so I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee, with Teitel. Walking over to Steinmetz’s at ten I passed Mrs. Krantz on East Houston Street, going fast, no hat.” ¶ The part worth keeping came last. East Houston Street was where Doyle lived. ¶ I wrote it down and underlined nothing. It was too early to underline.

I headed east for Mrs. Krantz’s flat, a couple of blocks away. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ The milkman had been to the Excelsior and left a bottle outside every door on every floor, and nobody in the building had seen him come or go. That’s the kind of building it is: no doorman, no janitor in sight, and a landlord who lives uptown and sends a man on the first of the month. There were marble stairs to the second floor and plain wood after that, where the builder ran out of marble or interest. ¶ Mrs. Krantz was drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in. She had a pince-nez on a black ribbon, which she puts on to read a rent book and takes off to read a face. ¶ Russo had said Mrs. Krantz was with him at Steinmetz’s at eight. That was reason enough. ¶ Nobody in the place was paid to notice who came and went, so nobody had. ¶ It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it, and I said it.

I walked east to Mrs. Krantz’s flat. It was a couple of blocks, and I took all of it. The street was empty and clear and very quiet, and my heels were the loudest thing on it. ¶ Mrs. Krantz’s flat looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Mrs. Krantz was writing in a rent book with a fountain pen. ¶ Russo had said Mrs. Krantz was with him at Steinmetz’s at eight. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ Looking at a banister as if it owed her money: that was the last I saw of her.

I set off west for Steinmetz’s. It was a couple of blocks. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ I went back to Steinmetz’s, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Demos was seating a man who would rather have stood. Teitel, Russo and Mabry were still there. ¶ Russo had said Mabry was with him here at seven. Mrs. Krantz had said she was here at eight. That settled where I was going. ¶ Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

A fair few blocks uptown and west, and I was at Rafferty’s. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ Rafferty’s again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was darning a lodger’s sock on the first landing. ¶ Mrs. Krantz had said she was here at seven. That settled where I was going. ¶ Writing in the rent book in pencil and going over it in ink: that was the last I saw of her.

Midnight. The office was where I’d left it, at the top of four flights on Mulberry Street, which is the only thing about it you could count on. I’d paid the landlady on my way up, and she’d counted it on the landing in front of me. The stairs felt shorter for it. The office looked the same as always, which was its own kind of relief. ¶ Somebody came up the stairs. Nobody comes up those stairs after midnight with good news; the good news waits for morning, like a gentleman. My visitor knocked twice and waited to be asked in, as if somebody’s mother was listening. ¶ She sat down in the good chair without being asked. “Bertha Krantz. I was Francis Doyle’s old sweetheart. Somebody has killed him.” ¶ The dead man was the alderman’s clerk. He was found in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street at half past eleven by Miss Nowak, who’d come round to collect a debt. The police put it down as a robbery gone wrong. ¶ “When did he die?” ¶ “I’ll tell you what the police didn’t ask,” Mrs. Krantz said. “Shot at eight or nine o’clock. Nobody heard it over the radios.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening he was at the Lyric,” she said. “His usual. He was a man of habits, and that was one of them.” ¶ “Who’d want him dead?” ¶ “Amato swore at him in the street on Monday, in front of the fruit man,” Mrs. Krantz said. “He and Doyle had been at each other’s throats for years.” ¶ She opened her bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I took the money. By the end of the week it would belong to my landlady, but for tonight the two of us were getting along fine.

I got down and went over the floor with a flashlight, board by board. ¶ Mrs. Krantz watched from the landing with her coat buttoned to the neck, as if the cold were in the room. ¶ A revolver lay under the chair, one chamber fired. I knew whose it was before I looked: it belongs in the hall-stand drawer at Rafferty’s, and the whole block knows it, because the landlady shows it to anybody who’s late with the rent. Doyle had been shot from across his own table. ¶ So the gun came from Rafferty’s. Doyle died at eight or nine, and whoever fired it had been at Rafferty’s before that, to take it. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

I set off uptown and west for the card room over Feingold’s garage. It was a couple of blocks. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The card room over the garage was down to one table, four players and a pot nobody mentioned. The el had stopped for the night, and the room was quiet enough to hear a card being thought about. The windows were painted black on the inside, so the morning wouldn’t get ideas. There was a long table in green baize, worn white in front of the dealer’s chair. ¶ Miss Nowak, in a fur collar, was on a hard chair by the wall, turning her hat round and round in her hands. She had nails painted red and bitten, both. ¶ Miss Nowak had found Doyle. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Nobody there was paid to keep track of anybody. ¶ It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it, and I said it.

Mrs. Krantz had pointed me at Amato. That was one thing. How Amato felt about the whole business was another, and I wanted to hear it. ¶ He sat me down at the kitchen table, under a light that was hard on both of us. He had a St. Christopher medal on a chain round his neck and another on the dashboard of his cab, in case one of them is off duty. ¶ I asked the man in a grey fedora about Doyle. “I just drive. People get in, people get out. I don’t look in the mirror.” ¶ “Doyle had my cab license pulled for a week because I wouldn’t drive his cousin for nothing. A week is a lot of fares.” ¶ That was the man in a grey fedora’s reason, in his own words. Mrs. Krantz hadn’t mentioned it. A reason isn’t an hour, though. ¶ There was Parnell, a ginger cat, asleep on a different stair every time anybody comes in, as if he were keeping count for her.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, downtown and east to Doyle’s place, a fair few blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. A cab sat at the curb with its engine running and its driver asleep, waiting for somebody who wasn’t coming out in this. ¶ Back at Doyle’s place, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ My client, Mrs. Krantz, had beaten me there and stood just inside the door, gloves in her hand. ¶ This was where Doyle had died. Everything else would be somebody’s story, and the room wouldn’t. ¶ Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

A few blocks uptown and west, and I was at the Lyric. It was raining the steady kind of rain that has nowhere else to be. ¶ The Lyric had emptied as far as a theater ever empties, which isn’t far: programs on the seats, somebody’s glove, a bag of sunflower seeds spilled in the twelfth row. Up in the ventilator over the gallery, the pigeons were rehearsing. There was a pair of silver candlesticks for the Sabbath scene in the second act, real silver, counted by the stage manager before the curtain and after. ¶ Pinsky was mouthing the third act from the back of the house. He had a white mustache waxed to points so fine they quiver when he disapproves. Mabry, with a cane, sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with his coat folded on his knees. ¶ Doyle had been here earlier in the evening. Amato had said Mabry was with him at Rafferty’s at eight. It was reason enough to look. From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “I seat by the chart. Every seat sold is a cross, every cross has a face, and I could draw you the face.” ¶ There was the daughter’s death scene in the third act, eleven minutes long, which the usher mouths along with from the back of the house, every word.

Amato had said Mrs. Greco was with him at Rafferty’s at seven. I knew a little of her evening and nothing of her reasons, and I wanted both. She kept me standing in the hall, which told me how long the visit was going to be. ¶ I mentioned Doyle to her and let the quiet do some of the asking. “Not my business. My business is the stove.” ¶ “Doyle knew what I got up to at Steinmetz’s, and let me know he knew.” ¶ That was Mrs. Greco’s reason, in her own words. Mrs. Krantz hadn’t mentioned it. Plenty of people have a reason. Fewer have the hour to go with it. ¶ Tasting the gravy off a wooden spoon: that was the last I saw of her.

A fair few blocks downtown and east, and I was at Doyle’s place. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ Back at Doyle’s place. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Mrs. Krantz let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ Doyle had died here, and a room like that is worth a second look. ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

It was a couple of blocks from there to the Grasso flat, east, with my collar up. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ The Grasso flat over the delicatessen on Second Avenue was three small rooms kept very clean, with oilcloth on the kitchen table and a calendar from the delicatessen on the wall. An aspidistra in a brass pot stood in the corner, dusted leaf by leaf. ¶ Grasso stood in the doorway of the parlor and looked at the place where Caruso ought to be, which is a thing you can do for a long time without it helping. ¶ No clerk, no doorman, nobody watching the stairs: nobody saw who came. ¶ If he went at ten, the flat had been empty, and anybody who’d heard Grasso at the chop house had known the way in. That was a room, more or less. It was a big room. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

The chop house was a couple of blocks east, near enough for anybody to walk it there and back inside the hour. I made a note of that. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ I went into the Grand Street chop house. It was dark wood and white tablecloths, with the grill at the back cooling down and ticking to itself. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Fairbanks was going from table to table with a cloth over her arm, straightening chairs that were already straight. Lathrop sat at a table by the mirror with a glass of tea, drinking it the old way, through a lump of sugar held in his teeth. Alfano sat at a table near the kitchen door with a newspaper folded to the crossword and a cup of coffee going cold. Round and pleasant and dressed a little too well for a cigar store, she kept her eyes on the door, in case it was the police or a winner. ¶ Nobody sits down in a restaurant without the head waiter deciding where, and Fairbanks had been doing the deciding. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Lathrop had a cup he’d stopped drinking and a newspaper he’d stopped reading, and was keeping both for company. ¶ I sat down across from him with a cup of coffee for company. ¶ “Fairbanks has you here at nine. Fill in the rest of the evening for me, in order.” ¶ He went slowly, the way people do who like to get things right. ¶ “At eight I dropped a parcel off at Mrs. Nagy’s, with Ainsworth. Around nine I went to the chop house for a glass of tea, and stayed the rest of the evening. Alfano, Lefkowitz and Dettweiler were there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ Lathrop said the chop house at ten. Fairbanks had Alfano, Dettweiler and Lou here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ I could have used a glass from the samovar. I could have used a lot of things. ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. He went at ten o’clock. Lathrop had told me the chop house at ten, and Fairbanks’s list said otherwise. Alfano was at the chop house at ten; Fairbanks said so. Lefkowitz hadn’t told me where he was at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Lou at the chop house at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Lathrop now. Or I could find out first from the landlady at Mrs. Nagy’s who’d been in. ¶ Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t, and I didn’t know yet which was which.

I waited for a gap in Mrs. Nagy’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. “Who was in tonight?” I said. “All of them, hour by hour, and who you didn’t know.” ¶ She started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Lathrop and Ainsworth. Nobody else. Nine, Ainsworth. Nobody else at all. Ten, Lefkowitz and Ainsworth. Nobody else, that hour.” ¶ Mrs. Nagy had Lathrop here at eight, same as he said. That put Lefkowitz here at ten, by her count. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

Midnight. I was in the office on Mulberry Street with my feet on the desk and the radio turned down low. My ribs hurt when I breathed deep, so I breathed shallow. Rain ran down the window in the lamplight, and I sat and listened to it and did not move much. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. A man stood in the doorway, cap on, deciding if I was worth coming in for. Narrowly. ¶ “Fritz’s gone,” Weisglass said. “My dachshund. He sleeps in his basket by the stove, and he isn’t there.” ¶ I got up and offered him the chair, and he sat down in it carefully, the way people sit in chairs they don’t trust. ¶ “I sat in the Blue Lantern from eight until ten,” he said, “complaining to anybody who’d listen that my parlor window won’t latch, and that I was off to my sister’s for the night.” ¶ “What time are we talking about?” ¶ He had worked it out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “The boy from the delicatessen came up with an order at a quarter past ten and passed somebody on the dark stairs, going down in a hurry.” ¶ “Who’d have a reason?” ¶ “Talk to Grasso,” he said, without having to think about it. “Fritz bit him at Easter, and he swore he’d see the back of him.” ¶ Then, smaller: “Dettweiler, a sewing-machine operator, lost her job on Friday, and asked me what Fritz was worth. And Salerno, a night-school teacher, and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ “Ten dollars,” Weisglass said. “It’s what I have. Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

I went over the parlor, and then the door, and then the parlor again. ¶ Weisglass stood in the hall with his hands in his pockets, so as not to touch anything, which was more than whoever came before me had managed. ¶ The basket by the stove was empty. The parlor window was up six inches, and there was soot on the sill from the fire escape. Whoever it was had known which window. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Weisglass at the Blue Lantern between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made the Blue Lantern the place to start counting. ¶ Somebody at the Blue Lantern would have kept count of faces, and that would be the doorkeeper. ¶ Bless This House, said the sampler. It hadn’t said anything about the people coming into it.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Hargrove. ¶ She saw me coming before I’d decided to come. That’s the job. I asked her who she’d seen come and go since the evening started. ¶ She looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶ “Benny the pawnbroker’s runner was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Dettweiler, Salerno and Mr. Weisglass telling the room about his window. Nobody else. Nine, Salerno and Mr. Weisglass, still telling it. Nobody else at all. Ten, just Benny. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Benny, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “And under the coat?” ¶ “Something alive. It moved about.” ¶ Dettweiler and Salerno heard about the window at eight. Grasso never heard Weisglass tell the room. Whatever went out of the Weisglass flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Benny. The hour that mattered was ten. Hargrove had Benny. ¶ I could feel the door behind me, ready to swing wide the moment I turned. It’s nice to be wanted gone that efficiently.

The chop house was a good walk downtown and east. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ I went into the Grand Street chop house. It was dark wood and white tablecloths, with the grill at the back cooling down and ticking to itself. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Quill was going from table to table with a cloth over his arm, straightening chairs that were already straight. Salerno was at a corner table with a plate of toast, eating it slowly, a corner at a time, like somebody paying by the bite. He was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until he needed one, and then only the one. Petrosino sat with his coat on and his plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. ¶ Dettweiler had said she was here at nine, and that Salerno was with her at the Blue Lantern at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. Nobody sits down in a restaurant without the head waiter deciding where, and Quill had been doing the deciding. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

I found a chair at the chop house and sat down with the form. I read the night back to myself, from the office to here, and started at the top of the form. ¶ My ribs had let me breathe through all of it, if shallow. I thanked them and didn’t push my luck.

It was a couple of blocks from there to the Prentiss flat, uptown and east, with my collar up. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ The Prentiss flat over the delicatessen on Second Avenue was three small rooms kept very clean, with oilcloth on the kitchen table and a calendar from the delicatessen on the wall. An aspidistra in a brass pot stood in the corner, dusted leaf by leaf. ¶ Prentiss stood in the doorway of the parlor and looked at the place where Fritz ought to be, which is a thing you can do for a long time without it helping. ¶ No one was posted to see who came and went. ¶ If he went at eleven, the flat had been empty, and anybody who’d heard Prentiss at Moskowitz’s had known the way in. That was a room, more or less. It was a big room. ¶ It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it, and I said it.

Moskowitz’s was only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ I went down to Moskowitz’s, a Romanian restaurant four steps down on Second Avenue. The place smelled of garlic and grilled meat, there was a basket of bread on every table, and the piano in the corner had a cloth over it for the night. The day’s specials were chalked on a slate by the door, and the soup had been crossed out. ¶ Hochstetter was going from table to table with a cloth over his arm, straightening chairs that were already straight. Winslow sat at a table near the kitchen door with a newspaper folded to the crossword and a cup of coffee going cold. She had a pianist’s back, bolt upright, and hands that seemed to be waiting to be counted in. Moretti was at a corner table with a plate of toast, eating it slowly, a corner at a time, like somebody paying by the bite. Renfro had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. ¶ A head waiter seats everybody who comes in, which means a head waiter knows where everybody sat. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Hochstetter’s list had Winslow here at eight. That was reason enough to ask. I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” Winslow put down what she was holding and gave me her attention. ¶ “I was at Moskowitz’s at eight, with Renfro. Then at nine I went home to listen to the radio, and stayed the rest of the evening. Moretti was there at nine and ten; at eleven it was just me.” ¶ So here at eight, with Renfro, which was what Hochstetter had. That part of the evening, at least, somebody else could vouch for. For eleven, the hour that mattered, she said home at Mrs. Nagy’s. I wrote it down and left it standing, for now. ¶ Carbone hadn’t told me his evening yet, and he was at the Automat. ¶ Nobody counted anybody in. I nearly counted them in myself, out loud, just to get things started.

I kept my voice down. Carbone kept his eyes on me. ¶ “Hochstetter has you at Moskowitz’s at nine and ten. That’s one hour. Tell me about the others.” ¶ He took a moment to put the evening in order before he handed it over. ¶ “At eight I dropped a parcel off at Mrs. Nagy’s, with Moretti. Around nine I went to Moskowitz’s for the blue-plate supper, and stayed the rest of the evening. Renfro was there at nine and ten; at eleven it was just me.” ¶ Carbone said Moskowitz’s at eleven. Hochstetter had Moretti, Renfro and Pardo at Moskowitz’s at eleven o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ The flat fingertips were typing on nothing, a line at a time. Nobody was dictating. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. He went at eleven o’clock. Winslow, Carbone and Renfro were at Moskowitz’s while Prentiss told the room; Moretti wasn’t. Winslow said home at eleven, and nobody else had said so yet. Carbone had told me Moskowitz’s at eleven, and Hochstetter’s list said otherwise. Moretti was at Moskowitz’s at eleven; Hochstetter said so. Renfro was at Moskowitz’s at eleven; Hochstetter said so. And whatever it was had gone to Pardo at Moskowitz’s at twelve. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the landlady at Mrs. Nagy’s who’d been in. ¶ That was the night so far: a lot of people who were somewhere, and one hour nobody wanted to talk about.

Carbone had named Bellucci: the Automat at eleven, the two of them. An owned-up story needs somebody to stand behind it. I said who I was, and he took it about as well as people do. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said to Bellucci. “The whole evening, in order.” ¶ He didn’t seem to mind being asked, which is how most people seem. ¶ “I was home from eight through ten, by myself. Then at eleven I went to the Automat to meet Carbone.” ¶ That put Carbone here at eleven, on his word. ¶ The landlady at Mrs. Nagy’s would know who’d been in. ¶ The tin sign on the wall had outlasted the company and would outlast me.

I asked Mrs. Nagy for a minute, and she gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. ¶ “I need the whole night,” I said. “Everybody who was here, hour by hour, and anybody you didn’t know.” She seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Carbone and Moretti. Nobody else. Nine and ten, Winslow and Moretti. Nobody else at all. Eleven, nobody but me.” ¶ Winslow said home at eleven. The landlady had nobody here at eleven o’clock. Two stories about her at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. Mrs. Nagy had Carbone here at eight, same as he said. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. The retainer was still folded in my breast pocket. I’d checked for it twice on the walk up, which wasn’t like me. I put it in the drawer, where it would keep its shape better than I would. ¶ The street door went downstairs, and somebody started up, taking the stairs slowly, like somebody not sure they were the right stairs. My visitor was already diagnosing the room, the stairs and my lack of a secretary before he sat down. ¶ He didn’t wait to be asked. “Cornelius Kavanagh. Morris Lefkowitz’s cousin. He’s dead, and nobody is doing anything about it.” ¶ The dead man was an alderman’s clerk. Alfano, who’d come to settle a bet, found him in his own two rooms over the bakery on Hester Street at half past eleven. The police called it his heart and went home. ¶ “When?” ¶ He said it slowly, so that I’d get it right. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “He’d been at Moskowitz’s earlier in the evening,” my client said. “His usual.” ¶ “Who didn’t like him?” ¶ “There’s Alfano,” he said. “I don’t like gossip, but she owed Lefkowitz the rent on a shop, and it was being called in. The woman downstairs told me.” ¶ Kavanagh put fifty dollars on the desk in tens, squared the edges and pushed them across. “I want a name. The right one.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

I bent over the table and took it a piece at a time, from one edge to the other. ¶ Kavanagh turned his back while I worked, and I was grateful. I don’t like an audience for this part. ¶ A cup of cocoa sat on the table, gone cold and bitter at the bottom. Beside it was a brown bottle with a druggist’s label made out to the Delmonico rooms. Somebody had made Lefkowitz cocoa, which is a kind thing to do, and then made sure it was the last. ¶ So the laudanum came from the Delmonico rooms, and laudanum takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Lefkowitz had been at the Delmonico rooms earlier, to get it. ¶ There were papers at Lefkowitz’s place, and papers sometimes say why. ¶ I put everything back where it had been, as near as I could.

It was a couple of blocks from there to Moskowitz’s, uptown and west, with my collar up. The street was as empty as a street gets, which in this city is never quite empty. ¶ I went down to Moskowitz’s, a Romanian restaurant four steps down on Second Avenue. The place smelled of garlic and grilled meat, there was a basket of bread on every table, and the piano in the corner had a cloth over it for the night. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Corrigan was going from table to table with a cloth over his arm, straightening chairs that were already straight. Abramowitz sat with her coat on and her plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, she wore clothes too good to have been bought. She’d made every stitch. Alfano sat at a table near the kitchen door with a newspaper folded to the crossword and a cup of coffee going cold. Winslow was finishing a plate of something with the care of somebody who had paid for it. ¶ A head waiter shows everybody to a table, so Corrigan would know who had come in tonight and where they’d been put. ¶ I took a seat where I could see the door, which is the only habit of mine that ever paid.
