Abramowitz watched me come over the way you watch weather. ¶ I got as near to her as manners allowed and said my name. ¶ “Corrigan has you here at eight. Now tell me the rest of it, from the beginning.” She counted back through the evening under her breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “At seven I went up to the Delmonico rooms to see about some money owed, with Alfano. Eight o’clock I went to Moskowitz’s for a glass of tea, with Winslow and Lefkowitz. Then at nine I went in to the print shop to set type for the morning. Then I closed up at ten and went to Moskowitz’s for the blue-plate supper. I had nobody with me at nine or ten.” ¶ Abramowitz said Moskowitz’s at ten. The head waiter had Alfano and Winslow here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. They couldn’t both be true, and Corrigan had no reason to be the wrong one. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. Kavanagh had said nine or ten, and Lefkowitz was at Moskowitz’s at nine, alive. The laudanum came from the Delmonico rooms, so whoever used it had been there first. Winslow hadn’t. Abramowitz had told me Moskowitz’s at ten, and Corrigan’s list said otherwise. Alfano was at Moskowitz’s at ten; Corrigan said so. Winslow was at Moskowitz’s at nine and ten; Corrigan said so. Sirkin hadn’t told me where he was at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the landlady at the Delmonico rooms who’d been in. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

Mrs. Lindemann met me at the foot of the stairs, which is where she met everybody. I asked her for everybody she’d seen tonight, in order, and nobody left out because she liked them. ¶ She looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Abramowitz and Alfano. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Alfano and Sirkin. Nobody else at all. Ten, nobody but me. The laudanum in my medicine cupboard was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Abramowitz, Alfano and Sirkin had been here earlier, when the laudanum was there for the taking. Mrs. Lindemann had Abramowitz here at seven, same as she said. I wrote down what the list had at ten, the hour that mattered: nobody. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

The print shop was a good walk uptown and west, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ I went in at the print shop on Centre Street, which runs a night shift. The presses were running with a noise like a train going over a long bridge, and everything in the room smelled of ink and hot oil. A wooden chair with one short leg stood by the wall, and rocked whenever anything touched it. ¶ Reinhardt was at her desk, going down a sheet of names with a ruler, line by line. ¶ Reinhardt runs the night shift, and knows who came on, who went off, and who said they’d only be a minute. ¶ There was one light, and everybody had arranged to be just outside it.

Midnight. My office was a desk, two chairs and a window on Mulberry Street, and the window was the only one of them with a view. Rent was three weeks gone. The envelope wasn’t going to pay itself by sitting on the desk. I lit a cigarette off the lamp and let the smoke do the worrying. ¶ I heard steps on the stairs, stopping on every landing to think it over. My visitor talked the whole walk to the chair: her sister, her landlord, and eventually the reason she’d come. ¶ She sat down in the good chair without being asked. “Margaret Feeney. I was Percival Renfro’s business partner. Somebody has killed him.” ¶ Renfro was a bail bondsman. Hurwitz, who’d come to settle a bet, found him in his own walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street at half past eleven. The police called it his heart and went home. ¶ “When was this?” ¶ My client had it all by heart, which is how you know somebody has been lying awake. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “He’d been at the chop house earlier in the evening,” she said. “His usual.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad he’s gone?” ¶ “If you want a name, it’s Sirkin,” she said. “He had a file on him.” ¶ “Fifty dollars,” Feeney said, and put it on the desk. “Find out who did this to him, and tell me before you tell anybody else.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

I bent over the table and took it a piece at a time, from one edge to the other. ¶ I worked slowly. Feeney waited in the hall, and the stairs creaked every time she shifted her weight. ¶ There were two glasses on the table. One smelled of rye and nothing else. The other smelled of rye and something sweet and chemical, like a hospital left out in the sun. Under the table, where it had rolled, was an empty brown bottle with a paper label from Mrs. Nagy’s. The lodgers there keep it on the hall shelf. Renfro had been drinking with somebody he knew. ¶ So the chloral came from Mrs. Nagy’s, and chloral takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Renfro had been at Mrs. Nagy’s earlier, to get it. ¶ That was all the room had to tell me, and it had told it without being asked twice.

I set off east for the chop house. It was a couple of blocks. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went into the Grand Street chop house. It was dark wood and white tablecloths, with the grill at the back cooling down and ticking to itself. A big samovar sat at the end of the counter, steaming quietly to itself. ¶ Donnelly stood by the reservation book at the door with a pencil, crossing out tables nobody would want now. Hurwitz had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, he wore clothes too good to have been bought. He’d made every stitch. Sirkin was at a corner table with a plate of toast, eating it slowly, a corner at a time, like somebody paying by the bite. Crowninshield sat with her coat on and her plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. ¶ A head waiter seats everybody who comes in, which means a head waiter knows where everybody sat. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Hurwitz had said he was here at eight and ten. The head waiter sees everybody and says nothing, unless somebody asks. I was going to ask. ¶ I went over to where Donnelly could see the whole room, which was where she always was. I asked her to give me the night the way only the head waiter could: every face, every hour. ¶ She went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Sirkin and Crowninshield. Nobody else. Eight, Hurwitz and Crowninshield. Nobody else at all. Nine, Bellucci and Renfro. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Sirkin and Crowninshield. Nobody else.” ¶ Hurwitz said the chop house at ten. Donnelly had Sirkin and Crowninshield here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. Crowninshield hadn’t been at Mrs. Nagy’s while it was there to take. Feeney had said nine or ten. Renfro was at the chop house at nine, alive. ¶ I could have used a glass from the samovar. I could have used a lot of things. ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. Feeney had said nine or ten, and Renfro was at the chop house at nine, alive. The chloral came from Mrs. Nagy’s, so whoever used it had been there first. Crowninshield hadn’t. Hurwitz had told me the chop house at ten, and Donnelly’s list said otherwise. Sirkin was at the chop house at ten; Donnelly said so. Bellucci was at the chop house at nine; Donnelly said so. Crowninshield was at the chop house at ten; Donnelly said so. ¶ Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t, and I didn’t know yet which was which.

Sirkin had said Crowninshield was with him at Mrs. Nagy’s at nine, so I went over. I kept my voice down. She kept her eyes on me. Young and tidy and a little tired, she still had the mark of the headset band pressed into her hair. ¶ I asked her to walk me through her night, every stop of it. ¶ Crowninshield smoothed the front of her coat, as if the evening were on it, and began. ¶ “I was at the chop house from seven through eight. Sirkin was there at seven; Hurwitz was there at eight. Come nine, I went round to Mrs. Nagy’s to borrow a collar stud, with Sirkin. Around ten I couldn’t settle, so I went to the chop house for coffee, with Sirkin. Walking over to the chop house at ten I passed Bellucci on Grand Street, going fast, no hat.” ¶ So here at ten and seven, with Sirkin, which was what Donnelly had. That much of it stood up, and it stood up where I could check it. The part worth keeping came last. Grand Street was where Renfro lived. ¶ Hurwitz had said he was here at nine, and that was worth the walk to Sokol’s back room. ¶ My hat had left a mark in my hair too. Nobody was paying me by the hour for mine.

I asked Hanrahan for a minute, and he gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. ¶ I asked Hanrahan who he’d seen come and go since the evening started. He started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Ten o’clock, Hurwitz. Nobody else. I came on at ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ That put Hurwitz here at ten, by his count. ¶ Bellucci had walked from Mrs. Nagy’s to the chop house at nine. I wanted to know what he’d passed on the way. ¶ The toes were still ready to be somewhere else. So were mine, but mine were further from the door.

Bellucci let me in as far as the kitchen, which in that house was as far as anybody got. ¶ I asked him to tell me his evening, from the beginning, and not to leave out the dull parts. He put down what he was holding and gave me his attention. ¶ “I was home at seven. Then at eight I took a letter round to Mrs. Nagy’s, with Sirkin. Come nine, I went to the chop house for a glass of tea, with Renfro. Around ten I went home to bed. At seven and ten I was on my own.” ¶ Bellucci said home at ten. Crowninshield passed him on Grand Street at ten. They couldn’t both be true, and I knew which one I’d bet on. The rest held where I could check it: Sirkin had him at Mrs. Nagy’s at eight, same as he said. ¶ The door opened. It was neither. It hardly ever is, which is how bookmakers stay in business.

Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants. I had money in the desk drawer for once. I’d opened the drawer twice to make sure, and once more just to visit. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor came in talking about the stairs, how many and how dark, and was still counting them sitting down. I’d never dared. ¶ “Gretchen Brauer,” she said, and put her hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Nunzio Bellucci’s business partner. He’s dead, and I don’t like how.” ¶ The dead man was a bail bondsman. At half past eleven, Doyle, who’d come up for the Thursday card game, found him in his own flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street. The police had a look and called it the work of a burglar he disturbed. ¶ “When?” ¶ “Here’s what they don’t want to hear,” she said. “The woman across the landing heard a fall at nine or ten o’clock; she’d dozed off over the radio and can’t say which.” ¶ “He’d been at the Blue Lantern earlier in the evening,” she said. “His usual.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad he’s gone?” ¶ “I found a letter from Rosenbaum in his desk,” Brauer said. “She owed Bellucci four hundred dollars. Start there.” ¶ She counted fifty dollars onto the blotter and kept a finger on the last bill. “Find out who did it. Then tell me first.” ¶ I took the money and my hat, in that order.

I got down and went over the floor with a flashlight, board by board. ¶ Brauer stayed by the door. People in a room with a dead man stand where they can leave. ¶ A carving knife lay on the floor by the door. The handle had a mark burnt into it, the mark every knife in the kitchen at Mrs. Nagy’s has so that nobody walks off with one. Somebody had. Bellucci had opened the door to somebody and turned his back. ¶ So the knife came from Mrs. Nagy’s. Bellucci died at nine or ten, and whoever used it had been at Mrs. Nagy’s before that, to take it. ¶ The little swing in the empty birdcage moved when the door went. That was all that moved.

I set off downtown and west for the Palace. It was a few blocks. Behind a window somewhere a radiator was knocking, trying to wake a building that didn’t want waking. ¶ The back row of the Palace, a picture house on Delancey Street, was the darkest place on Delancey Street you could sit for a dime. That’s what the back row is for, and the management has known it for years. A wooden chair with one short leg stood by the wall, and rocked whenever anything touched it. ¶ Doyle, in a green hat, looked up when I came in, and then looked as if he wished he hadn’t. ¶ Doyle had found Bellucci. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ There was nobody on duty, and nobody to ask who had been by. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Doyle had said Lathrop was with him here at ten. That was reason enough to ask. I found her at the far end, where the light gave up, and stood where she could see me without having to want to. ¶ I asked her to tell me her evening, from the beginning, and not to leave out the dull parts. ¶ She smoothed the front of her coat, as if the evening were on it, and began. ¶ “At seven I went to the Palace because the picture had Ronald Colman in it, and I was there all evening. At seven, eight and nine it was just me; Doyle was there at ten.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Lathrop said the Palace. Whether anything else I held touched it, I’d have to see. ¶ Somebody leaned on the chair with the short leg, and it told the whole room about it.

I waited for a gap in Ellery’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. “You’ve been here all night,” I said. “Who came in, and when?” ¶ He didn’t look at the room to answer. He didn’t need to. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Vitale and Schilling. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Vitale and Bellucci. Nobody else at all. Ten, somebody in a camel coat, back to the room, I couldn’t swear who. Nobody else, that hour.” ¶ I wrote down what Ellery had at nine and ten, the hours that mattered: Vitale and Bellucci at nine and somebody in a camel coat at ten. ¶ I could feel the door behind me, ready to swing wide the moment I turned. It’s nice to be wanted gone that efficiently.

Mrs. Nagy’s was a good walk uptown and east, and I took it at a good clip. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ I went to Mrs. Nagy’s rooms on East Fourth Street. It was a tall thin house that leaned a little on its neighbor, like a lodger who has had one too many. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Nagy sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Vitale, with a bandaged hand, was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into his collar. Prentiss, in a sailor’s pea coat, was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. ¶ Schilling had said he was here at eight and nine, and that Vitale was with him at the Blue Lantern at seven. It was reason enough to look. Mrs. Nagy kept the house, and the house kept no secrets from her, or not for long. ¶ The hall had a coat stand with nobody’s coat on it.

A few blocks downtown, and I was at Rosenbaum’s flat. A newspaper went by in the gutter. It might have been the same one. It was making better time than I was. ¶ I went round to Rosenbaum’s flat on Pitt Street. It was a walk-up like every walk-up on Pitt Street: a hall that smelled of other people’s suppers and a stair with a bend in it. The wallpaper roses had faded to the color of weak tea, except in the corners the light never reached. ¶ Rosenbaum, in a fur collar, was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. She had long, cold-looking fingers and a habit of humming under her breath, always the same few bars and never the end of them. ¶ Mrs. Nagy’s list had Rosenbaum at Mrs. Nagy’s at seven, and that was worth the walk. It was the kind of place nobody kept an eye on. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

I found somewhere to sit and took out the form. I put down what I had, and what I had would have to stand up by itself. ¶ The new money would go in the desk drawer with the old. The drawer had never had company before.

It was a few blocks from there to the Krantz flat, east, with my collar up. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There were brass mailboxes with little windows, so the whole building can see who gets letters and who gets bills. ¶ Mrs. Krantz stood in the doorway of the parlor and looked at the place where Duchess ought to be, which is a thing you can do for a long time without it helping. ¶ No clerk, no doorman, nobody watching the stairs: nobody saw who came. ¶ If she went at ten, she went after the meeting, and everybody at the meeting had known the way in. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

The Lyric was a few blocks uptown and west, and I took it at a good clip. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ Only the lobby of the playhouse was lit, where the cleaners had started on the brass and stopped for a glass of tea. The poster by the doors still said THE RABBI’S DAUGHTER, ELEVENTH TRIUMPHANT WEEK, and under it somebody had written, in pencil, and twelfth. There was the usher’s seating chart on a clipboard, every seat sold a pencil cross. ¶ Pinsky was pointing his flashlight at a man who was talking. He had his seating chart under one arm on a clipboard, the way other men carry a newspaper. Lieb stood at the back with his hat in his hand, as if he had just come in or was just going. Doyle sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with his coat folded on his knees. ¶ Mrs. Krantz had pointed me at Lieb, who asked twice whether Duchess had papers at the meeting. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “I seat by the chart. Every seat sold is a cross, every cross has a face, and I could draw you the face.” ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Pinsky was mouthing the third act from the back of the house. “Who was in tonight?” I said. “You’d know. Knowing is most of your job.” ¶ He seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Eight, the curtain goes up, and I go to the back of the house, where an usher belongs and an actor once didn’t. Benny the pawnbroker’s runner was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight and nine, Belkin. Nobody else. Ten, Doyle and Belkin. And nobody else. Every cross on the chart has a face, and I’ve given you every face. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Benny, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “What was under the coat?” ¶ “I couldn’t say. Only that it moved.” ¶ Lieb said the Lyric at ten. Pinsky had Doyle, Belkin and Benny here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. Two stories about him at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. Whatever went out of the Krantz flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Benny. ¶ It turned out Belkin was three rows back with his hat over his eyes. ¶ Sweeping sunflower shells out of the gallery: that was the last I saw of him. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. She went at ten o’clock. Lieb had told me the Lyric at ten, and Pinsky’s list said otherwise. Doyle was at the Lyric at ten; Pinsky said so. Miss Nowak hadn’t told me where she was at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Benny at the Lyric at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Lieb now. Or I could find out first from the head waiter at Steinmetz’s who’d been in. ¶ Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t, and I didn’t know yet which was which.

Demos was writing covers in the book at his stand. ¶ I asked him who he’d seen come and go since the evening started. He went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Eight, the full room, and one stands at the stand like a traffic policeman in a tailcoat. Eight o’clock, Mabry. Nobody else. Nine, Lieb, Doyle, Miss Nowak and Mabry. Nobody else at all. Ten, Miss Nowak and Mabry. No one else, sir. Not in my room. Not without my say-so.” ¶ Demos had Lieb here at nine, same as he said. That put Miss Nowak here at ten, by his count. ¶ Seating a man who would rather have stood: that was the last I saw of him.

Midnight. I was in the office on Mulberry Street with my feet on the desk and the radio turned down low. My ribs hurt when I breathed deep, so I breathed shallow. Rain ran down the window in the lamplight, and I sat and listened to it and did not move much. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. My visitor didn’t sit until I told her to. She needed help, she said. That was the speech. ¶ “Fritz’s gone,” Dr. Hirsch said. “My dachshund. He sleeps in his basket by the stove, and he isn’t there.” ¶ I got up and offered her the chair, and she sat down in it carefully, the way people sit in chairs they don’t trust. ¶ “I sat in Sokol’s from eight until ten,” she said, “complaining to anybody who’d listen that my parlor window won’t latch, and that I was off to my sister’s for the night.” ¶ “What time are we talking about?” ¶ She had worked it out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “The woman upstairs heard feet on the stairs in the middle of the Atwater Kent Hour, which runs from ten o’clock.” ¶ “Who’d have a reason?” ¶ “I keep thinking about Miss Lowenthal,” she said. “She stood at my elbow at Sokol’s the whole time, and I didn’t think anything of it at the time. And she has always wanted Fritz, and asked me the price.” ¶ Then, smaller: “Russo, the card-room keeper, says my IOU to him is overdue, and that Fritz would square it. And Miss Nowak, the switchboard operator, owes Fishel money, and he wants it by Saturday.” ¶ “Ten dollars,” Dr. Hirsch said. “It’s what I have. Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

I went over the parlor, and then the door, and then the parlor again. ¶ Dr. Hirsch stood in the hall with her hands in her pockets, so as not to touch anything, which was more than whoever came before me had managed. ¶ The basket by the stove was empty. The parlor window was up six inches, and there was soot on the sill from the fire escape. Whoever it was had known which window. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Dr. Hirsch at Sokol’s between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made Sokol’s the place to start counting. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Sokol. ¶ He was slicing rye for a free lunch nobody eats. “You’ve been here all night,” I said. “Who came in, and when?” ¶ He looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶ “Eight’s the regulars. I pour before they ask. It saves them the strain. Fishel the bookmaker was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Miss Lowenthal, Russo and Dr. Hirsch telling the room about her window. Nobody else. Nine, Miss Lowenthal and Dr. Hirsch, still telling it. Nobody else at all. Ten, nobody else. That’s everybody. I counted the glasses twice. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Fishel, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “And under the coat?” ¶ “Something alive. It moved about.” ¶ Whatever went out of the Hirsch flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Fishel. The hour that mattered was ten. Sokol had Fishel. ¶ Looking in on the ovens through the door marked FLOUR: that was the last I saw of him.

Steinmetz’s was a couple of blocks downtown and east. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ The front of Steinmetz’s was dark, but the kitchen door at the back stood propped open on the alley, letting out steam and the sound of a pot being scrubbed by somebody with opinions about it. The chop house window still said CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS in gold, with the R gone from OYSTERS. There was the head waiter’s book on its stand by the door, every table and the time it sat written in ink. ¶ Demos was seating a man who would rather have stood. He had a white napkin over one forearm even off duty; he says he feels undressed without it. Miss Lowenthal had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. Miss Moskin sat with her coat on and her plate pushed away, finishing a glass of seltzer. ¶ Russo had said he was here at nine, and that Miss Lowenthal was with him at Sokol’s at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “I seat every table myself, and I write the covers in the book with the time beside them. Nobody sits in my room without my say-so.” ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

I found a chair at Steinmetz’s and sat down with the form. I read the night back to myself, from the office to here, and started at the top of the form. ¶ My ribs had let me breathe through all of it, if shallow. I thanked them and didn’t push my luck.

It was a few blocks from there to the Doyle flat, east, with my collar up. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There were brass mailboxes with little windows, so the whole building can see who gets letters and who gets bills. ¶ Doyle stood in the doorway of the parlor and looked at the place where Mimi ought to be, which is a thing you can do for a long time without it helping. ¶ No one was posted to see who came and went. ¶ If she went at ten, the flat had been empty, and anybody who’d heard Doyle at Steinmetz’s had known the way in. That was a room, more or less. It was a big room. ¶ It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it, and I said it.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, west to Steinmetz’s, a couple of blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ Steinmetz’s was a chop house on Grand Street with sawdust on the floor, white cloths on the tables and a slate by the door with the specials chalked on it. After midnight it had the late crowd: men off the newspaper trucks, a table of musicians, and a couple sharing one steak and not speaking. The head waiter had seated each of them as if they’d booked. There was one curtained booth at the back, for parties who don’t want to be a party. ¶ Demos was seating a man who would rather have stood. He had hair parted dead center and flattened with something that smells of violets. Dr. Hirsch was finishing a plate of something with the care of somebody who had paid for it. Teitel sat at a table near the kitchen door with a newspaper folded to the crossword and a cup of coffee going cold. Miss Nowak had a table by the window and a glass of tea gone cold. ¶ From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “I seat every table myself, and I write the covers in the book with the time beside them. Nobody sits in my room without my say-so.” ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Demos’s list had Miss Nowak here at eight and eleven. That was reason enough to ask. ¶ There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. She was pale under a cloche hat, with a red mark across the top of her head from the headset that her hair doesn’t quite hide. I asked her to walk me through her night, every stop of it. ¶ Miss Nowak took a moment to put the evening in order before she handed it over. ¶ “Number, please. Sorry. I mean, what would you like to know? I’ll put you through. I was at Steinmetz’s at eight, with Dr. Hirsch. Eight’s when I feel lucky. I don’t know why. It’s cost me a fortune. Around nine I went home, because my feet hurt, and stayed through ten. Teitel was there at nine; at ten it was just me. At eleven I went to Steinmetz’s to read the late paper over a plate of soup, with Dr. Hirsch and Teitel.” ¶ So here at eleven, with Dr. Hirsch and Teitel, and here at eight, which was what Demos had. At an hour that mattered, somebody else could vouch for it. ¶ Mrs. Sobel could tell me her own evening, and she was at the bakery cellar at Sokol’s. ¶ There was the slate by the door with the specials chalked on it, where the soup is crossed off at whatever hour you come in.

I said who I was, and Mrs. Sobel took it about as well as people do. ¶ “Demos has you at Steinmetz’s at nine. That’s one hour. Tell me about the others.” ¶ She nodded, as if it were a fair question, and maybe it was. ¶ “Sit, sit. I delivered half this street. I can deliver an evening. At eight I went up to Rafferty’s to see about some money owed, with Teitel. Eight, my feet go up, wherever I am. They’ve earned it. Come nine, I couldn’t settle, so I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee, and stayed through ten. Dr. Hirsch was there at nine; at ten it was just me. Around eleven I went round to the bakery cellar at Sokol’s to see a man about a horse, alone.” ¶ Mrs. Sobel said Steinmetz’s at ten. Demos had Dr. Hirsch, Teitel and Benny at Steinmetz’s at ten o’clock, and nobody else. Two stories about her at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. ¶ People always remember their own evenings well. It’s other people’s they go vague on. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. She went at ten o’clock. Dr. Hirsch, Mrs. Sobel and Miss Nowak were at Steinmetz’s while Doyle told the room; Teitel wasn’t. Dr. Hirsch was at Steinmetz’s at ten; Demos said so. Teitel was at Steinmetz’s at ten; Demos said so. Mrs. Sobel had told me Steinmetz’s at ten, and Demos’s list said otherwise. Miss Nowak said home at ten, and nobody else had said so yet. And whatever it was had gone to Benny at Steinmetz’s at eleven. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the landlady at Rafferty’s who’d been in. ¶ Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t, and I didn’t know yet which was which.

Mrs. Sobel had named Miss Moskin: the bakery cellar at Sokol’s at ten, the two of them. An owned-up story needs somebody to stand behind it. I got as near to her as manners allowed and said my name. She had a copy of Variety rolled in her coat pocket, folded open at the uptown casting news. ¶ I asked her for her evening, all of it, and kept the other story in my pocket. ¶ Miss Moskin answered straight off, the way people do with an evening they’ve only just finished. ¶ “Oh, my evening. Let me do it properly. You have to set the scene, or it doesn’t play. I was home from eight through nine. Come ten, I went to the bakery cellar at Sokol’s to meet Mrs. Sobel. Around eleven I went home to listen to the radio. Eleven, I’m tired, and I won’t admit it, because tired is for the chorus. Nobody was with me at eight, nine or eleven.” ¶ That put Mrs. Sobel here at ten, on her word. ¶ The landlady at Rafferty’s would know who’d been in. ¶ Everybody’s evening sounds tidy when they tell it. I wrote it down anyway.

There was a pot of tea stewing on the back of the stove at all hours, offered to everybody, and always too strong to refuse politely. I asked Mrs. Rafferty to give me the night the way only the landlady could: every face, every hour. ¶ She didn’t look at the room to answer. She didn’t need to. ¶ “Eight, I’ve the tea on and a sock on the egg and one ear on the door. Eight o’clock, Teitel and Mrs. Sobel. Nobody else. Nine, Teitel and Miss Nowak. Nobody else at all. Ten and eleven, nobody but me.” ¶ Miss Nowak said home at ten. The landlady had nobody here at ten o’clock. They couldn’t both be true, and she had no reason to be the wrong one. Mrs. Rafferty had Mrs. Sobel here at eight, same as she said. ¶ Counting the umbrellas on their hooks: that was the last I saw of her.

Russo’s place was a few blocks east, and I took it at a good clip. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Steam heat is the whole reason anybody pays what they pay to live in the Excelsior’s flats, and against the cold the lobby was warm enough to make your nose run. A row of brass mailboxes with little windows showed who had letters and who had bills. Upstairs a phonograph was playing the same record for the third time, to somebody who didn’t care for it. There was a gas ring in every kitchen, and on the third floor a smell of gas the tenants have been mentioning to each other since spring. ¶ Russo was in the chair by the table, with his head on his arms, like a man asleep over his accounts. He had a fresh deck in his breast pocket, still in its band, and his green eyeshade in his hand. ¶ Mrs. Krantz, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ Nobody minded who came and went. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him. I went through his papers with the lamp pulled close, the way you read a will you aren’t in. ¶ There was a page in there for everybody with a grudge against him, in a careful hand. Every one of them had a reason, and he’d written every one down. ¶ Mrs. Greco: a copy of the family will, with her name underlined. Miss Lowenthal: an IOU from her friend, with her name pencilled beside it. Dr. Hirsch: an IOU in her hand, and a note of what was still owing. Doyle: a note about him and the Peacock, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. ¶ A reason is the easy half. The other half was a way to the rat poison, and that was at the flats over Lipsky’s. ¶ The usher at the Lyric sees every face that comes through the door. I wanted all of them. ¶ I left it as I found it, give or take my fingerprints.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Pinsky. There were sunflower-seed shells in the gallery aisles, swept up every night and back by the second act. ¶ “Who was in tonight?” I said. “All of them, hour by hour, and who you didn’t know.” He didn’t look at the room to answer. He didn’t need to. ¶ “Seven, I open the doors and take up the chart. Every seat sold, a cross. I’m very good at crosses. Seven o’clock, Mrs. Greco, Miss Lowenthal and Doyle. Nobody else. Eight, Dr. Hirsch and Doyle. Nobody else at all. Nine, Doyle and Russo. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Mrs. Greco and Doyle. And nobody else. Every cross on the chart has a face, and I’ve given you every face.” ¶ I wrote down what Pinsky had at nine and ten, the hours that mattered: Doyle at both, Russo at nine and Mrs. Greco at ten. ¶ The one to ask was the janitor at the flats over Lipsky’s, who’d been there all night. ¶ Marking crosses on his seating chart: that was the last I saw of him.

I waited until Dr. Hirsch had finished what she was doing, which took longer than it needed to. “Pinsky has you at the Lyric at eight. That’s one hour. Tell me about the others.” ¶ She thought about it the way you’d think about a step in the dark, and then took it. ¶ “I keep good records. You’ll find my evening as precise as a filling, and about as much fun. At seven I went up to the flats over Lipsky’s to see about some money owed. At eight I had a ticket for the Lyric, with Doyle. Eight, I start to want a cigarette, and I make myself wait till nine. Discipline. Nine o’clock I went round to the back room at Wexler’s to see about a pledge. Then I locked up at ten and went to the Lyric to see the new play. Nobody was with me at seven, nine or ten.” ¶ Dr. Hirsch said the Lyric at ten. Pinsky had Mrs. Greco and Doyle at the Lyric at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ Nobody had fixed the chair with the short leg. In a room like that, a folded matchbook under the leg counts as a carpenter. ¶ I found a doorway and stood in it, and let the whole night go past me again, in order. ¶ Here’s what I had. Mrs. Krantz had said nine or ten, and Russo was at the Lyric at nine, alive. The rat poison came from the flats over Lipsky’s, so whoever used it had been there first. Doyle hadn’t. Dr. Hirsch had told me the Lyric at ten, and Pinsky’s list said otherwise. Mrs. Greco was at the Lyric at ten; Pinsky said so. Doyle was at the Lyric at nine and ten; Pinsky said so. Miss Lowenthal hadn’t told me where she was at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the janitor at the flats over Lipsky’s who’d been in. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

Dr. Hirsch had named Mabry: the back room at Wexler’s at ten, the two of them. An owned-up story needs somebody to stand behind it. I got as near to him as manners allowed and said my name. He had a pencil mustache trimmed so thin it looks drawn on, and might have been. ¶ I asked Mabry to tell me his evening, and who he’d seen. ¶ He didn’t seem to mind being asked, which is how most people seem. ¶ “Sure. Let me count it off for you. One, two, a-one two three four: seven o’clock. I was home from seven through nine, by myself. Then at ten I went to the back room at Wexler’s to meet Dr. Hirsch. Eight’s a slow hour. Slow tempo. I like a slow eight.” ¶ That put Dr. Hirsch here at ten, on his word. ¶ The janitor at the flats over Lipsky’s would have seen everybody who came in. ¶ I wrote it down. An evening told straight through always sounds simpler than it was to live.

Wojcik was shoveling coal into the boiler. ¶ “I need the whole night,” I said. “Everybody who was here, hour by hour, and anybody you didn’t know.” He went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Seven, I bank the boiler for the night. She sulks. Then she settles. Seven o’clock, Dr. Hirsch. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Mrs. Greco and Miss Lowenthal. Nobody else at all. Ten, nobody. The rat poison on the cellar shelf was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Dr. Hirsch, Mrs. Greco and Miss Lowenthal had been here earlier, when the rat poison was there for the taking. Wojcik had Dr. Hirsch here at seven, same as she said. The hour that mattered was ten. The list had nobody. ¶ Sweeping a stoop he had swept an hour ago: that was the last I saw of him.

I sat down at the kitchen table with the form, under the one good light. I read the night back to myself, from the office to here, and started at the top of the form. ¶ The new money would go in the drawer beside the old. It was getting crowded in there, and I didn’t mind.

I walked east to Doyle’s place. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. A dance hall upstairs was letting out, and the street was full of people saying goodnight at length. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There was a gas ring in every kitchen, and on the third floor a smell of gas the tenants have been mentioning to each other since spring. ¶ Doyle was where they’d found him, in the chair by the table, as if he’d sat down to wait for something and it had come. He had a carnation in his buttonhole and his little black book in his waistcoat, the rubber band still round it. ¶ Dr. Hirsch let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ Nobody there was paid to keep track of anybody. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I stood a moment and let my eyes catch up with the rest of me.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, so I went through them. Doyle kept his papers in a box file, and I sat down with it under the lamp. ¶ He had a page on everybody who held something against him, typed and clipped together, and every page said what the grudge was. He’d kept them square, so that nobody got top billing. ¶ Amato: a complaint he’d made against him, in triplicate. Teitel: an IOU in his hand, and a note of what was still owing. Mrs. Krantz: a bundle of her letters, tied with string and never given back. Mabry: an IOU from his friend, with his name pencilled beside it. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Rafferty’s and the chloral. ¶ Doyle had been here earlier in the evening, and that was worth the walk to Steinmetz’s. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Teitel. There was sawdust on the floor, fresh at noon and swept into the corners at closing, where it waits for morning. He had a necktie of his own so loud it seems to be shouting for the others. ¶ “Where were you tonight?” I said. “All of it. I’ve got time, and I hope you have.” He put down what he was holding and gave me his attention. ¶ “Sit, sit. My night you can have, and a tie to go with it. At seven I went to Rafferty’s for the company, and stayed through nine. Nine, business. I think about it; it doesn’t think about me. Mabry was there at seven; Mrs. Krantz was there at eight; Amato and Mrs. Krantz were there at nine. At ten I couldn’t settle, so I went to Steinmetz’s for coffee, with Amato.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Teitel said Rafferty’s at nine and Steinmetz’s at ten. I put it with the rest and didn’t argue with it yet. ¶ There was the slate by the door with the specials chalked on it, where the soup is crossed off at whatever hour you come in.

Demos’s list had Mabry here at eight. I wanted the rest of it in his own words. I sat down where he could see me, and didn’t hurry. He had a callus on his upper lip from the cornet, which he touches when he’s thinking. ¶ I asked him to walk me through his night, every stop of it. ¶ He had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “Sure. Let me count it off for you. One, two, a-one two three four: seven o’clock. I was home at Rafferty’s at seven, with Teitel. Then at eight I went to Steinmetz’s for the blue-plate supper, with Amato and Doyle. Come nine, I went round to the bakery cellar at Sokol’s to see a man about a horse. Around ten I went to Steinmetz’s for a glass of tea. Ten, I start hearing tunes in everything: car horns, the el, a woman laughing two streets off. At nine and ten I was on my own.” ¶ Mabry said Steinmetz’s at ten. Demos had Amato and Teitel here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ I wrote it down and underlined nothing. It was too early to underline. ¶ I sat down on the nearest thing that would hold me. It was the only thing in the room that didn’t want something from me. ¶ Here’s what I had. Dr. Hirsch had said nine or ten, and Doyle was at Steinmetz’s at nine, alive. The chloral came from Rafferty’s, so whoever used it had been there first. Mabry and Teitel had been at Rafferty’s earlier, when the chloral was there for the taking; Amato hadn’t. Amato was at Steinmetz’s at ten; Demos said so. Mabry had told me Steinmetz’s at ten, and Demos’s list said otherwise. Teitel was at Steinmetz’s at ten; Demos said so. Mrs. Krantz hadn’t told me where she was at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

Mrs. Krantz’s flat was a couple of blocks east. The dance hall crowd would have finished saying goodnight by now. It had taken them long enough, but they’d done it properly. ¶ The milkman had been to the Excelsior and left a bottle outside every door on every floor, and nobody in the building had seen him come or go. That’s the kind of building it is: no doorman, no janitor in sight, and a landlord who lives uptown and sends a man on the first of the month. There were marble stairs to the second floor and plain wood after that, where the builder ran out of marble or interest. ¶ Mrs. Krantz was counting bills with a rubber thumb. She was a stout woman in gray, buttoned to the throat, carrying a leather satchel with a brass lock on it. ¶ Amato had said Mrs. Krantz was with him at Rafferty’s at nine, and that was worth the walk. ¶ Nobody kept watch there. It wasn’t that kind of place. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

A couple of blocks uptown and west, and I was at the bakery cellar at Sokol’s. The sky had gone gray along the bottom edge, and a milk wagon was working the next block. ¶ I found the bakery cellar at Sokol’s. It was the kind of place people go to so they can say they were somewhere else. There was the door from the bakery to the bar, with FLOUR painted on it, which has fooled nobody for years. ¶ Fishel was behind the counter, writing in a ledger by the light of a green-shaded lamp. He had a pearl-gray fedora he never takes off indoors, because, he says, it’s worth more than the indoors. ¶ Fishel had the room from the hour that mattered, and not before. Before that, he said, it was anybody’s. ¶ Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

Midnight. My office was a room at the top of the stairs on Mulberry Street, with a desk, a lamp and a coat stand that had outlasted two tenants. I had money in the desk drawer for once. I’d opened the drawer twice to make sure, and once more just to visit. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor came in talking about the stairs, how many and how dark, and was still counting them sitting down. I’d never dared. ¶ “Beatrice Lowenthal,” she said, and put her hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Francis Doyle’s neighbor. He’s dead, and I don’t like how.” ¶ Doyle was the alderman’s clerk. At half past eleven, Amato, who’d come to return a borrowed book, found him in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street. The police had a look and called it a robbery gone wrong. ¶ “When?” ¶ “Here’s what they don’t want to hear,” Miss Lowenthal said. “The police surgeon puts it at nine or ten o’clock, by the warmth of him.” ¶ “He’d been at the Lyric earlier in the evening,” she said. “His usual.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad he’s gone?” ¶ “Ask about Mabry,” Miss Lowenthal said. “He was squeezing Mabry’s friend for money. I had that from the woman downstairs.” ¶ She counted fifty dollars onto the blotter and kept a finger on the last bill. “Find out who did it. Then tell me first.” ¶ I took the money and my hat, in that order.

I got down and went over the floor with a flashlight, board by board. ¶ Miss Lowenthal stayed by the door. People in a room with a dead man stand where they can leave. ¶ A revolver lay under the chair, one chamber fired. I knew whose it was before I looked: it belongs in the hall-stand drawer at Rafferty’s, and the whole block knows it, because the landlady shows it to anybody who’s late with the rent. Doyle had been shot from across his own table. ¶ So the gun came from Rafferty’s. Doyle died at nine or ten, and whoever fired it had been at Rafferty’s before that, to take it. ¶ That was all the room had to tell me, and it had told it without being asked twice.

I set off uptown and west for the Lyric. It was a few blocks. Behind a window somewhere a radiator was knocking, trying to wake a building that didn’t want waking. ¶ Over the doors of the Lyric the marquee was dripping rain onto Second Avenue letter by letter. In the lobby the carpet had a dark wet path from the doors to the center aisle, and somebody had laid newspapers across it, this week’s reviews on top, the good ones. There were sunflower-seed shells in the gallery aisles, swept up every night and back by the second act. ¶ Pinsky was sweeping sunflower shells out of the gallery. He had a white mustache waxed to points so fine they quiver when he disapproves. Mabry, in a sailor’s pea coat, was sitting near the front, very upright, with both hands on the back of the seat in front. ¶ Doyle had been here earlier in the evening. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “I seat by the chart. Every seat sold is a cross, every cross has a face, and I could draw you the face.” ¶ Somewhere behind the curtain a rope creaked, which in a theater counts as conversation.

Miss Lowenthal had pointed me at Mabry. That was reason enough to ask. ¶ I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. He had a pencil mustache trimmed so thin it looks drawn on, and might have been. “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” ¶ He didn’t seem to mind being asked, which is how most people seem. ¶ “Sure. Let me count it off for you. One, two, a-one two three four: seven o’clock. I was home at Rafferty’s from seven through nine. Miss Nowak was there at seven; Miss Nowak, Mrs. Krantz and Teitel were there at eight; Miss Nowak and Teitel were there at nine. Eight’s a slow hour. Slow tempo. I like a slow eight. Then at ten I went round to Mrs. Krantz’s for a game of gin.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Mabry said Mrs. Krantz’s flat. I put it with the rest and didn’t argue with it yet. ¶ There was the daughter’s death scene in the third act, eleven minutes long, which the usher mouths along with from the back of the house, every word. ¶ I found a doorway and stood in it, and let the whole night go past me again, in order. ¶ Here’s what I had. Miss Lowenthal had said nine or ten o’clock. The revolver had come from Rafferty’s. I had an evening from Mabry, and a list from Pinsky. I didn’t have Amato’s, Miss Nowak’s, Mrs. Krantz’s or Teitel’s evenings yet. ¶ That was everything I had, and it wasn’t enough yet.

Mrs. Rafferty was counting the umbrellas on their hooks. I asked her to take me through the night, hour by hour, everybody in the place. ¶ She answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Seven, I take my chair and the mending, and the house knows I’m on. Seven o’clock, Miss Nowak and Mabry. Nobody else. Eight, Miss Nowak, Mabry, Mrs. Krantz and Teitel. Nobody else at all. Nine, Miss Nowak, Mabry and Teitel. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Amato and Teitel. And that’s the lot. If there’d been another one on my stairs, I’d have his name and his mother’s maiden name. The revolver in the hall-stand drawer was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ The hour that mattered was ten. Mrs. Rafferty had Amato and Teitel. ¶ Pouring tea nobody asked for: that was the last I saw of her.

Mrs. Krantz was writing in a rent book with a fountain pen. “Mrs. Rafferty has you at Rafferty’s at eight. Now tell me the rest of it, from the beginning.” ¶ She went slowly, the way people do who like to get things right. ¶ “My evening is in order. Everything I do is in order. You may have it in order. I was home at seven, alone. Come eight, I went round to Rafferty’s to borrow a collar stud, with Miss Nowak, Mabry and Teitel. Around nine I went to the Lyric to see the new play, with Amato and Doyle. At ten I had a game of gin at home, with Mabry. Ten, I think about the first of the month. I always think about the first of the month.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Mrs. Krantz said home, here at Mrs. Krantz’s flat. I didn’t believe it or disbelieve it. I wrote it down. ¶ Drinking lemon tea with the lemon left in: that was the last I saw of her.

I waited until Miss Nowak had finished what she was doing, which took longer than it needed to. I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. ¶ She thought about it the way you’d think about a step in the dark, and then took it. ¶ “I don’t mind telling you. I’m very good at times; it’s my whole job. I was home at Rafferty’s from seven through nine. Mabry was there at seven; Mabry, Mrs. Krantz and Teitel were there at eight; Mabry and Teitel were there at nine. Then at ten I went round to the back booth at Sokol’s to see a man about a horse, with Fishel. Ten I’m supposed to be in. Number four on the card. I know number four by heart.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Miss Nowak said the back booth at Sokol’s. I wrote it down and left it standing, for now. ¶ It turned out Fishel was in the corner, out of the light. ¶ Flour gets on everybody who goes through to the bar, and the whole block could find Sokol’s by the white footprints, the police included.

I sat at the end of the table with the form, where the light was worst. I put down what I had, and what I had would have to stand up by itself. ¶ The new money would go in the desk drawer with the old. The drawer had never had company before.

I walked uptown and east to the Feldman flat. It was a good walk, and I took all of it. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ I went to the Feldman flat on the third floor of 40 Avenue B. It was a good flat for Avenue B, with a carpet in the hall and lace on every table, kept the way people keep things they have finished paying for. A china shepherdess stood on a doily, looking at the room with painted patience. ¶ Feldman showed me where the watch had been kept and touched the place once, lightly, the way you touch a sore tooth. ¶ It was the kind of place nobody kept an eye on. ¶ If it went at ten, the flat had been empty, and anybody who’d heard Feldman at the Orpheum had known the way in. That was a room, more or less. It was a big room. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

A few blocks west, and I was at the Orpheum. Close enough to make it there and back in an hour, which I wrote down. A trolley went by, with the same people asleep on it for all I knew, going round again for the company. ¶ I went in at the Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight. The last show had let out, the screen was a big gray blank, and the rows were full of peanut shells and dropped programs. Above the lobby doors a painted plaster mask grinned down at everybody who came in, with the tip of its nose missing. ¶ Zeldin was in the lobby, counting the evening’s ticket stubs into bundles and putting a rubber band round each one. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. Bidwell sat in the back row with her hat on her knee, watching the picture without looking at it. Hauck sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with his coat folded on his knees. ¶ Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Zeldin. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Bidwell had moved down a few rows since I came in, as if the show might start again if she waited long enough. ¶ I got as near to her as manners allowed and said my name. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, she wore clothes too good to have been bought. She’d made every stitch. ¶ “Zeldin has you here at nine. I’m asking everybody the same. Where else were you tonight?” ¶ She looked at me for a while first, as if deciding what sort of question it was. ¶ “At eight I took a letter round to Kowalski’s, with Whitfield and Abramowitz. Then at nine I had a ticket for the Orpheum, and stayed the rest of the evening. Hauck, Whitfield and Stannard were there at nine; at ten it was just me.” ¶ Bidwell said the Orpheum at ten. Zeldin had Hauck, Stannard and Benny here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it. ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at ten o’clock. Bidwell had told me the Orpheum at ten, and Zeldin’s list said otherwise. Hauck was at the Orpheum at ten; Zeldin said so. Whitfield hadn’t told me where he was at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Benny at the Orpheum at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Bidwell now. Or I could find out first from the landlady at Kowalski’s who’d been in. ¶ Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t, and I didn’t know yet which was which.

I waited for a gap in Mrs. Kowalski’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. ¶ I asked Mrs. Kowalski to give me the night the way only the landlady could: every face, every hour. She counted it off on her fingers, and ran out of fingers before she ran out of night. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Bidwell, Whitfield and Abramowitz. Nobody else. Nine, Abramowitz. Nobody else at all. Ten, Whitfield and Abramowitz. Nobody else, that hour.” ¶ Mrs. Kowalski had Bidwell here at eight, same as she said. That put Whitfield here at ten, by her count. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

Midnight. My office was a desk, two chairs and a window on Mulberry Street, and the window was the only one of them with a view. The fee sat on the blotter where I’d dropped it, more money than the desk usually saw in a month. I left the lamp burning longer than I needed, so the two of them could get acquainted. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor came in talking about the stairs, how many and how dark, and was still counting them sitting down. I’d never dared. ¶ “It’s my late husband’s gold watch,” Quill said. “I keep it under a glass dome on the parlor mantel, and it’s gone.” ¶ “I sat in the Kit Kat from eight until ten,” he said, “telling anybody who’d listen that I was off to my sister’s for the night, and the key was under the mat.” ¶ “And when did the watch go missing?” ¶ He had it worked out, the way people do when they can’t sleep. “St. Teresa’s was striking ten when the woman across the hall heard the door.” ¶ “Who’d want to take it?” ¶ “It’s Vogel,” Quill said. “She stood at my elbow at the Kit Kat the whole time. And she is three weeks behind on the rent, and once asked what the watch would pawn for.” ¶ He looked at the window, then back at me. “Feldman, a typist, lost her job on Friday, and asked me what the watch was worth. And Stannard, a bus conductor, and I haven’t spoken since the business over the coal bill.” ¶ He put ten dollars on the desk and smoothed it flat with his palm. “Find out who, and where.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

I went over Quill’s parlor from the door to the far wall, slowly. ¶ Quill stood in the hall with his hands in his pockets, so as not to touch anything, which was more than whoever came before me had managed. ¶ The glass dome on the mantel was empty. The key was back under the mat, and there wasn’t a mark on the door. Whoever it was had known exactly where to look. ¶ So it was somebody who’d heard Quill at the Kit Kat between eight and ten, and had come here after. That made the Kit Kat the place to start counting. ¶ Somebody at the Kit Kat would have kept count of faces, and that would be the doorkeeper. ¶ The china shepherdess went on minding her doily. Some jobs are small and you do them anyway.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Ruggiero. I asked her for a minute, and she gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. ¶ “I need the whole night,” I said. “Everybody who was here, hour by hour, and anybody you didn’t know.” She started at the top of the evening and went down it like a column of figures. ¶ “Benny the pawnbroker’s runner was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Mr. Quill telling the room about his key. Nobody else. Nine, Feldman, Vogel and Mr. Quill, still telling it. Nobody else at all. Ten, just Benny. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Benny, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “And under the coat?” ¶ “Something small. I didn’t see what.” ¶ Feldman and Vogel heard about the key at nine. Stannard never heard Quill tell the room. Whatever went out of the Quill flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Benny. For ten, the hour that mattered, Ruggiero had Benny. ¶ I could feel the door behind me, ready to swing wide the moment I turned. It’s nice to be wanted gone that efficiently.

Rafferty’s lay a couple of blocks uptown and west. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Rafferty’s rooming house on Mott Street smelled of boiled cabbage and lye soap, and the stairs creaked a different note on every step. A framed sign in the hall said that baths were on Saturdays and the hot water was by arrangement. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Vogel was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. Alfano was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ Feldman had said she was here at eight, with Vogel, and that was worth the walk. Mrs. Rafferty kept the house, and the house kept no secrets from her, or not for long. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

I sat on a hard chair in the hall with the form on my knee. A name wants a line under it, and a line wants somebody’s word under that. I went down the form one line at a time. ¶ The fee on my blotter would have company soon. The lamp could make the introductions.

The Abramowitz flat lay a couple of blocks downtown and east. The fog had swallowed the far end of the street and was in no hurry to give it back. ¶ I went up to the Abramowitz flat over the delicatessen on Second Avenue. The delicatessen downstairs was shut, but the smell of pickles and smoked fish came up the stairs with me and stayed for the visit. A china shepherdess stood on a doily, looking at the room with painted patience. ¶ Abramowitz showed me where the cigarette case had been kept and touched the place once, lightly, the way you touch a sore tooth. ¶ Anybody could have come and gone, and nobody would have known it. ¶ If it went at eleven, the flat had been empty, and anybody who’d heard Abramowitz at Hanley’s had known the way in. That was a room, more or less. It was a big room. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

It was a fair few blocks to Hanley’s, uptown and east. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. Behind a window somewhere a radiator was knocking, trying to wake a building that didn’t want waking. ¶ Hanley’s, a saloon with sawdust on the floor, was the oldest bar on Houston Street and acted like it. The sawdust gets changed on Mondays whether it needs it or not, and it always needs it. There was a radio on a shelf behind the bar, playing dance music so softly it might have been coming from next door. ¶ Prentiss was behind the bar, setting clean glasses upside down in rows on a towel. She had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Zeldin was on a stool with his hat pushed back, turning a coin over and over on the bar. Renfro had a stool at the end of the bar and was looking at the mirror behind it, which looked back. Winslow sat at a little table by the wall, with a beer going flat in front of him. ¶ Nobody gets a drink in a place like that without the one who pours it looking at them, and Prentiss looks at everybody twice. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Prentiss’s list had Zeldin here at eight, so that was where I went next. I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, he wore clothes too good to have been bought. He’d made every stitch. ¶ I asked him to walk me through his night, every stop of it. ¶ He minded a little, then decided it was cheaper not to. ¶ “I was at Hanley’s at eight, with Winslow. Then at nine I went to the Delmonico rooms to help write letters home, and stayed through ten, with Renfro. Come eleven, I went down to Hanley’s to hear the piano, on my own.” ¶ Zeldin said Hanley’s at eleven. Prentiss had Renfro, Winslow and Lou here at eleven o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it. ¶ I lit a cigarette I didn’t want, to give my hands something to do while my head did the rest. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at eleven o’clock. Bidwell, Zeldin and Winslow were at Hanley’s while Abramowitz told the room; Renfro wasn’t. Zeldin had told me Hanley’s at eleven, and Prentiss’s list said otherwise. Renfro was at Hanley’s at eleven; Prentiss said so. Winslow was at Hanley’s at eleven; Prentiss said so. Bidwell hadn’t told me where he was at eleven, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out what Bidwell had to say for himself. ¶ Some of it would hold and some of it wouldn’t, and I didn’t know yet which was which.

I headed downtown for the Delmonico rooms, a fair few blocks away. The fog was still at the end of whatever street I was on. It followed me better than I follow people. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. The stair had a brass rod on every step, and one of them was loose. ¶ Mrs. Lefkowitz sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Bidwell was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ Mrs. Lefkowitz kept the house, and the house kept no secrets from her, or not for long. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

The card room was a good walk uptown and west. A milkman was leaving bottles on the steps, two by two, as quietly as a man can do anything with glass. ¶ The card room over the Bowery garage had no sign and no name on the door, only a light under it. A gambling room doesn’t advertise. The people who need it always find it. A wooden chair with one short leg stood by the wall, and rocked whenever anything touched it. ¶ Dandridge was shuffling a deck with one hand, not to play, just to keep the hand busy. Hands clasped in front, weight back on her heels, she stood as though poured there and left to set. ¶ A game is only as good as the people at it, so whoever runs one takes a good look at everybody who comes up the stairs. ¶ It was the sort of room people say they were never in. I made a note that I was.

I sat down with the form and a pencil. I read the night back to myself, from the office to here, and started at the top of the form. ¶ The rent envelope on my desk could stop worrying. For once I had something to put in it.

Crowninshield’s place was a few blocks downtown and east. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ I went to Crowninshield’s rooms behind the tailor’s on Allen Street. The passage from Allen Street smelled of pressed wool and machine oil, and it ended at a door the police had pulled shut on their way out. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Crowninshield lay on the floor where he’d fallen, on his side, with his knees drawn up a little. ¶ Hochstetter let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ There was nobody on duty, and nobody to ask who had been by. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, so I went through them. I went through his papers with the lamp pulled close, the way you read a will you aren’t in. ¶ The papers held a page on everybody who had it in for him, kept like a doctor’s files, one grudge to a page and every page full. ¶ Hargrove: a column of payments, every month for years, and her name at the top. Schilling: an IOU for four hundred dollars, in her hand. Colquitt: the lease on a shop, the rent owing, and a carbon of his letter calling it in. Bidwell: a court transcript, his own testimony against his brother. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from the Delmonico rooms and the revolver. ¶ The ticket seller at the Bijou sees every face that comes through the door. I wanted all of them. ¶ The empty birdcage hung in its corner. It had been empty a long time and was used to it.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Tramonti. I asked Mrs. Tramonti for a minute, and she gave me one, and kept an eye on the room the whole of it. ¶ “I need the whole night,” I said. “Everybody who was here, hour by hour, and anybody you didn’t know.” She seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Hargrove and Schilling. Nobody else. Eight, Hargrove and Bidwell. Nobody else at all. Nine, Hargrove and Schilling. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, nobody but me. The revolver in the hall-stand drawer was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Hargrove, Bidwell and Schilling had been here earlier, when the revolver was there for the taking. Colquitt hadn’t been here while it was there to take. That put Hargrove and Schilling here at nine, by her count. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

The Bijou lay a couple of blocks uptown and east. The cold was at its worst, the kind that finds the hole in your glove you didn’t know you had. ¶ I went to the Bijou, a picture house on Clinton Street. It was a narrow little house with a ticket window the size of a mail slot and a smell of floor polish and oranges. A life-size cardboard cowboy stood in the lobby, fading, and tipping his hat at the box office. ¶ Lathrop was by the inner doors, sorting a stack of programs into the ones that could be used again and the ones that couldn’t. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. Hargrove was in the lobby, reading the bills for next week as if they might change. Colquitt was in the back row with a bag of peanuts, shelling them one at a time and not eating them. Schilling sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with her coat folded on her knees. ¶ Bidwell had said he was here at seven, and that Hargrove was with him at his place at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. Nobody gets into a theater without going past the front of the house, and the front of the house was Lathrop. ¶ I stood at the back a moment, where the people who work a theater always stand.

Schilling was reading the program for the third time, in case the cast had changed. ¶ I sat one seat over. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, she wore clothes too good to have been bought. She’d made every stitch. ¶ “Lathrop has you here at eight. Fill in the rest of the evening for me, in order.” ¶ She had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “At seven I went round to the Delmonico rooms to borrow a collar stud, with Hargrove. Eight o’clock I had a ticket for the Bijou, with Colquitt and Crowninshield. Then at nine I went round to the Delmonico rooms to return a borrowed umbrella, with Hargrove. Come ten, I went to the second show at the Bijou, by myself.” ¶ Schilling said the Bijou at ten. Lathrop had Hargrove and Colquitt here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. The rest held where I could check it: Mrs. Tramonti had her at the Delmonico rooms at seven and at the Delmonico rooms at nine, same as she said. ¶ Somebody at Sokol’s back room would have kept count of faces, and that would be the man who takes the slips. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it.

I waited for a gap in Sweeney’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. ¶ I asked him who’d been here tonight, and said I’d take it untidy, the way it happened. Sweeney went through it the way you’d count change, carefully and out loud. ¶ “Ten o’clock, Bidwell. Nobody else. I came on at ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ That put Bidwell here at ten, by his count. ¶ The toes were still ready to be somewhere else. So were mine, but mine were further from the door.

From there to Callahan’s place was a couple of blocks. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ Callahan’s walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street was one room at the top of the stairs. The police had been and gone, and the room had the look rooms get when a lot of people have stood in them and nobody sat down. A coal merchant’s calendar hung by the stove, still turned to last month. ¶ Callahan was in the chair with his head to one side, like a man dozing over the evening paper, except that nobody dozes that still. ¶ Weisglass was there, with a cup of something she hadn’t touched and her coat still buttoned. ¶ There was no one to notice who passed through. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him. His papers were in a box under the bed, the kind of box a man keeps for the things he’d rather not file. ¶ The papers held a page on everybody who had it in for him, kept like a doctor’s files, one grudge to a page and every page full. ¶ Ellery: the lease on a shop, the rent owing, and a carbon of his letter calling it in. Pickering: a file he’d kept on him, thick enough to matter. Stannard: a notice to quit, from when he threw her out of a lease. Crowninshield: the order that closed her business, with his signature on it. ¶ I put the pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from Kowalski’s and the laudanum. ¶ Weisglass had pointed me at Stannard, and that was worth the walk to Moe’s. ¶ The coal merchant’s calendar had a picture of a smiling family round a stove. Last month had been good to somebody.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Stannard. ¶ I took the stool beside her and let her finish her drink before I spoiled it. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, she wore clothes too good to have been bought. She’d made every stitch. I asked her for her evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. ¶ She had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “At seven I went round to Kowalski’s to return a borrowed umbrella. Come eight, I wanted company, so I went to Moe’s, with Crowninshield and Callahan. Around nine I went to the Palace to sit through the double bill. At ten I went over to Moe’s for a drink. Nobody was with me at seven, nine or ten.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Stannard said the Palace at nine and Moe’s at ten. I put it with the rest and didn’t argue with it yet. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it.

Hauck’s list had Crowninshield here at seven, eight and ten, so I went over. I leaned on the bar next to her and ordered nothing, which got noticed. She was neat in a way that took effort: every button done, the collar pinned, the hair flat. The hands stayed folded until she needed one, and then only the one. ¶ I asked Crowninshield to walk me through her night, every stop of it. She didn’t seem to mind being asked, which is how most people seem. ¶ “I was at Moe’s from seven through eight. Ellery was there at seven; Stannard and Callahan were there at eight. Around nine I dropped a parcel off at Kowalski’s, with Ellery. At ten I went to Moe’s, as most nights, with Ellery. Walking over to Moe’s at ten I passed Pickering on Grand Street, going fast, no hat.” ¶ So here at ten and seven, with Ellery, which was what Hauck had. That much of it stood up, and it stood up where I could check it. The part worth keeping came last. Grand Street was where Callahan lived. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully.

I headed west for the Palace, a few blocks away. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ I went in at the back row of the Palace, a picture house on Delancey Street. It was a big shabby picture house with the gilt coming off the plaster, and the back row sat under the balcony, where the light from the screen never quite reached. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Bellucci stood at the back of the house with a flashlight, pointed at the floor, ready.
