The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. ¶ Bellucci sees every face that comes in from the street, if only for the second it takes to look at a ticket. ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

I set off downtown and east for Pickering’s flat. It was a few blocks. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ I went round to Pickering’s flat on Norfolk Street. It was a walk-up like every walk-up on Norfolk Street: a hall that smelled of other people’s suppers and a stair with a bend in it. A kettle sat on a gas ring on the shelf, gone cold. ¶ Pickering was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into his collar. ¶ Nobody there was paid to keep track of anybody. ¶ It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it, and I said it.

Midnight. My office on Mulberry Street had my name on the door, a bottle in the drawer and the landlady’s bill under the bottle, where I could keep an eye on it. I favored the side that still ached and lowered myself into the chair in three stages, like a drawbridge. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. My visitor came in with an apology for the hour and a second one for the first, and was well into a third before sitting down. ¶ “My name is Thomas Kavanagh,” he said. “I’m Alonzo Prentiss’s business partner. He’s dead.” ¶ The dead man had been a pawnbroker. He was found in his own walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street at half past eleven. The one who found him was Havemeyer, who’d come to return a borrowed book. The police wrote it down as his heart. ¶ “When?” ¶ He said it slowly, so that I’d get it right. “The coroner says laudanum in a drink, taken at nine or ten o’clock; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “He was at Moskowitz’s earlier in the evening,” my client said. “His usual. He liked his usual.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad he’s gone?” ¶ “There’s Bellucci,” Kavanagh said. “I don’t like gossip, but he owed Prentiss the rent on a shop, and it was being called in. The woman downstairs told me.” ¶ He opened his bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

I bent over the table and took it a piece at a time, from one edge to the other. ¶ Kavanagh didn’t come in. I didn’t ask him to. ¶ A cup of cocoa sat on the table, gone cold and bitter at the bottom. Beside it was a brown bottle with a druggist’s label made out to Rafferty’s. Somebody had made Prentiss cocoa, which is a kind thing to do, and then made sure it was the last. ¶ So the laudanum came from Rafferty’s, and laudanum takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Prentiss had been at Rafferty’s earlier, to get it. ¶ I wrote down what I’d found and where, before I could start remembering it differently.

It was a good walk to Rafferty’s, uptown and west. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. The cat from the step was on a different step now. Even the cat had somewhere to be. ¶ Rafferty’s rooming house on Mott Street smelled of boiled cabbage and lye soap, and the stairs creaked a different note on every step. A holy picture hung in the hall, with a little lamp in a red glass under it. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Bellucci, in a camel coat, was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. Sirkin, with a bandaged hand, answered the door in his stocking feet, with the lamp behind him. Havemeyer, in a grey fedora, was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. ¶ The laudanum had come from here. Kavanagh had pointed me at Bellucci, and that was worth the walk. ¶ Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Rafferty had the look of a landlady who made a point of it. ¶ A clock in the hall was keeping time for nobody in particular.

Havemeyer had said he was here at eight and ten, and the landlady would know who’d been in. ¶ I went over to Mrs. Rafferty and waited until she had a moment, which took a moment. I asked her to count the night for me, face by face. ¶ She seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Lathrop, Dettweiler and Sirkin. Nobody else. Eight, Dettweiler, Sirkin and Havemeyer. Nobody else at all. Nine, Dettweiler and Sirkin. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Bellucci and Sirkin. Nobody else. The laudanum in my medicine cupboard was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Mrs. Rafferty had Sirkin at both, Dettweiler at nine and Bellucci at ten. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it. ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. Kavanagh had said nine or ten o’clock. The laudanum had come from Rafferty’s. I had an evening from Havemeyer, and a list from Mrs. Rafferty. I didn’t have Lathrop’s, Bellucci’s, Dettweiler’s or Sirkin’s evenings yet. ¶ That was everything I had, and it wasn’t enough yet.

I waited for a gap in Margolis’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. ¶ I asked her who’d been here tonight, and said I’d take it untidy, the way it happened. She looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Bellucci and Havemeyer. Nobody else. Eight and nine, Bellucci and Prentiss. Nobody else at all. Ten, somebody in a green hat, back to the room, I couldn’t swear who. Nobody else, that hour.” ¶ At nine and ten, when it counted, Margolis had Bellucci and Prentiss at nine and somebody in a green hat at ten. ¶ I read the slate by the door again. Still no soup, which seemed about right for the night.

It was no distance to the Palace: round the corner, and there it was. Delancey Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ The back row of the Palace, a picture house on Delancey Street, was the darkest place on Delancey Street you could sit for a dime. That’s what the back row is for, and the management has known it for years. A bare bulb hung on a cord, swinging a little whenever the door shut. ¶ Quill was by the inner doors, sorting a stack of programs into the ones that could be used again and the ones that couldn’t. The uniform coat had the theater’s name on the collar, and the cap had been reshaped by a hundred hot nights. ¶ Havemeyer had said he was here at nine. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ Quill sees every face that comes in from the street, if only for the second it takes to look at a ticket. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

I walked downtown and east to Lathrop’s flat. It was a good walk, and I took all of it. Water ran down the gutters in a hurry, carrying a newspaper with it. ¶ Lathrop’s flat on Pitt Street was two rooms and a kitchen at the top of the stairs, behind a doormat that had given up saying welcome years ago. A kettle sat on a gas ring on the shelf, gone cold. ¶ Lathrop, in a sailor’s pea coat, was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. Round and pleasant and dressed a little too well for a cigar store, he kept his eyes on the door, in case it was the police or a winner. ¶ Dettweiler had said Lathrop was with him at Rafferty’s at seven. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ Nobody kept a list of who came and went, on paper or in their head. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

I sat on a hard chair in the hall with the form on my knee. I read the night back to myself, from the office to here, and started at the top of the form. ¶ I stayed where I was. Getting up is three stages as well, and I wasn’t ready to start.

I walked east to the Krantz flat. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There were marble stairs to the second floor and plain wood after that, where the builder ran out of marble or interest. ¶ Mrs. Krantz showed me where the spoons had been kept and touched the place once, lightly, the way you touch a sore tooth. ¶ It was the kind of place nobody kept an eye on. ¶ If it went at ten, it went after the supper, and everybody at the supper had known the way in. ¶ I found somewhere to stand that wasn’t in anybody’s way.

It was a fair few blocks from there to the Peacock, uptown and west, with my collar up. A trolley went by, with the same people asleep on it for all I knew, going round again for the company. ¶ Down in the cellar club it was the last set, for the serious drinkers, and the band had slowed to match them. Smoke hung under the low ceiling like a second ceiling. Through the velvet curtain at the foot of the stairs, four couples on the dance floor were holding each other up. There was the smell of lilies coming down through the floorboards from the undertaker’s, which the gin covers until about one. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was eating a pickle out of a paper bag on her stool. She had big hands folded in her lap, the knuckles flattened by a career she doesn’t discuss. Belkin had a table near the empty bandstand and was tapping the time of a song nobody was playing. Lieb had a table near the empty dance floor and was turning a glass slowly round and round by its stem. ¶ Mrs. Krantz had pointed me at Belkin, who counted the spoons out loud at the supper. It was reason enough to look. ¶ From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “Every face comes to my slot first. I don’t like most of them, so the ones I let in, I remember.” ¶ I found a place at the bar and let the room settle around me.

Mrs. Szabo was knitting a muffler with no end in sight. ¶ I asked her who she’d seen come and go since the evening started. She seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Eight, the dinner crowd. Dinner crowd’s easy. They only want to sit down. Miss Marsh the cigarette girl was there all evening, every hour of it. Eight o’clock, Mabry. Nobody else. Nine and ten, Belkin and Mabry. Nobody else. I’d remember. I don’t like enough faces to forget any. Eleven: somebody came in with something under a coat and went straight to Marsh, and it changed hands. I was watching the coat, not the face.” ¶ “Did you see what was under the coat?” ¶ “Something small. I didn’t ask it its name.” ¶ Lieb said the Peacock at ten. Mrs. Szabo had Belkin, Mabry and Miss Marsh here at ten o’clock, and nobody else. One of them was wrong. Whatever went out of the Krantz flat, something came in here under a coat at eleven and went to Miss Marsh. ¶ It turned out Mabry was at the far end of the bar, nursing something. ¶ Explaining to a large man why he was going home: that was the last I saw of her. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at ten o’clock. Belkin was at the Peacock at ten; Mrs. Szabo said so. Lieb had told me the Peacock at ten, and Mrs. Szabo’s list said otherwise. Teitel hadn’t told me where he was at ten, and nobody else had either. And whatever it was had gone to Marsh, the cigarette girl at the Peacock at eleven. ¶ I could put it to Lieb now. Or I could find out first from the janitor at the flats over Lipsky’s who’d been in. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

Wojcik was answering the fourth floor by banging a pipe with a wrench. I asked him who’d been in tonight, everybody, hour by hour. ¶ He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Eight, I sit. Pipe. Steps. Street. Eight o’clock, Amato. Nobody else. Nine, Teitel, Lieb and Amato. Nobody else at all. Ten, Teitel and Amato. That’s all. Nobody gets up that stoop without stepping on my shadow.” ¶ Wojcik had Lieb here at nine, same as he said. That put Teitel here at ten, by his count. ¶ Shoveling coal into the boiler: that was the last I saw of him.

Midnight. My office was a desk, two chairs and a window on Mulberry Street, and the window was the only one of them with a view. The fee sat on the blotter where I’d dropped it, more money than the desk usually saw in a month. I left the lamp burning longer than I needed, so the two of them could get acquainted. ¶ A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock. My visitor came in talking about the stairs, how many and how dark, and was still counting them sitting down. I’d never dared. ¶ “It’s my late husband’s gold watch,” Dr. Hirsch said. “I keep it under a glass dome on the parlor mantel, and it’s gone.” ¶ “I had people in at eight for cards,” she said. “Russo and Miss Lowenthal. Nobody else.” ¶ “I went out after them,” she said, “and I left the key under the mat for my sister. I told the table I would.” ¶ “And when did the watch go?” ¶ “And I know when,” she said. “The man below heard the door go just after the ten o’clock el went by; he sets his watch by it.” ¶ “Who’d want it?” ¶ “I keep thinking about Russo,” she said. “He took the watch out from under its dome and weighed it in his hand at the card party, and I didn’t think anything of it at the time. And he says my IOU to him is overdue, and that the watch would square it.” ¶ She looked at the window, then back at me. “Miss Nowak, the switchboard operator, owes Fishel money, and he wants it by Saturday. And Miss Lowenthal, the piano teacher, has always wanted the watch, and asked me the price.” ¶ Dr. Hirsch counted out ten dollars in ones and change, and the change was the part that got to me. “Who, and where. That’s all I’m asking.” ¶ I took the money, and the night along with it.

I went over Dr. Hirsch’s parlor from the door to the far wall, slowly. ¶ Dr. Hirsch stood in the hall with her hands in her pockets, so as not to touch anything, which was more than whoever came before me had managed. ¶ The glass dome on the mantel was empty. The key was back under the mat, and the door hadn’t a mark on it. Whoever it was had let themselves in and put the key back after, which is manners of a kind. ¶ So whoever it was knew the way in, and the people who knew were the ones at the card party in the Hirsch flat at eight. Dr. Hirsch had given me their names. ¶ I put everything back where it had been, as near as I could.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Russo. There were sunflower-seed shells in the gallery aisles, swept up every night and back by the second act. He had a pinstripe suit pressed to a knife edge, and one gold tooth that shows when he wins. ¶ I asked him for his evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. Russo answered without looking at me, which is a way of answering. ¶ “Sure. Cut the deck. I’ll deal you the evening. I was at Dr. Hirsch’s at eight, for the card party, with Miss Lowenthal. Around nine I left the card party when the gin ran out and went to Steinmetz’s for the blue-plate supper, with Amato. Nine, I watch. I always watch at nine. It’s when people get brave. At ten I had a ticket for the Lyric, by myself.” ¶ So the Hirsch flat at eight, with Miss Lowenthal, which was what Dr. Hirsch had said. So far as it went, it stood up. For ten, the hour that mattered, he said the Lyric. I took it down the way it was given. ¶ Pinsky had been there all evening with nothing to do but notice. ¶ There was the daughter’s death scene in the third act, eleven minutes long, which the usher mouths along with from the back of the house, every word.

From there to Steinmetz’s was a fair few blocks. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The front of Steinmetz’s was dark, but the kitchen door at the back stood propped open on the alley, letting out steam and the sound of a pot being scrubbed by somebody with opinions about it. The chop house window still said CHOPS STEAKS OYSTERS in gold, with the R gone from OYSTERS. There was an umbrella stand made from an elephant’s foot, which the owner swears is a cow’s. ¶ Demos was writing covers in the book at his stand. He had hair parted dead center and flattened with something that smells of violets. Miss Lowenthal was at a corner table with a plate of toast, eating it slowly, a corner at a time, like somebody paying by the bite. Amato sat at a table near the kitchen door with a newspaper folded to the crossword and a cup of coffee going cold. ¶ Russo had said he was here at nine. Pinsky’s list had Miss Lowenthal at the Lyric at nine, and that was worth the walk. From his post Demos could see the whole dining room, from his stand by the door. “I seat every table myself, and I write the covers in the book with the time beside them. Nobody sits in my room without my say-so.” ¶ I looked the place over the way you read a bill: twice, and slowly.

I spread the form on the tablecloth, next to the sugar. A name wants a line under it, and a line wants somebody’s word under that. I went down the form one line at a time. ¶ The fee on my blotter would have company soon. The lamp could make the introductions.

The Belkin flat lay a few blocks east. The fog had swallowed the far end of the street and was in no hurry to give it back. ¶ The Excelsior was a block of private flats on East Houston Street, six floors with its name over the door in gold script, and a lobby with a mirror, a potted palm and nobody at the desk, because there isn’t a desk. Everybody who lives there has a key to the front door. After midnight the lobby light was on, because it’s nobody’s job to turn it off. There were marble stairs to the second floor and plain wood after that, where the builder ran out of marble or interest. ¶ “That’s where the brooch lives,” Belkin said, and then, more quietly, “lived.” ¶ Anybody could have come and gone, and nobody would have known it. ¶ If it went at ten, the flat had been empty, and anybody who’d heard Belkin at the Peacock had known the way in. That was a room, more or less. It was a big room. ¶ The place had the stillness of somewhere something has happened, and it wasn’t saying what.

It was a fair few blocks to the Peacock, uptown and west. I made a note of it: tonight was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The Peacock was a cellar club under Kornblum & Sons, Funeral Directors, on Chrystie Street. You went down an outside stair beside the undertaker’s window, past a coffin on display with its lid up and the price folded discreetly on the pillow, to a steel door with a slot in it. After midnight the band was still going, and you could feel the bass drum through the door before you heard it. There was the cigarette girl’s tray, Luckies and Camels on the top layer and, underneath, a layer nobody buys cigarettes from. ¶ Mrs. Szabo was eating a pickle out of a paper bag on her stool. She had big hands folded in her lap, the knuckles flattened by a career she doesn’t discuss. Miss Moskin was at the bar with her back to the room, watching the room in the mirror. Doyle sat at the back with his coat still on, as if he might leave at any minute and had been thinking so for an hour. Mrs. Krantz had a table near the empty dance floor and was turning a glass slowly round and round by its stem. ¶ From her post Mrs. Szabo could see the street door through the slot, and the stairs down. “Every face comes to my slot first. I don’t like most of them, so the ones I let in, I remember.” ¶ Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

Mrs. Szabo’s list had Miss Moskin here at nine and eleven, so that was where I went next. I took the stool beside her and let her finish her drink before I spoiled it. She had a copy of Variety rolled in her coat pocket, folded open at the uptown casting news. ¶ I asked Miss Moskin to walk me through her night, every stop of it. She had the answer ready, which is either honesty or rehearsal. ¶ “Oh, my evening. Let me do it properly. You have to set the scene, or it doesn’t play. I was home at the flats over Lipsky’s at eight, with Doyle. Come nine, I went to the Peacock, where the band was new, with Doyle. Around ten I went home to listen to the radio, on my own. At eleven I went to the Peacock to see who was about, with Doyle and Mrs. Krantz. Eleven, I’m tired, and I won’t admit it, because tired is for the chorus.” ¶ So here at eleven, with Doyle and Mrs. Krantz, and here at nine, which was what Mrs. Szabo had. That much of it stood up, and it stood up where I could check it. ¶ Dr. Hirsch could tell me her own evening, and she was at the card room over Feingold’s garage. ¶ There was a stuffed peacock by the bar, molting, with one glass eye; the other was lost in a bet in 1924, and nobody will say who won it.

There were ashtrays that are never emptied, only added to, so that there are eleven of them now. ¶ “Mrs. Szabo has you at the Peacock at eight. I’m asking everybody the same. Where else were you tonight?” Dr. Hirsch took a moment to put the evening in order before she handed it over. ¶ “I keep good records. You’ll find my evening as precise as a filling, and about as much fun. I was at the Peacock at eight. Then at nine I took a letter round to the flats over Lipsky’s. Nine, I have the cigarette. One. I make it last like a good filling. Come ten, I had a table at the Peacock. Around eleven I went up to the card room over Feingold’s garage to watch the game and not play. All of it on my own.” ¶ Dr. Hirsch said the Peacock at ten. The doorkeeper had Doyle, Mrs. Krantz and Miss Marsh at the Peacock at ten o’clock, and nobody else. They couldn’t both be true, and Mrs. Szabo had no reason to be the wrong one. ¶ The el shakes the table every time it passes, and every man who ever lost a hand up here has blamed it on the el. ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. It went at ten o’clock. Miss Moskin, Doyle and Dr. Hirsch were at the Peacock while Belkin told the room; Mrs. Krantz wasn’t. Miss Moskin said home at ten, and nobody else had said so yet. Doyle was at the Peacock at ten; Mrs. Szabo said so. Mrs. Krantz was at the Peacock at ten; Mrs. Szabo said so. Dr. Hirsch had told me the Peacock at ten, and Mrs. Szabo’s list said otherwise. And whatever it was had gone to Marsh, the cigarette girl at the Peacock at eleven. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the janitor at the flats over Lipsky’s who’d been in. ¶ It was the middle of the night and the middle of the job, and neither one felt like an end.

Dr. Hirsch had named Miss Nowak: the card room over Feingold’s garage at ten, the two of them. An owned-up story needs somebody to stand behind it. I got as near to her as manners allowed and said my name. She was pale under a cloche hat, with a red mark across the top of her head from the headset that her hair doesn’t quite hide. ¶ I asked her where she’d spent the night, plainly, the way you’d ask anybody. ¶ Miss Nowak smoothed the front of her coat, as if the evening were on it, and began. ¶ “I don’t mind telling you. I’m very good at times; it’s my whole job. I was home from eight through nine. Come ten, I went to the card room over Feingold’s garage to meet Dr. Hirsch. Around eleven I turned in early, home. Nobody was with me at eight, nine or eleven.” ¶ That put Dr. Hirsch here at ten, on her word. ¶ The one to ask was the janitor at the flats over Lipsky’s, who’d been there all night. ¶ I wrote it all down. My handwriting at that hour looks like a spider fell in the ink, but I can read it, mostly.

Wojcik was shoveling coal into the boiler. ¶ I asked him to give me the night the way only the janitor could: every face, every hour. He seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Eight, I sit. Pipe. Steps. Street. Eight o’clock, Miss Moskin and Doyle. Nobody else. Nine, Dr. Hirsch. Nobody else at all. Ten and eleven, nobody.” ¶ Miss Moskin said home at ten. The janitor had nobody here at ten o’clock. One of them was wrong. Wojcik had Dr. Hirsch here at nine, same as she said. ¶ Answering the fourth floor by banging a pipe with a wrench: that was the last I saw of him.

Midnight. My office was two rooms at the top of a walk-up on Mulberry Street, and the second room was mostly for show. I had money in the desk drawer for once. I’d opened the drawer twice to make sure, and once more just to visit. ¶ The street door went downstairs, and somebody started up, taking the stairs slowly, like somebody not sure they were the right stairs. My visitor came in talking about the stairs, how many and how dark, and was still counting them sitting down. I’d never dared. ¶ “Lazar Belkin,” he said, and put his hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Francis Doyle’s neighbor. He’s dead, and I don’t like how.” ¶ The dead man had been the alderman’s clerk. He was found in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street at half past eleven. The one who found him was Dr. Hirsch, who’d come to settle a bet. The police wrote it down as his heart. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ “Here’s what they don’t want to hear,” he said. “The coroner says rat poison in a drink, taken at nine or ten o’clock; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “He’d been at Steinmetz’s earlier in the evening,” my client said. “His usual.” ¶ “Who’d want him dead?” ¶ “If you want a name, it’s Amato,” Belkin said. “He and Doyle had been at each other’s throats for years.” ¶ He opened his bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.

I went over Doyle’s table slowly, touching nothing I didn’t have to. ¶ I worked slowly. Belkin waited in the hall, and the stairs creaked every time he shifted his weight. ¶ A cup of cocoa gone cold, bitter at the bottom. Beside it a tin with a skull on the label, from the cellar shelf at the flats over Lipsky’s. Somebody made him cocoa. ¶ So the rat poison came from the flats over Lipsky’s, and rat poison takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Doyle had been at the flats over Lipsky’s earlier, to get it. ¶ I hadn’t been through the papers at Doyle’s place yet, and a dead man’s papers can be talkative. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

The flats over Lipsky’s were a few blocks uptown, near enough for anybody to walk it there and back inside the hour. I made a note of that. Steam came up out of the street gratings, the only warm thing on the block, and a row of pigeons was sitting on one with their eyes shut. ¶ Every radiator in the flats over Lipsky’s had gone cold, and somebody on the fourth floor was banging one with a shoe, a message the janitor could read from the cellar and was choosing not to. Frost had made ferns on the shop window, over a bolt of blue serge marked down twice. There was the coal bin in the cellar, padlocked, with a chalk tally on the wall of whose scuttle got what, and two of the tallies rubbed out by a thumb. ¶ Wojcik was answering the fourth floor by banging a pipe with a wrench. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. Amato was eating a sandwich on the running board. ¶ The rat poison had come from here. Belkin had pointed me at Amato, and that was worth the walk. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe from supper till bed, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ My feet were glad to stop, and said so.

Wojcik’s list had Amato here at eight and nine. That was reason enough to ask. He was sleeping in his cab with his cap over his face. He had a St. Christopher medal on a chain round his neck and another on the dashboard of his cab, in case one of them is off duty. ¶ I asked him for his evening, in order, the way you’d ask for a receipt. He told it the way you give somebody directions, landmark by landmark. ¶ “Where to? Ha. Sorry. Habit. Go ahead, ask. I was at Steinmetz’s at seven, with Mrs. Krantz. Then at eight I went home to listen to the radio, and stayed the rest of the evening. Dr. Hirsch was there at eight and nine; at ten it was just me. Nine’s dead. Nine’s always dead. You could roll a bowling ball down Delancey at nine.” ¶ Amato said home at ten. Wojcik had nobody here at ten o’clock. One of them was wrong. ¶ Arguing with a horse cab about the right of way: that was the last I saw of him. ¶ I stopped and took stock. Something had come loose, and I wanted to see what it was fastened to. ¶ Here’s what I had. It happened at nine or ten o’clock, and I didn’t know which yet. The rat poison came from the flats over Lipsky’s, so whoever used it had been there first. Mabry, Amato and Dr. Hirsch had been at the flats over Lipsky’s earlier, when the rat poison was there for the taking; Mrs. Krantz hadn’t. Amato had told me home at ten, and Wojcik’s list said otherwise. Dr. Hirsch was at the flats over Lipsky’s at nine; Wojcik said so. Mabry and Mrs. Krantz hadn’t told me where they were at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to find out from the head waiter at Steinmetz’s who’d been in. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

Demos was folding napkins into shapes nobody asked for. ¶ I asked him who’d been here tonight, and said I’d take it untidy, the way it happened. He didn’t look at the room to answer. He didn’t need to. ¶ “Seven, sir: the early covers. People who dine at seven are not interesting, but they tip. Seven o’clock, Mrs. Krantz and Amato. Nobody else. Eight, Mabry, Mrs. Krantz and Doyle. Nobody else at all. Nine, Mrs. Krantz and Doyle. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Mrs. Krantz and Dr. Hirsch. No one else, sir. Not in my room. Not without my say-so.” ¶ Demos had Amato here at seven, same as he said. That put Mrs. Krantz and Dr. Hirsch here at ten, by his count. Belkin had said nine or ten. Doyle was at Steinmetz’s at nine, alive. ¶ That made Mabry the next question, and he was close enough to ask. ¶ Seating a man who would rather have stood: that was the last I saw of him.

A couple of blocks uptown and west, and I was at the back booth at Sokol’s. My knees had the temperature a block before any thermometer did. They’ve had more practice. ¶ I found the back booth behind the flour sacks at Sokol’s. It was the kind of place people go to so they can say they were somewhere else. There was the door from the bakery to the bar, with FLOUR painted on it, which has fooled nobody for years. ¶ Fishel was behind the counter, writing in a ledger by the light of a green-shaded lamp. He had a pearl-gray fedora he never takes off indoors, because, he says, it’s worth more than the indoors. ¶ Fishel had the room from the hour that mattered, and not before. Before that, he said, it was anybody’s. ¶ It was the sort of room people say they were never in. I made a note that I was.

Midnight, and the office on Mulberry Street was as quiet as an office gets when nobody is paying for it to be loud. My head kept its own time, behind the clock over the safe and louder. I put the lamp low and thanked it. ¶ Somebody came up the stairs. Nobody comes up those stairs after midnight with good news; the good news waits for morning, like a gentleman. My visitor came in with an apology for the hour and a second one for the first, and was well into a third before sitting down. ¶ “Oscar Lieb,” he said, and put his hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Francis Doyle’s neighbor. He’s dead, and I don’t like how.” ¶ The dead man had been the alderman’s clerk. He was found in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street at half past eleven. The one who found him was Mrs. Greco, who’d come to return a borrowed book. The police wrote it down as his heart. ¶ “When was this?” ¶ “The police can call it what they like,” he said. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening he was at the Lyric,” my client said. “His usual. He was a man of habits, and that was one of them.” ¶ “Who had a reason?” ¶ “Ask about Amato,” he said. “He and Doyle had been at each other’s throats for years. I had that from the woman downstairs.” ¶ “Fifty dollars,” Lieb said, and put it on the desk. “Find out who did this to him, and tell me before you tell anybody else.” ¶ I took the money. The case came with it, the way a cold comes with a wet night.

I went over Doyle’s table slowly, touching nothing I didn’t have to. ¶ Lieb watched from the landing with his coat buttoned to the neck, as if the cold were in the room. ¶ A cup of cocoa gone cold, bitter at the bottom. Beside it a tin with a skull on the label, from the cellar shelf at the flats over Lipsky’s. Somebody made him cocoa. ¶ So the rat poison came from the flats over Lipsky’s, and rat poison takes twenty minutes to an hour to do its work. Whoever brought it to Doyle had been at the flats over Lipsky’s earlier, to get it. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

It was a few blocks to the Lyric, uptown and west. A trolley went by, with the same people asleep on it for all I knew, going round again for the company. ¶ Only the lobby of the playhouse was lit, where the cleaners had started on the brass and stopped for a glass of tea. The poster by the doors still said THE RABBI’S DAUGHTER, ELEVENTH TRIUMPHANT WEEK, and under it somebody had written, in pencil, and twelfth. There were sunflower-seed shells in the gallery aisles, swept up every night and back by the second act. ¶ Pinsky was marking crosses on his seating chart. He had his seating chart under one arm on a clipboard, the way other men carry a newspaper. Miss Nowak stood at the back with her hat in her hand, as if she had just come in or was just going. Mrs. Greco was in the lobby, reading the bills for next week as if they might change. ¶ From his post Pinsky could see the whole house, from the back of the center aisle. “I seat by the chart. Every seat sold is a cross, every cross has a face, and I could draw you the face.” ¶ I stood still and listened. Places tell you things if you let them finish.

Mrs. Greco had said she was here at seven, eight and ten, and Pinsky had been here all night to see who came and went. ¶ He was sweeping sunflower shells out of the gallery. “Who was in tonight?” I said. “You’d know. Knowing is most of your job.” ¶ He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Seven, I open the doors and take up the chart. Every seat sold, a cross. I’m very good at crosses. Seven o’clock, Mrs. Greco and Doyle. Nobody else. Eight, Amato, Mrs. Greco and Doyle. Nobody else at all. Nine, Doyle. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Miss Nowak and Mrs. Greco. And nobody else. Every cross on the chart has a face, and I’ve given you every face.” ¶ Mrs. Greco hadn’t been at the flats over Lipsky’s while it was there to take. Pinsky had her here at seven, same as she said. That put Miss Nowak here at ten, by his count. Lieb had said nine or ten. Doyle was at the Lyric at nine, alive. ¶ Mouthing the third act from the back of the house: that was the last I saw of him.

The janitor knocks his pipe out on the stoop rail so often the rail has a dent in it the shape of the bowl. “You’ve been here all night,” I said. “Who came in, and when?” ¶ Wojcik counted it off on his fingers, and ran out of fingers before he ran out of night. ¶ “Seven, I bank the boiler for the night. She sulks. Then she settles. Seven o’clock, Amato and Miss Nowak. Nobody else. Eight, Miss Nowak and Mrs. Krantz. Nobody else at all. Nine, Miss Nowak and Mrs. Greco. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, nobody. The rat poison on the cellar shelf was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Amato, Miss Nowak and Mrs. Krantz had been here earlier, when the rat poison was there for the taking. Wojcik had Mrs. Greco here at nine, same as she said. I wrote down what the list had at ten, the hour that mattered: nobody. ¶ Sitting on the cellar steps with his pipe: that was the last I saw of him.

Mrs. Krantz was counting bills with a rubber thumb. ¶ “Wojcik has you at the flats over Lipsky’s at eight. Now tell me the rest of it, from the beginning.” ¶ She went slowly, the way people do who like to get things right. ¶ “My evening is in order. Everything I do is in order. You may have it in order. I was home at seven. Eight o’clock I dropped a parcel off at the flats over Lipsky’s, with Miss Nowak. Eight, I do the arithmetic. It is never in my favor and never wrong. Then at nine I went back to my room to write letters, and stayed the rest of the evening. Nobody was with me at seven, nine or ten.” ¶ Mrs. Krantz said home at ten. Mrs. Greco passed her on East Houston Street at ten. They couldn’t both be true, and I knew which one I’d bet on. The rest held where I could check it: Wojcik had her at the flats over Lipsky’s at eight, with Miss Nowak, same as she said. ¶ Looking at a banister as if it owed her money: that was the last I saw of her. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. Lieb had said nine or ten, and Doyle was at the Lyric at nine, alive. The rat poison came from the flats over Lipsky’s, so whoever used it had been there first. Amato, Miss Nowak and Mrs. Krantz had been at the flats over Lipsky’s earlier, when the rat poison was there for the taking; Mrs. Greco hadn’t. Miss Nowak was at the flats over Lipsky’s at nine and the Lyric at ten; Wojcik and Pinsky said so. Mrs. Greco was at the flats over Lipsky’s at nine and the Lyric at ten; Wojcik and Pinsky said so. Mrs. Krantz had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Greco’s story said otherwise. Amato hadn’t told me where he was at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to get over to the back booth at Sokol’s. ¶ That was everything I had, and it wasn’t enough yet.

I took out my pencil, which makes some people nervous and makes the rest feel important. “Wojcik has you at the flats over Lipsky’s at seven. Where were you the rest of the evening? All of it, in order.” ¶ He didn’t seem to mind being asked, which is how most people seem. ¶ “My night? I’ll give it to you like a fare: the long way, and you don’t argue with the meter. I was home at the flats over Lipsky’s at seven, with Miss Nowak. Come eight, I went to the Lyric to see the new play, with Mrs. Greco and Doyle. Eight, I eat. Most men eat sitting at a table. I’m not most men. Around nine I went round to the back booth at Sokol’s to see a man about a horse. At ten I went home. At nine and ten I was on my own.” ¶ Amato said home at ten. Wojcik had nobody at the flats over Lipsky’s at ten o’clock. Two stories about him at the same hour, and only one of them could stand. ¶ Flour gets on everybody who goes through to the bar, and the whole block could find Sokol’s by the white footprints, the police included.

Amato had named Dr. Hirsch: the back booth at Sokol’s at ten, the two of them, so I went to see if it held. ¶ I found her at the far end, where the light gave up, and stood where she could see me without having to want to. She had very clean hands with very short nails, and a gold wedding band she wears on a chain round her neck instead of on the hand. ¶ I asked her to tell me her evening, and who she’d seen. ¶ Dr. Hirsch counted back through the evening under her breath before saying any of it out loud. ¶ “I keep good records. You’ll find my evening as precise as a filling, and about as much fun. I was home from seven through nine, by myself. Ten o’clock I went to the back booth at Sokol’s to meet Amato. Eight, I start to want a cigarette, and I make myself wait till nine. Discipline.” ¶ That put Amato here at ten, and she would swear to it. ¶ I wrote it down and thanked her. She didn’t look as if thanks were what she’d been expecting.

Midnight. My office on Mulberry Street had my name on the door, a bottle in the drawer and the landlady’s bill under the bottle, where I could keep an eye on it. I favored the side that still ached and lowered myself into the chair in three stages, like a drawbridge. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. My visitor came in with an apology for the hour and a second one for the first, and was well into a third before sitting down. ¶ “My name is Assunta Greco,” she said. “I’m Francis Doyle’s neighbor. He’s dead.” ¶ The dead man had been the alderman’s clerk. He was found in his own flat in the Excelsior on East Houston Street at half past eleven. The one who found him was Mabry, who’d come to return a borrowed book. The police wrote it down as his heart. ¶ “When?” ¶ Mrs. Greco said it slowly, so that I’d get it right. “His mantel clock was knocked over and stopped at five past, but it was never right: nine or ten o’clock, I’d say.” ¶ “He was at the Lyric earlier in the evening,” she said. “His usual. He liked his usual.” ¶ “Anybody who’d be glad he’s gone?” ¶ “There’s a letter from Mrs. Krantz in his desk,” Mrs. Greco said. “It was on top, and I didn’t look any further. She and Doyle were sweethearts once, and it ended badly.” ¶ She opened her bag and counted out fifty dollars, slowly, so I’d know what it cost. “Find out who.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him, and I went through them one at a time. His papers were in a box under the bed, the kind of box a man keeps for the things he’d rather not file. ¶ He had a page on everybody who held something against him, typed and clipped together, and every page said what the grudge was. He’d kept them square, so that nobody got top billing. ¶ Amato: a complaint he’d made against him, in triplicate. Mabry: an IOU from his friend, with his name pencilled beside it. Mrs. Krantz: a bundle of her letters, tied with string and never given back. Teitel: an IOU in his hand, and a note of what was still owing. Miss Nowak: a note about her and the Peacock, in the dead man’s hand, with a date. ¶ I put Doyle’s pages back in their box. A grudge on paper is a long way from the chloral. ¶ There was a potted palm in the lobby, long dead, which one of the tenants still waters on his way out, out of courtesy.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Mrs. Krantz. ¶ She was counting bills with a rubber thumb. “Tell me where you were tonight,” I said. “Every hour, and anybody who can say so.” ¶ She went slowly, the way people do who like to get things right. ¶ “My evening is in order. Everything I do is in order. You may have it in order. I was home at seven. At eight I dropped a parcel off at Rafferty’s, with Miss Nowak and Amato. Nine o’clock I went home to iron a shirt for the morning. Then at ten I went to the Lyric, because a friend was in the show. Ten, I think about the first of the month. I always think about the first of the month. At seven, nine and ten I was on my own.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Mrs. Krantz said home at nine and the Lyric at ten. Whether anything else I held touched it, I’d have to see. ¶ Writing in a rent book with a fountain pen: that was the last I saw of her.

Pinsky was pointing his flashlight at a man who was talking. I asked him to give me the night the way only the usher could: every face, every hour. ¶ He looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶ “Seven, I open the doors and take up the chart. Every seat sold, a cross. I’m very good at crosses. Seven o’clock, Teitel, Amato and Doyle. Nobody else. Eight, Teitel, Mabry and Doyle. Nobody else at all. Nine, Teitel and Doyle. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, somebody in a fur collar, back to the room, I couldn’t swear who. And nobody else. Every cross on the chart has a face, and I’ve given you every face.” ¶ At nine and ten, when it counted, Pinsky had Teitel and Doyle at nine and somebody in a fur collar at ten. ¶ Mouthing the third act from the back of the house: that was the last I saw of him. ¶ I found a doorway and stood in it, and let the whole night go past me again, in order. ¶ Here’s what I had. Mrs. Greco had said nine or ten o’clock. The chloral had come from Rafferty’s. I had an evening from Mrs. Krantz, and a list from Pinsky. I didn’t have Miss Nowak’s, Teitel’s, Mabry’s or Amato’s evenings yet. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

I went round the corner to Rafferty’s. A cab sat at the curb with its engine running and its driver asleep, waiting for somebody who wasn’t coming out in this. ¶ The skylight over Rafferty’s stairwell was letting the rain into a bucket on the top landing, with a newspaper under the bucket and a second newspaper under the first. The rest of the rooming house was dry and accounted for, including the umbrellas in the hall, each on its own hook with a lodger’s name inked above it. There was a pot of tea stewing on the back of the stove at all hours, offered to everybody, and always too strong to refuse politely. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty was pouring tea nobody asked for. She had a ring of keys at her belt the size of a saucer, and she knows each key by the sound it makes. Teitel, in a camel coat, was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into his collar. Mabry, in a grey fedora, was writing a tune on the back of a menu. Amato, in a sailor’s pea coat, was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ Miss Nowak had said she was here at seven, eight and nine. Pinsky’s list had Teitel at the Lyric at seven, eight and nine. It was reason enough to look. From her post Mrs. Rafferty could see the front door, the stairs and every landing to the top. ¶ I wiped my feet, because somebody in that house would notice if I didn’t.

Mabry had said he was here at seven and ten, and Mrs. Rafferty had been here to see who came and went. She was darning a lodger’s sock on the first landing. ¶ I asked her who she’d seen come and go since the evening started. She seemed pleased somebody had asked. Nobody ever asks the one who sees everybody. ¶ “Seven, I take my chair and the mending, and the house knows I’m on. Seven o’clock, Miss Nowak and Mabry. Nobody else. Eight, Miss Nowak, Mrs. Krantz and Amato. Nobody else at all. Nine, Miss Nowak and Amato. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, Teitel and Amato. Nobody else. Nobody gets past the basket. The chloral on my hall shelf was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ The hour that mattered was ten. Mrs. Rafferty had Teitel and Amato. ¶ Writing in the rent book in pencil and going over it in ink: that was the last I saw of her.

Fishel saw me coming before I’d decided to come. That’s the job. ¶ “Who was in tonight?” I said. “You’d know. Knowing is most of your job.” He answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Ten, the big money comes, if it comes. It comes in small bills, and nervous. Ten o’clock, Mabry and two men I didn’t know. I wasn’t minding the room before ten. Before that I couldn’t tell you.” ¶ For ten, the hour that mattered, Fishel had Mabry and two men nobody could put a name to. ¶ Flour gets on everybody who goes through to the bar, and the whole block could find Sokol’s by the white footprints, the police included.

Midnight. The office was where I’d left it, at the top of four flights on Mulberry Street, which is the only thing about it you could count on. Rent was three weeks gone. The envelope wasn’t going to pay itself by sitting on the desk. I lit a cigarette off the lamp and let the smoke do the worrying. ¶ There was a knock, and then the door opened before I’d said anything, which is how people knock when they’ve made up their minds. My visitor came in unhurried, as if the hour happened to other people. ¶ “Chandler Ainsworth,” he said, and put his hat on my desk like a deposit. “I was Otto Wehrle’s cousin. He’s dead, and I don’t like how.” ¶ Wehrle was a landlord. He was found in his own walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street at half past eleven by Brauer, who heard his radio still going and knocked. The police put it down as his heart. ¶ I pointed my client at the chair. He took it, and held his hat on his knees. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ He had it all by heart, which is how you know somebody has been lying awake. “The woman across the hall heard him laughing with somebody all through the Eveready Hour, which runs from nine o’clock. The coroner says laudanum, taken then; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “Who had a reason?” ¶ “I found a letter from Coffin in his desk,” my client said. “He had been squeezing her for years. Start there.” ¶ “Fifty dollars,” Ainsworth said, and put it on the desk. “Find out who did this to him, and tell me before you tell anybody else.” ¶ I took the money. The case came with it, the way a cold comes with a wet night.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Brauer. She sat me down at the kitchen table, under a light that was hard on both of us. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, she wore clothes too good to have been bought. She’d made every stitch. ¶ I asked her where she’d been tonight, and who with, hour by hour. She thought for a second, the way anybody does, and started at the beginning. ¶ “I was home at the Delmonico rooms all evening. Coffin, Sirkin and Hanrahan were there at eight; Hanrahan was there at nine and ten.” ¶ For nine, the hour that mattered, Brauer said home, here at the Delmonico rooms. Whether anything else I held touched it, I’d have to see. ¶ It turned out Hanrahan was in the front room, in the good chair. ¶ I still hadn’t looked properly at the table at Wehrle’s place. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, uptown to Wehrle’s place, a couple of blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ Wehrle’s walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street was one room at the top of the stairs. The police had been and gone, and the room had the look rooms get when a lot of people have stood in them and nobody sat down. A coal merchant’s calendar hung by the stove, still turned to last month. ¶ Wehrle was in the chair by the table, with his head on his arms, like a man asleep over his accounts. ¶ Ainsworth, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ No one was posted to see who came and went. ¶ If it happened at nine, it happened in this room, and whoever did it had walked in here with the laudanum already in hand. ¶ Nobody offered to take my hat. I hadn’t expected anybody to.

The Orpheum lay a couple of blocks uptown and west. It was the hour when the city stops pretending. Even the lit signs looked tired. ¶ The Orpheum, a picture house with continuous shows till midnight, had stopped the pictures for the night. Without one, a picture house is just three hundred red seats staring at a wall, which describes most of my evenings. The lobby carpet was red and gold swirls, worn down to the threads in a path from the door to the seats. ¶ Havemeyer was by the inner doors, sorting a stack of programs into the ones that could be used again and the ones that couldn’t. He had a roll of tickets on a spindle and a coin changer on his belt, and a callus on one thumb from tearing stubs, the only part of the job that showed. Coffin was sitting near the front, very upright, with both hands on the back of the seat in front. Sirkin was in the lobby, reading the bills for next week as if they might change. ¶ Havemeyer sees every face that comes in from the street, if only for the second it takes to look at a ticket. ¶ The air smelled of dust and velvet and other people’s oranges.

Coffin had said she was here at nine and ten. The one to ask was the usher, who’d been here the whole time. I stood beside Havemeyer at the back, where he could see every seat in the place. ¶ “You’ve been here all night,” I said. “Who came in, and when?” He counted it off on his fingers, and ran out of fingers before he ran out of night. ¶ “Eight o’clock, Bellucci. Nobody else. Nine, Coffin and Bellucci. Nobody else at all. Ten, Coffin, Sirkin and Bellucci. Nobody else, that hour.” ¶ Havemeyer had Coffin here at nine, same as she said. ¶ That made Sirkin the next question, and he was close enough to ask. ¶ The thumb with the callus was twitching for a stub. I didn’t have one. I rarely have a ticket for anything.

I headed uptown and west for the Orpheum, a fair few blocks away. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ I went back to the Orpheum, because there’s no such thing as a place you’re finished with. ¶ Havemeyer was in the lobby, counting the evening’s ticket stubs into bundles and putting a rubber band round each one. Coffin sat in an aisle seat about halfway down, with her coat folded on her knees. Sirkin stood at the back with his hat in his hand, as if he had just come in or was just going. Bellucci was in the back row with a bag of peanuts, shelling them one at a time and not eating them. ¶ Havemeyer’s list had Sirkin here at ten, and Bellucci here all evening, and that was worth the walk. ¶ I walked along the worn path in the carpet. I was adding to it.

I took the form out and smoothed it flat on my knee. I didn’t have all of it. The form didn’t care. Forms never do. ¶ The rent envelope on my desk could stop worrying. For once I had something to put in it.

I went round the corner to the Velvet Room. Elizabeth Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ I went down to the Velvet Room, six steps down under a hat shop. Upstairs the hat shop had gone dark, and down here the lamps were low and the talk was lower, the way it gets after midnight when the loud things have all been said. Over the bar hung a mirror gone cloudy at the corners, which is the kindest way to be looked at after midnight. ¶ Reinhardt was polishing a glass that was already clean, which is what bartenders do instead of watching you. He had a pleasant, forgettable face, which in that trade is the whole trick, and eyes that went to the door every time it opened, and came back. Callahan was at the far end of the bar, reading the racing page and making little marks beside the horses. Corrigan was in a booth by the wall, alone with a glass of beer and a newspaper. ¶ Margolis had been here earlier in the evening. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ A bartender who stands behind a bar all night knows who drank at it. ¶ I found a place at the bar and let the room settle around me.

Bellucci had pointed me at Callahan, and I still didn’t know what he thought about any of it. I leaned on the bar next to him and ordered nothing, which got noticed. ¶ I asked Callahan whether there was anything I ought to know where Margolis was concerned. Callahan’s mouth went flat. He didn’t like the question, and didn’t mind my knowing it. ¶ “I owed Margolis the rent on my shop,” he said, “and he was calling it in. He was very polite about it, which was worse.” ¶ That was his reason, in his own words. It was what Bellucci had said in the office, near enough. A reason is the easy half. For nine, he had told me the Velvet Room at nine. ¶ The mirror behind the bar went on being kind to everybody, me included.

It was a few blocks from there to Feld’s studio, downtown and east, with my collar up. A policeman on his round tried a shop door, found it locked, and looked almost disappointed. ¶ Feld’s photographic studio on Canal Street was shut for the night. The studio had a painted garden on the back wall and a velvet chair in front of it, for people to look their best in. A brass scale with a set of little weights stood at one end of the counter, perfectly balanced. ¶ Dandridge was tidying the shelves behind the counter, turning every label to face the front. ¶ Callahan had said he was here at eight. It was a thread, and I meant to pull it. ¶ From behind his counter Dandridge can see the door and everybody who uses it. ¶ I stood out of the way, which in a place like that is a job in itself.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, uptown to Margolis’s place, a couple of blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. The policeman was trying doors on this street too. We were working the same night from different ends. ¶ Margolis’s flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street was as high up as the building went. The police had been and gone, and left the place with its lamp lit and its door shut, like a shop on a holiday. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Margolis was in his chair, sitting very still, the way nobody living ever sits for long. ¶ Bellucci let me in and then stayed in the hall, the way people do when they don’t want to look at a room. ¶ No one was posted to see who came and went. ¶ If it happened at nine, it happened in this room, and whoever did it had walked in here with the cyanide already in hand. ¶ I took my hat off. It seemed like the thing to do.

I walked uptown and west to the Velvet Room. It was a few blocks, and I took all of it. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Back at the Velvet Room. Nothing had moved but the clock. ¶ Reinhardt stood at the register end of the bar with his arms folded, as if the till might try something. Callahan was on a stool with his hat pushed back, turning a coin over and over on the bar. Corrigan had a stool at the end of the bar and was looking at the mirror behind it, which looked back. Vitale sat at a little table by the wall, with a beer going flat in front of him. ¶ Vitale had said he was here all evening. Dandridge’s list had Corrigan at Feld’s studio at eight. That was reason enough. ¶ Somebody came in behind me. The eyes went to the door and came back, and I was glad to see I’d been promoted to furniture.

Midnight. I was in the office on Mulberry Street with my feet on the desk and the radio turned down low. My head ached from the night before. I’d sent two aspirin after it, and they hadn’t found it yet. The fog outside made the street lamp a smudge, and my eyes were grateful. ¶ Somebody was coming up. At this hour it’s either trouble or a client, and in my experience they climb at the same speed. My visitor talked the whole walk to the chair: her sister, her landlord, and eventually the reason she’d come. ¶ “I’m Esther Hurwitz,” she said, sitting down on the edge of the chair. “I was Edward Callahan’s landlady. He’s dead.” ¶ Callahan had been a bail bondsman. He was found in his own flat on the top floor of 12 Ludlow Street at half past eleven. The one who found him was Quill, who’d come to return a borrowed book. The police wrote it down as his heart. ¶ “Do they know when?” ¶ My client had it all by heart, which is how you know somebody has been lying awake. “The woman across the hall heard him laughing with somebody all through the A&P Gypsies, which runs from ten o’clock. The coroner says laudanum, taken then; it takes twenty minutes to an hour.” ¶ “He’d been at the Shamrock earlier in the evening,” she said. “His usual.” ¶ “Who’d want him dead?” ¶ “Start with Bellucci,” she said. “He threw him out of a lease.” ¶ Hurwitz put fifty dollars on the desk in tens, squared the edges and pushed them across. “I want a name. The right one.” ¶ I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.

Hurwitz had pointed me at Bellucci. A where without a why is half an answer, and I wanted the other half from him. I sat down where he could see me, and didn’t hurry. He had fingertips gone flat from typing all day, and was dressed for an office in a good plain way that no office would ever notice. ¶ I asked Bellucci about Callahan. He answered as if he’d been asked before, by somebody, about something. ¶ “Callahan threw me out of a lease,” he said. “Eight years in that place, and out in a week. You don’t forget a thing like that.” ¶ That was his reason, in his own words. Hurwitz hadn’t mentioned it. A reason is the easy half. ¶ The flat fingertips were typing on nothing, a line at a time. Nobody was dictating.

Bellucci had said Quill was with him here at ten, and I still didn’t know what she thought about any of it. I took the stool beside her and let her finish her drink before I spoiled it. Round and pleasant and dressed a little too well for a cigar store, she kept her eyes on the door, in case it was the police or a winner. ¶ I mentioned Callahan to her and let the quiet do some of the asking. She let out a breath and told me what she thought. ¶ “Callahan jilted my sister a week before the wedding,” she said. “She cried for a month, and I heard every minute of it through the wall.” ¶ That was Quill’s reason, in her own words. Hurwitz hadn’t mentioned it. Plenty of people have a reason. Fewer have the hour to go with it. ¶ The door opened. It was neither. It hardly ever is, which is how bookmakers stay in business.

The Palace was a good walk uptown and west, which is no distance at all if you aren’t the one walking it. The fog had come up off the river and was taking the streetlamps one at a time. ¶ The back row of the Palace, a picture house on Delancey Street, was the darkest place on Delancey Street you could sit for a dime. That’s what the back row is for, and the management has known it for years. An old tin sign for a cough syrup nobody makes any more was nailed to the wall. ¶ Sirkin looked up when I came in, and then looked as if she wished she hadn’t. She had long, cold-looking fingers and a habit of humming under her breath, always the same few bars and never the end of them. ¶ Bellucci had said Sirkin was with him at the Delmonico rooms at nine, and that was worth the walk. ¶ No clerk, no doorman, nobody watching the stairs: nobody saw who came. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

Bellucci had said Sirkin was with him at the Delmonico rooms at nine. Where is only half of it. The other half is why. I found her at the far end, where the light gave up, and stood where she could see me without having to want to. ¶ I said Callahan’s name and watched what her face did with it. She looked at me the way people do when they can see where a question is going. ¶ “Callahan knew where I was in 1921,” she said, “and he liked me to know he knew. That’s all I’ll say about 1921.” ¶ That was Sirkin’s reason, in her own words. Hurwitz hadn’t mentioned it. A reason isn’t an hour, though. For ten, she had told me home at ten. ¶ The tin sign was still promising relief. It had been promising it for years.

I set off uptown and west for the Palace. It was a good walk. I could still smell the chestnut man’s brazier, or thought I could. It was the warmest thing that had happened to me all night. ¶ The Palace again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Sirkin was sitting where she could see the door, with her hat on and her coat buttoned. ¶ The place was out of the night, and so, for a while, was I.

Mrs. Thorndike met me at the foot of the stairs, which is where she met everybody. ¶ “Who was in tonight?” I said. “You’d know. Knowing is most of your job.” She looked at the door, as if the night were written on it, and started. ¶ “Seven and eight, Bellucci and Steinbach. Nobody else. Nine, Bellucci and Sirkin. Nobody else at all. Ten, nobody but me. The laudanum in my medicine cupboard was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Sirkin said home at ten. The landlady had nobody here at ten o’clock. One of them was wrong. Mrs. Thorndike had Bellucci at seven and Steinbach at seven, same as they’d said. ¶ The red lamp under the holy picture was still burning, for whoever needed it most. ¶ I went over it once more, the way you go over a bill you know is wrong. ¶ Here’s what I had. It happened at ten o’clock. Bellucci said the Shamrock at ten, and nobody else had said so yet. Sirkin had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Thorndike’s list said otherwise. Steinbach said the Shamrock at ten, and nobody else had said so yet. Quill hadn’t told me where she was at ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to go over the table. ¶ It was the middle of the night and the middle of the job, and neither one felt like an end.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, downtown to the Delmonico rooms, a fair few blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ The Delmonico rooms again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Mrs. Thorndike sat in the open door of the front room with a basket of mending, where the stair was never out of sight. ¶ The holy picture had its eyes on me, with an expression I couldn’t afford.

Kowalski’s was a fair few blocks uptown and east, and I took it at a good clip. The cold had got into the gutters, and the gutters had given up. ¶ I went to Mrs. Kowalski’s boarding house on Orchard Street. It was a narrow brick house with a scrubbed stoop and a smell of beet soup that had got into the walls and settled. A framed sign in the hall said that baths were on Saturdays and the hot water was by arrangement. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. Petrosino was at the sink with her sleeves rolled up, and dried her hands slowly before she turned round. ¶ Bernstein had pointed me at Petrosino. That settled where I was going. Mrs. Kowalski kept the house, and the house kept no secrets from her, or not for long. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

I waited for a gap in Mrs. Kowalski’s night, and when one came I stepped into it. ¶ I asked Mrs. Kowalski who she’d seen come and go since the evening started. She answered at once. It was all there, the way it always is with somebody whose job is to notice. ¶ “Seven o’clock, Petrosino and Quill. Nobody else. Eight, Callahan and Quill. Nobody else at all. Nine, Quill. Nobody else, that hour. Ten, nobody but me. The carving knife in my kitchen drawer was there at seven. I didn’t look again.” ¶ Petrosino said home at ten. Mrs. Kowalski had nobody here at ten o’clock. One of them was wrong. That put Quill here at nine, by her count. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it. ¶ I stopped where I was and went over it again, slowly, the way you reread a letter from the bank. ¶ Here’s what I had. It happened at nine or ten o’clock, and I didn’t know which yet. Petrosino had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Kowalski’s list said otherwise. Quill was at Kowalski’s at nine; Mrs. Kowalski said so. Callahan and Mosley hadn’t told me where they were at nine or ten, and nobody else had either. ¶ Before I did anything about it, I wanted to go over the floor. ¶ Every story was somebody’s, and not all of them could be true at once.

Petrosino had told me home at ten, and Mrs. Kowalski’s list said otherwise. I wanted to hear what she made of the pair of them. She saw the notebook in my hand and knew what it meant before I opened my mouth. ¶ “Here’s my trouble,” I said. “You told me home at ten. Mrs. Kowalski had nobody at Kowalski’s at ten o’clock.” ¶ She sat very still and let me finish. “I know how it looks,” she said. “I didn’t kill anybody. I’m still not saying.” ¶ Petrosino’s ten o’clock still had Mrs. Kowalski’s list against it, and nothing new beside it. A refusal isn’t a confession. But if she wasn’t home at ten, somebody saw her where she was, and if nobody had, that would say something too. ¶ I hadn’t been over the floor at Ruggiero’s place yet, and it was where the night started. ¶ The sign about the bath had the last word in the hall, the way signs in rooming houses always do.

Kowalski’s was only round the corner, which I wrote down: the whole night was going to be about who could walk where in an hour. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ Kowalski’s looked the same the second time, which in my line of work is never quite true. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. Petrosino was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. ¶ I gave the place a minute to show me what it had.

It was a couple of blocks to Kowalski’s, east. The cold was at its worst, the kind that finds the hole in your glove you didn’t know you had. ¶ Kowalski’s again. The welcome was about what it had been the first time. ¶ Mrs. Kowalski had the parlor door open and the parlor lamp on, so that nothing in the hall could happen without an audience. Petrosino was at the window with the curtain held back an inch, keeping an eye on the street. ¶ The stairs had opinions about my weight and shared them all the way up.

I got down and went over the floor with a flashlight, board by board. ¶ Bernstein watched from the landing with her coat buttoned to the neck, as if the cold were in the room. ¶ A carving knife lay on the floor by the door. The handle had a mark burnt into it, the mark every knife in the kitchen at Kowalski’s has so that nobody walks off with one. Somebody had. Ruggiero had opened the door to somebody and turned his back. ¶ So the knife came from Kowalski’s. Ruggiero died at nine or ten, and whoever used it had been at Kowalski’s before that, to take it. ¶ Ainsworth would have seen everybody who came in. ¶ The calendar by the stove was still on last month. Nobody was going to turn it now.

Ruggiero’s place was round the corner. Anybody could have made it there and back in an hour, and I wrote that down. A coal cart was making its first round, and the man on it had a scarf wound up to his eyes and no intention of talking. ¶ Back at Ruggiero’s place, I had my hands in my pockets and my questions in order. ¶ Bernstein had got there before me and looked up when I came in, the way people look up when they’re paying for your time. ¶ A man’s papers are where he keeps the people who wanted something from him. It was reason enough to look. ¶ It was warmer in than out, which was the best thing I could say for it, and I said it.

Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time. I gave up on bed around eleven and made my peace with the desk chair, which had never once let me sleep. The stairs outside creaked twice, some tenant getting home. ¶ The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make. My visitor set an engraved card on the desk before she said a word. I felt underdressed. ¶ She didn’t wait to be asked. “Rachel Lefkowitz. Abraham Kessler’s business partner. He’s dead, and nobody is doing anything about it.” ¶ Kessler was a landlord. Wehrle, who’d come up for the Thursday card game, found him in his own rooms behind the tailor’s on Allen Street at half past eleven. The police called it a robbery gone wrong and went home. ¶ I offered my client the chair. She looked at it the way you’d look at a dog that might bite, and sat anyway. ¶ “When did he die?” ¶ “I’ll tell you what the police didn’t ask,” she said. “The police surgeon puts it at nine or ten o’clock, by the warmth of him.” ¶ “Earlier in the evening he was at Moskowitz’s,” she said. “His usual. He was a man of habits, and that was one of them.” ¶ “Who’d want him dead badly enough to see to it?” ¶ “Ask about Wehrle,” Lefkowitz said. “He closed her business. I had that from the woman downstairs.” ¶ She put fifty dollars on the desk. “Find out who. The police aren’t going to.” ¶ I took the money. By the end of the week it would belong to my landlady, but for tonight the two of us were getting along fine.

Brauer was in the room, and I hadn’t heard from him yet. That was one thing. How Brauer felt about the whole business was another, and I wanted to hear it. I sat down where he could see me, and didn’t hurry. ¶ I said Kessler’s name and watched what Brauer’s face did with it. He answered as if he’d been asked before, by somebody, about something. ¶ “I owed Kessler four hundred dollars,” he said. “Four hundred. I used to say it in my sleep.” ¶ That was his reason, in his own words. Lefkowitz hadn’t mentioned it. A reason isn’t an hour, though. ¶ One of those folded hands came unfolded, did something small, and went back. I’ve seen banks spend less carefully.

Brauer had said Schilling was with him here at seven, and I still didn’t know what she thought about any of it. I didn’t waste her time. She looked like somebody who kept count of it. ¶ I mentioned Kessler to her and let the quiet do some of the asking. Her mouth went flat. She didn’t like the question, and didn’t mind my knowing it. ¶ “Kessler testified against my brother,” she said. “Stood up in court in a new suit and did it. I remember the suit.” ¶ That was Schilling’s reason, in her own words. Lefkowitz hadn’t mentioned it. A reason is the easy half. ¶ The samovar hissed once as I passed, as if it had an opinion.

From there to Salerno’s flat was a good walk. Behind a window somewhere a radiator was knocking, trying to wake a building that didn’t want waking. ¶ I went round to Salerno’s flat on Pitt Street. It was a walk-up like every walk-up on Pitt Street: a hall that smelled of other people’s suppers and a stair with a bend in it. The wallpaper roses had faded to the color of weak tea, except in the corners the light never reached. ¶ Salerno was in the front room with a book, one finger in it to keep the place. She had fingertips gone flat from typing all day, and was dressed for an office in a good plain way that no office would ever notice. ¶ Wehrle had said Salerno was with her at her place at seven. That was reason enough. ¶ There was nobody on duty, and nobody to ask who had been by. ¶ I took one more look at the wallpaper roses. Faded, but still trying. I could sympathize.

I headed downtown and west for the Delmonico rooms, a few blocks away. The moon was out and doing a thorough job of it, every railing and every step picked out in white. ¶ The Delmonico rooms over the fish market were up a steep stair from Catherine Street, three floors of them. The market below was shut and its stalls hosed down, but the smell of fish hadn’t gone anywhere. A holy picture hung in the hall, with a little lamp in a red glass under it. ¶ Mrs. Abramowitz was in the hall with a dustpan, sweeping a stair that had been swept already. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs. ¶ Salerno had said she was here at seven. That was reason enough for the walk. Nobody comes or goes in a rooming house without the landlady knowing, and Mrs. Abramowitz had the look of a landlady who made a point of it. ¶ I passed the holy picture on the stairs and kept my eyes front. I don’t like being looked at that kindly.

Wehrle had said Salerno was with her at her place at seven, and I still didn’t know how she felt about any of it. I said who I was, and she took it about as well as people do. ¶ “Tell me about Kessler,” I said to her. She looked at me the way people do when they can see where a question is going. ¶ “Kessler jilted my sister a week before the wedding,” she said. “She cried for a month, and I heard every minute of it through the wall.” ¶ That was Salerno’s reason, in her own words. Lefkowitz hadn’t mentioned it. Plenty of people have a reason. Fewer have the hour to go with it. For nine and ten, she had told me home at nine and home at ten. ¶ The faded roses on the wallpaper had had better years. So had I.

It was no distance to Kessler’s place: round the corner, and there it was. The streetlamps went out all at once while I was under one, which felt personal. ¶ I went to Kessler’s rooms behind the tailor’s on Allen Street. The passage from Allen Street smelled of pressed wool and machine oil, and it ended at a door the police had pulled shut on their way out. An empty birdcage hung in the corner, with nothing in it but a little swing. ¶ Kessler lay on the floor where he’d fallen, on his side, with his knees drawn up a little. ¶ Lefkowitz, my client, was already there, keeping one eye on the door and the other on me. ¶ Anybody could have come and gone, and nobody would have known it. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

I walked it at an ordinary pace, downtown and east to the Delmonico rooms, a fair few blocks, and wrote it down. An hour only holds so many walks like that. The first light was coming up over the river, thin and gray, and the streetlamps hadn’t heard about it yet. ¶ The Delmonico rooms again, a little later and a little quieter. ¶ Mrs. Abramowitz sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. ¶ The revolver had come from here, and that was worth the walk. ¶ I wiped my feet, late. It didn’t do much for me, but the stairs appreciated it.

Getting to Rafferty’s meant a couple of blocks uptown. The rain had the street to itself and was making the most of it. ¶ I went up the stoop at Rafferty’s rooming house on Mott Street. It was four floors of narrow rooms and one long stair, with a gas lamp on each landing turned down to a little blue bead. On the landing a rubber plant had grown up to the ceiling and was thinking about going further. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty sat on a kitchen chair at the foot of the stairs, with a rent book in her lap and a shawl round her shoulders. She had a big ring of keys at her waist and reading glasses pushed up into her hair, and looked at my shoes before my face, to see what they’d do to the stairs.
