Carbone, in a camel coat, was finishing a late supper at the kitchen table, with a napkin still tucked into her collar. Stannard, with a cane, was at the sink with her sleeves rolled up, and dried her hands slowly before she turned round. ¶ Corrigan had pointed me at Carbone. That settled where I was going. ¶ Mrs. Rafferty kept the house, and the house kept no secrets from her, or not for long. ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

I hadn’t come for the furniture. I’d come for Carbone. She sat me down at the kitchen table, under a light that was hard on both of us. ¶ I asked her to walk me through her night, every stop of it. She didn’t seem to mind being asked, which is how most people seem. ¶ “I was home at Rafferty’s all evening. Hochstetter and Havemeyer were there at seven; Hochstetter, Dettweiler and Havemeyer were there at eight; Hochstetter and Havemeyer were there at nine; Stannard was there at ten.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Carbone said home, here at Rafferty’s. I took it down the way it was given. ¶ The rubber plant was still growing on the landing. At least something in that house was getting somewhere.

I didn’t waste Havemeyer’s time. He looked like somebody who kept count of it. Thin, and bent at the shoulders from years over a sewing machine, he wore clothes too good to have been bought. He’d made every stitch. ¶ I asked him where he’d been tonight. All of it, in order. He didn’t ask why I wanted it. He just let me know it cost something. ¶ “At seven I went to Rafferty’s for the company, and stayed through nine. Hochstetter and Carbone were there at seven; Hochstetter, Carbone and Dettweiler were there at eight; Hochstetter and Carbone were there at nine. At ten I went round to Dettweiler’s for a game of gin.” ¶ For nine and ten, the hours that mattered, Havemeyer said Rafferty’s at nine and Dettweiler’s flat at ten. I didn’t believe it or disbelieve it. I wrote it down. ¶ I buttoned my coat. It came off a rack, and in that company it knew it.

Havemeyer had said Hochstetter was with him at Rafferty’s at nine. I knew a little of her evening and nothing of her reasons, and I wanted both. I found her at the far end, where the light gave up, and stood where she could see me without having to want to. ¶ I mentioned Lanza to her and let the quiet do some of the asking. She looked at me the way people do when they can see where a question is going. ¶ “Lanza threw me out of a lease,” she said. “I did everything right. It didn’t matter. It never does, with a man like that.” ¶ That was Hochstetter’s reason, in her own words. Corrigan hadn’t mentioned it. A reason isn’t an hour, though. ¶ I could have used gloves like that. Mine have all ten fingertips, and they still let the cold in.

I headed east for Dettweiler’s flat, a good walk away. A newsstand had its shutters down and the morning papers stacked outside in tied bundles, the day’s bad news already in them and waiting to be untied. ¶ I went round to Dettweiler’s flat on Cannon Street. It was a walk-up like every walk-up on Cannon Street: a hall that smelled of other people’s suppers and a stair with a bend in it. A gramophone with a big tin horn stood in the corner, with a record still on it. ¶ Dettweiler, in a fur collar, was still up, with the look of somebody who had been about to go to bed for an hour. Young and tidy and a little tired, she still had the mark of the headset band pressed into her hair. ¶ Hochstetter had said Dettweiler was with her at her place at eight. That was reason enough. Anybody could have come and gone, and nobody would have known it. ¶ The gramophone in the corner kept its record to itself. I wasn’t in the mood for a tune anyway.

Dettweiler’s flat was a good walk east. Cannon Street was running with water, curb to curb. ¶ Back at Dettweiler’s flat, everything was where I’d left it except the time. ¶ Dettweiler, in a fur collar, answered the door in her stocking feet, with the lamp behind her. ¶ Hochstetter had said Dettweiler was with her at her place at eight. That was reason enough for the walk. ¶ My hat had left a mark in my hair too. Nobody was paying me by the hour for mine.

I set off west for Lanza’s place. It was a few blocks. A cat on a step watched me go by and decided I was nobody’s business, which is the most a cat will do for you. ¶ Lanza’s walk-up over the drugstore on Grand Street was one room at the top of the stairs. The police had been and gone, and the room had the look rooms get when a lot of people have stood in them and nobody sat down. A coal merchant’s calendar hung by the stove, still turned to last month. ¶ Lanza lay by the door on his face. Nobody had moved him, and nobody had wanted to. ¶ Corrigan was there, with a cup of something he hadn’t touched and his coat still buttoned. ¶ No clerk, no doorman, nobody watching the stairs: nobody saw who came. ¶ If it happened at nine or ten, it happened in this room, and he’d let whoever did it in. ¶ I took my hat off. It seemed like the thing to do.

I found a chair at Dettweiler’s flat and sat down with the form. Whatever I wrote down, I’d have to be able to say whose word it stood on. ¶ The fee on my blotter would have company soon. The lamp could make the introductions.

It was a few blocks to the flats over Lipsky’s, uptown and east. A trolley went by with three people on it, all of them asleep, and the conductor looking as if he’d like to be. ¶ It was a clear night over Orchard Street, the kind that shows you every washing line strung between the buildings, and the tenement over Lipsky’s had more than its share. A whole family’s shirts hung out over the street on a pulley, white as a surrender, waiting for a sun that wasn’t due till six. The janitor knocks his pipe out on the stoop rail so often the rail has a dent in it the shape of the bowl. ¶ Wojcik was shoveling coal into the boiler. He had coal dust in the creases of his knuckles that no soap on Orchard Street has ever got out. Teitel was haggling with a customer who had already paid. ¶ Teitel had found Russo. That was reason enough. ¶ From his post Wojcik could see the street door and the stoop, from the cellar steps. “I sit on the cellar steps with my pipe from supper till bed, and every pair of shoes that goes up that stoop goes past my nose.” ¶ I stood still a moment and let the place get used to me.

Teitel had found Russo, and I still didn’t know how he felt about any of it. I said who I was, and Teitel took it about as well as people do. ¶ “Tell me about Russo,” I said to him. “What do I know? I sell neckties. A necktie doesn’t ask where a man’s been.” ¶ “Russo knew what I got up to at the card room over Feingold’s garage, and let me know he knew.” ¶ That was his reason, in his own words. Dr. Hirsch hadn’t mentioned it. A reason is the easy half. For nine, he had told me home at nine. ¶ Arranging neckties on his cart by color, then by price, then by color again: that was the last I saw of him.
